```csharp
                    .AddBranch("CalcHandling", new CalcHandlingFeeStep()),
                mergeStrategy: new SumNumericFieldsMerge())
        .Run(out ICompiledPipeline<OrderData> pipeline)
    .Build();

foreach (var total in new[] { 50m, 200m })
{
    var d = (await pipeline.RunAsync(new OrderData("Alice", total))).GetData();
    Console.WriteLine($"{d.Status}: total {d.Total}, tax {d.Tax}, shipping {d.Shipping}, handling {d.Handling}");
}

public sealed record OrderData(string CustomerName, decimal Total, string Status = "New",
    decimal Tax = 0m, decimal Shipping = 0m, decimal Handling = 0m);

public sealed class CalcShippingBranch : PureStep<OrderData>
{
    public override OrderData Execute(OrderData data) => data with { Shipping = 9.99m };
}

public sealed class CalcHandlingFeeStep : IStep<OrderData>
{
    public ValueTask<OrderData> ExecuteAsync(OrderData data, CancellationToken ct = default)
        => ValueTask.FromResult(data with { Handling = 1.5m });
}

public sealed class SumNumericFieldsMerge : IMergeStrategy<OrderData>
{
    public OrderData Merge(OrderData original, IReadOnlyList<OrderData> results)
        => original with
        {
            Tax      = results.Max(r => r.Tax),
            Shipping = results.Max(r => r.Shipping),
            Handling = results.Max(r => r.Handling),
        };
}
```

Output:

```text
Standard: total 50, tax 4.00, shipping 9.99, handling 1.5
VIP: total 160.0, tax 12.800, shipping 9.99, handling 1.5
```

##### Sagas: compensation on failure

A saga chains steps that each declare an undo. If a later step fails, every earlier compensation runs in reverse order. BeginSaga and EndSaga bracket the block, and the compiler refuses a pipeline whose saga is left open.

- BestEffort: The default. Every compensation runs even if one of them throws.
- AbortOnFirst: Stop compensating at the first compensation that fails.
- SwallowErrors: Run every compensation and swallow any exception from them.

```csharp
using EvalApp;

Eval.App("Saga")
    .WithResource(ResourceKind.Database, Tunable.FixedAt(2))
    .DefineDomain("Orders")
        .DefineTask<OrderData>("ProcessOrder")
            .BeginSaga(CompensationPolicy.BestEffort)
                .AddStepWithCompensation(
                    "ReserveInventory",
                    forward:    d => d with { Status = "Reserved" },
                    compensate: d => { Console.WriteLine("compensate: release the inventory"); return d with { Status = "Unreserved" }; })
                .AddGate(
                    ResourceKind.Database,
                    onWaiting: null,
                    configure: g => g.AddStep("WriteLedger", d => d with { Total = d.Total }),
                    compensate: new RevertLedgerStep())
                .AddStep(
                    "ChargePayment",
                    d => d.Total > 1_000_000m
                        ? throw new InvalidOperationException("Payment declined")
                        : d with { Status = "Charged" })
            .EndSaga()
        .Run(out ICompiledPipeline<OrderData> pipeline)
    .Build();

var ok = await pipeline.RunAsync(new OrderData("Ivy", 10m));
var failed = await pipeline.RunAsync(new OrderData("Jin", 2_000_000m));
Console.WriteLine($"ok: {ok.IsSuccess}, status {ok.GetData().Status}");
Console.WriteLine($"failed: {failed.IsFailure}, status after compensation {failed.GetData().Status}");

public sealed record OrderData(string CustomerName, decimal Total, string Status = "New");

public sealed class RevertLedgerStep : IStep<OrderData>
{
    public ValueTask<OrderData> ExecuteAsync(OrderData data, CancellationToken ct = default)
    {
        Console.WriteLine("compensate: revert the ledger entry");
        return ValueTask.FromResult(data with { Status = "LedgerReverted" });
    }
}
```

Output:

```text
compensate: revert the ledger entry
compensate: release the inventory
ok: True, status Charged
failed: True, status after compensation New
```

##### Middleware

IStepMiddleware<T> wraps each named step individually, for timing, retry, audit or per-step tracing. No middleware ships ready-made; it is a seam you implement. To wrap the steps of a ForEach item pipeline, register an IStepMiddleware for the item type on that sub-builder.

An exception thrown by a step comes back as a Failure. An exception thrown by middleware outside the call to next is thrown from RunAsync on a top-level pipeline, and is a Failure only when the pipeline is nested in another. A ForEach whose item pipeline is a single synchronous step normally runs as one fused loop, and attaching middleware turns that fast path off.

##### Dependency injection

AddStep<TStep>(name) and AddBranch<TStep>(name) resolve the step through an IStepFactory. The default creates it with a public parameterless constructor. ServiceProviderStepFactory asks your container first and falls back to that for anything not registered.

The compiler enforces the new() constraint whichever factory you register, so a type needs a literal parameterless constructor even if the container always supplies the real one. The factory path is for plain IStep<T> implementers. A side-effect step that needs a constructor-injected dependency uses AddStep<TStep>(name, factory) instead.

```csharp
using EvalApp;

// Any real IServiceProvider works; this minimal one keeps the sample dependency-free.
var services = new SimpleServiceProvider();
services.Register(typeof(ValidateOrderStep), new ValidateOrderStep("DI-resolved"));

Eval.App("Di")
    .WithStepFactory(new ServiceProviderStepFactory(services))
    .DefineDomain("Orders")
        .DefineTask<OrderData>("ProcessOrder")
            .AddStep<ValidateOrderStep>("Validate")     // resolved from the container, not Activator
        .Run(out ICompiledPipeline<OrderData> pipeline)
    .Build();

var result = await pipeline.RunAsync(new OrderData("Alice", 10m));
Console.WriteLine(result.GetData().Status);

public sealed record OrderData(string CustomerName, decimal Total, string Status = "New");

public sealed class ValidateOrderStep : IStep<OrderData>
{
    private readonly string _tag;
    // AddStep<TStep>() needs a literal parameterless constructor; the tagged one is what the container supplies.
    public ValidateOrderStep() : this("default") { }
    public ValidateOrderStep(string tag) => _tag = tag;
    public ValueTask<OrderData> ExecuteAsync(OrderData data, CancellationToken ct = default)
        => ValueTask.FromResult(data with { Status = _tag });
}

public sealed class SimpleServiceProvider : IServiceProvider
{
    private readonly Dictionary<Type, object> _services = new();
    public void Register(Type type, object instance) => _services[type] = instance;
    public object? GetService(Type serviceType) => _services.TryGetValue(serviceType, out var s) ? s : null;
}
```

Output:

```text
DI-resolved
```

##### Pipelines that run pipelines

A compiled pipeline is a value. A step can run another pipeline or itself, and a context can hold a registry of them, so an outer schedule loop drives an inner per-batch pipeline, or a pipeline recurses through a tree, without a hand-written loop around RunAsync. A loop of that kind is invisible to gates and to the tuner; this is how it becomes visible.

PipelineRef<T> forward-declares a pipeline before it is built, PipelineTrace tells same-named steps apart across levels, and a recursion that runs away fails cleanly with PipelineRecursionException instead of overflowing the stack.

##### Exclusive resources

Some things are not thread-safe: a GPU context, a native handle, a file with one writer. Declare an ExclusiveResource once and guard a scope, or named parallel branches, with Exclusive. A second concurrent entry fails loudly with ExclusiveViolationException, or queues if you choose that policy. The guard is re-entrant for recursion, and forks inside a held scope exclude each other instead of silently inheriting it.

##### One-thread hosts

Fanning out only pays when there is a second thread to fan out to. EvalApp detects a single-thread host once, at startup: a browser running Blazor WebAssembly, a process with one processor or one allowed CPU, or a host you declare with ExecutionHost.OverrideSingleThreaded or WithSingleThread. In that mode ForEach, parallel groups and ChunkedWork run inline on the caller, and long runs hand the thread back to the host every few milliseconds (ExecutionHost.YieldBudget) so a page or UI stays responsive. The cancellation token is checked at each yield.

A single very long synchronous step cannot be sliced. Split it into smaller steps or items. Inside a UI, use ChunkedWork.ForAsync and ChunkedWork.RunAsync, which work in time slices. On a multi-core host none of this is active and nothing is added to the fast path.

##### Licensing

No feature in EvalApp is gated behind a tier or a licence key. Every pipeline shape on this page runs at its full declared concurrency whether or not you pass a key, the tuner attaches whenever you call WithTuning, and Build(null) behaves exactly like Build(key).

The licence check exists so that every Evaluated Applications package validates a key the same way. LicenseValidator.ForEvalApp().Check(key) returns Unlicensed or Licensed and never throws, and CheckPeriodic(key, interval) is cheap enough for a hot loop. Verification is entirely offline, with ECDsa P-256, and makes no network call.

EvalApp is proprietary software under a commercial licence. Evaluation and non-commercial development are licensed without a key; commercial, production or revenue-generating use needs a separate licence.

##### Tuning and inspecting

Two opt-in modes. WithTuning is reactive: it rediscovers the operating point on each start, which suits a long-running, stable, single-instance service. WithBayesianTuning is predictive: a performance model persists across restarts, which suits frequent restarts and many instances. Both take an optional store path and share one phase machine, so switching between them does not reset what was learned.

The defaults come from a simulation harness and are what WithTuning uses out of the box. To override them, load your own JSON file with WithTunerSettings(path); the file is read when you call it, and a missing or invalid path throws at that point.

ICompiledPipeline<T> is opaque on purpose: a name and RunAsync. The read-only window on a plan is pipeline.Report(), which lists the plan's nodes and, for each ForEach, how many calls ran inline and how many fanned out. ExecutionHost.Yields counts the yields a process has taken.

```csharp
using EvalApp;

var store = Path.Combine(Path.GetTempPath(), "evalapp-tuning-sample.json");

Eval.App("Tuned")
    .WithResource(ResourceKind.Network, Tunable.Between(1, 8, 2))
    .WithTuning(storePath: store)
    .DefineDomain("Orders")
        .DefineTask<Batch>("Fetch")
            .ForEach(
                select: b => b.Items,
                merge: (b, items) => b with { Items = items.ToList() },
                collectionName: "Items",
                configure: sub => sub
                    .Gate(ResourceKind.Network, onWaiting: null, configure: g => g
                        .AddStep("Download", async (int i, CancellationToken ct) => { await Task.Delay(5, ct); return i + 1; })))
        .Run(out ICompiledPipeline<Batch> pipeline)
    .Build();

for (var run = 0; run < 5; run++)
    await pipeline.RunAsync(new Batch(Enumerable.Range(0, 16).ToList()));

// A read-only window on the compiled plan: each ForEach node counts its calls (and, in Inline and FanOut, how they ran).
foreach (var node in pipeline.Report().Of("ForEach"))
    Console.WriteLine($"{node.Label}: {node.Calls} calls");

File.Delete(store);

public sealed record Batch(List<int> Items);
```

Output:

```text
Items: 5 calls
```

##### Anti-patterns to avoid

The tuner and the gates can only account for work they can see. Anything that happens outside the declared pipeline is invisible to both.

- Task.WhenAll in a step: Use a declared ForEach instead.
- A background Task kept on the record: It races the pipeline, ungated.
- Async work around RunAsync: Work before or after the call, outside the pipeline, is unthrottled and untuned.
- A shared collection written from a ForEach item: It is not thread-safe. Let each item own its result and collect results in merge.
- Mutating the record: Use with. Mutation breaks the guarantee that makes parallel ForEach safe without locks.
- State in step instance fields: Steps are reused by every concurrent run. Per-run state belongs on the record.
- Rebuilding the pipeline per request: It discards everything the tuner has learned. Build once, run many times.
- Blocking calls in a synchronous step: Use the async overload, and pass the cancellation token to every awaited call.
- A hand-written loop or recursion around RunAsync: The loop is invisible to gates and the tuner. Layer and recurse through context instead.
- Guarding a non-thread-safe singleton with a comment: Use an ExclusiveResource.

##### Extension seams

Beyond the fluent API and the step base classes, four extension points are public: GlobalContext and DomainContext (subclass them for WithContext and DefineDomain), IMergeStrategy<T> (custom conflict handling for AddParallelGroup) and IPressureResource (a soft, non-blocking budget signal for Pressure and WithPressure). Everything else is internal to the engine.

Licence: Commercial licence for commercial use. Evaluation and non-commercial use are permitted. Terms at https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/licence/

### HoloDb: an embeddable SQL database for .NET

A SQL database inside your app that answers dashboard queries in microseconds, with transactions, similarity search and tables bigger than memory.

Page: https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/holodb/
- Package EvaluatedApplications.HoloDb, release 6.0.1: `dotnet add package EvaluatedApplications.HoloDb`
- Package EvaluatedApplications.HoloDb.Client, release 1.5.3: `dotnet add package EvaluatedApplications.HoloDb.Client`
- Package EvaluatedApplications.HoloDb.Protocol, release 1.1.3: `dotnet add package EvaluatedApplications.HoloDb.Protocol`
- Builds on: EvalApp, Phasor
- Used by: Prose, HoloGenome
- Tools: Umbrarium, preset demo, The Analyst, Prose

100,000,000 invoices. Dashboard answers in under a millisecond.

A SQL database inside your .NET app that keeps your totals ready, ranks rows by resemblance, runs in a browser tab and survives a crash. Declare what you ask often, or let it learn. Tables can be bigger than memory.

- 0.12 ms: to add up 100,000,000 invoices (HoloDb restored, warm median). Tuned DuckDB scanning them: 23.17 ms. Tuned SQL Server with an indexed view: 0.65 ms.
- 0.19 to 0.25 ms: for the four joins to 2,000,000 customers (HoloDb restored, warm median). Tuned SQL Server: 0.62 to 0.77 ms. Tuned DuckDB: 102.06 to 603.65 ms.
- 16 of 16: queries where HoloDb restored is ahead of tuned DuckDB, and 16 of 16 where it is ahead of tuned SQL Server. Ahead means more than 20 percent faster in both runs.
- 10 of 16: queries where HoloDb out of the box is ahead of tuned DuckDB. It is behind on 5 and too close to call on 1: scans that no structure covers. Against tuned SQL Server it is ahead on 7 and behind on 9.

HoloDb is an embeddable SQL database for .NET with ACID transactions, similarity search and maintained aggregates. Rows live in typed columns, and everything else is derived from them: a holographic vector built from a row's columns powers similarity search by content, exact integer accumulators answer aggregates without a scan, and exact derived summaries answer filters and group-bys. So the same copy of the data is read three ways. Exact lookup by primary key is ordinary SQL. Similarity search by content is the NEAREST clause. Analytics read a maintained total instead of scanning.

Applications that need relational storage, similarity search and fast dashboard rollups normally reach for three systems, a row store, a vector index and a cube or a pile of scans, and pay to keep them consistent. HoloDb is one embeddable package: a transactional store, an in-SQL similarity search, and aggregates whose response time does not grow with the table.

Why use it:
- No separate vector index. NEAREST ranks rows by resemblance to a partial description, in SQL, over the rows the table already holds. A close number or date, or a near-identical string, ranks ahead of a far or unrelated one, and the score is readable as a column.
- Aggregates do not scan. An integer column's running total is a maintained exact accumulator, so whole-table COUNT, SUM, MIN and MAX and single-column GROUP BY read that value directly, flat as the table grows from a thousand rows to tens of millions. An INT SUM never wraps: it is held in 128 bits, and the statement throws only if the true total leaves 64 bits.
- Real ACID, and past RAM. Write-ahead logging with an fsync on each durable commit, crash recovery bounded by live data and not by write history, reader and writer locking, and paged tables on an 8 KB buffer pool that let a table exceed memory.
- Damage is reported, never read as an answer. The columns are the source of truth, and every hologram, summary and index is derived from them. A paged table checks every data page, so a page that fails its checksum is refused with an error that names the page. In a test that flipped 61 bits in the data file of a 91 MB paged table, none gave a silently different answer: 36 were reported and 25 were in pages never read.

Capabilities:
- A substantial SQL dialect. CREATE TABLE, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, SELECT with DISTINCT, COUNT, SUM, MIN, MAX and AVG, INNER JOIN (several in one statement on in-memory tables, one on a paged table), WHERE with AND, OR, NOT, LIKE, IN, BETWEEN, IS NULL and IN (SELECT ...), GROUP BY and HAVING, ORDER BY, LIMIT, ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN, indexes, EXPLAIN, and explicit BEGIN, COMMIT and ROLLBACK.
- Real SQL NULL. Declare a column NULL and it holds true NULLs with three-valued logic: COUNT(col), SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX skip them, GROUP BY makes one NULL group, ORDER BY puts them first, and a join never matches one. Whole-table aggregates and one-column group-bys stay maintained answers with NULLs present: 0 rows read at 10,000 to 640,000 rows with half the values NULL. On an empty selection SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX are NULL and COUNT is 0, for a NOT NULL column as well.
- Parameterized queries. Every Execute has a ? placeholder overload with positional binding, correctly quoted and escaped, beside the raw SQL string form.
- Content similarity in SQL. NEAREST ranks by graded closeness for numbers, dates and text, with a score column on request. From 8,000 rows an approximate sublinear index ranks candidates, and below that or whenever the query has a WHERE the ranking is an exact scan.
- Constant-time exact aggregates. COUNT, SUM, MIN, MAX and single-column GROUP BY over integer columns are exact, not approximate. Real-number aggregates use a fast SIMD scan.
- Durable and larger than memory. A snapshot plus a short log gives recovery that tracks live data. Paged tables spill cold pages to disk and keep the maintained aggregates accurate there. Every 8 KB data page carries a checksum, UPDATE and DELETE move only the pages that change, and a statement may change more pages than the buffer pool holds: a rollback or a power cut still leaves the table as it was.
- Summaries and indexes that build themselves. With nothing declared, the engine watches which aggregate statements keep scanning and, when the scanning has cost as much as a summary would cost to build, builds it, in memory or on a paged table, and drops it again if the workload moves on. A predicate that matches a small fraction of a large table earns a sorted or an equality index the same way. EXPLAIN says what answered a query and why. SET summaries and SET indexes switch this between auto, declared and off, and the answers are the same either way.
- A table with no rows. CREATE SUMMARY TABLE makes a table that keeps only the exact plane and the position each feed has reached, so memory does not depend on how many rows passed through it. COUNT, SUM, AVG, GROUP BY, HAVING and a WHERE over the dimensions still answer exactly, and a replayed feed never counts twice. Anything that needs a row is refused with the reason.
- Atomic change batches and upsert. ApplyChanges applies a whole batch of upserts and deletes under one write lock, as one write-ahead-log commit group, so a reader sees the table before the batch or after it and never part of it. INSERT with ON CONFLICT (key) DO UPDATE SET is the SQL upsert. Both work on in-memory tables.
- Fast scans. A WHERE is evaluated over raw column arrays in tight loops, GROUP BY over INT and TEXT columns uses dense codes, and an equi-join on TEXT keys is a columnar hash join.
- Metering. A per-query usage meter reports the rows and bytes actually processed, for billing or observability.
- Embedded or networked. Use it in process, or run it as a server with a matching typed client and a columnar wire protocol. The same managed code also runs in a browser tab.
- The optional Pleroma plane and page store. Attach an exact, derived summary to chosen columns to answer filters, group-bys, distinct counts and joins without scanning, or keep exact Pleroma pages durably as the data itself.

Quick start:

```csharp
using HoloDb;

var db = new HoloDbService(new HoloDbOptions());           // in memory
db.Execute("CREATE TABLE users (id INT PRIMARY KEY, age INT, name TEXT)");
db.Execute("INSERT INTO users VALUES (1, 30, 'Ada'), (2, 24, 'Linus'), (3, 15, 'Kid')");

var result = db.Execute("SELECT name FROM users WHERE age >= 18 ORDER BY age DESC");
foreach (var row in result.Rows)
    Console.WriteLine(row["name"]);

var count = await db.ExecuteAsync("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users");
Console.WriteLine(count.Rows[0]["count(*)"]);
```

Output:

```text
Ada
Linus
3
```

Limits:
- Joins: INNER JOIN only. Several in one statement on in-memory tables, one on a paged table. LEFT, RIGHT, FULL, CROSS, NATURAL, USING and comma joins are refused.
- Aliases: No AS on columns or tables. Aggregate columns are named agg(col), such as count(*).
- ALTER TABLE: ADD COLUMN only, with a DEFAULT or NULL. No DROP COLUMN, RENAME COLUMN or RENAME TO.
- Expressions: No CASE, LENGTH(), OFFSET or UNION, and no arithmetic in the select list or inside SUM(v * 2). COUNT(DISTINCT col), LIKE and IN (SELECT ...) work on in-memory tables.
- Money: Constant-time totals are for INT columns. REAL SUM is a SIMD scan, and DECIMAL and NUMERIC are REAL (a double), so hold money as integer cents. There is no fixed-point type.
- Saved summaries: A summary made with CREATE INDEX ... USING SUMMARY, or built by the planner, is saved with the table and restored on open. A plane attached with the EnablePleroma call on an in-memory table is not saved: call it again after Open.
- Summary limits: A declared summary takes up to 4,095 distinct values per column (1,024 for one the planner builds) and a joint of 12 bits. A column over its limit goes to a scan and is never approximated.
- Joins on paged tables: The keyed summary holds up to 4,194,304 consecutive INT keys. The 100,000,000-invoice run joins 2,000,000 customers.
- Languages: A .NET library. The server speaks a TCP and TLS binary protocol whose only client is .NET. No JDBC, ODBC, Python, Node or Go client, and no PostgreSQL or MySQL wire.
- Concurrency: One process per database and one writer at a time. Simple aggregate reads run off a snapshot without the lock. A second process cannot open a paged database's files, and there is no MVCC: a long transaction blocks other writers.
- Table size: Tested to 100,000,000 rows (4.94 GB paged, 165 s to load). In-memory tables are bounded by RAM at about 110 bytes per row. A paged primary key loaded out of order keeps a RAM dictionary of about 35 bytes per row. Beyond 100,000,000 rows is untested.
- Backup: Offline: copy the files of a closed database. There is no online backup and no point-in-time recovery.
- Crash safety: One fsync per commit. Tests cut the log at every record boundary, flip bits in the log and the data file, and tear a page during a checkpoint. A real power cut, a disk that lies about fsync, a full disk and several processes are not tested.

Also:
- Upsert: a plain INSERT of an existing primary key throws. To insert or replace, use INSERT with ON CONFLICT (key) DO UPDATE SET column = EXCLUDED.column, or ApplyChanges with RowChange.Upsert. Both work on in-memory tables only, and a paged table refuses them.
- Keys: a table has one PRIMARY KEY, an INT or TEXT column.
- NULL: a column holds NULL only when it is declared NULL. An index takes NOT NULL columns only, paged tables and summary tables refuse NULL, and the Pleroma plane hands any statement that touches a column holding a NULL to the engine. A statement on a column holding NULLs that is not a maintained aggregate reads boxed rows, slower than a NOT NULL column. A table that declares a NULL column is not read lock-free.
- Similarity: NEAREST with a WHERE filters first and then ranks the survivors, and NEAREST does not combine with GROUP BY.
- Documentation: the package ships compiled, without XML documentation.

#### HoloDb docs: tables, SQL, transactions (https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/holodb/docs/)

The practical guide: put data in, get answers out. Every program on this page was compiled and run against the published package, and the output shown is what it printed.

##### Install and first query

Add the package from NuGet with dotnet add package EvaluatedApplications.HoloDb. It targets .NET 8 and later, and ships the compiled library only. HoloDbService is the wrapped, async-friendly entry point, and Execute runs SQL synchronously. ExecuteAsync offloads the work to the thread pool so a request thread is not blocked.

```csharp
using HoloDb;

var db = new HoloDbService(new HoloDbOptions());           // in memory
db.Execute("CREATE TABLE users (id INT PRIMARY KEY, age INT, name TEXT)");
db.Execute("INSERT INTO users VALUES (1, 30, 'Ada'), (2, 24, 'Linus'), (3, 15, 'Kid')");

var result = db.Execute("SELECT name FROM users WHERE age >= 18 ORDER BY age DESC");
foreach (var row in result.Rows)
    Console.WriteLine(row["name"]);

var count = await db.ExecuteAsync("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users");
Console.WriteLine(count.Rows[0]["count(*)"]);
```

Output:

```text
Ada
Linus
3
```

##### Tables and types

There are three storage types, each with the usual SQL aliases.

- INT: A .NET long. Aliases: INTEGER.
- REAL: A .NET double. Aliases: FLOAT, DOUBLE, DECIMAL, NUMERIC. DECIMAL and NUMERIC map to a 64-bit float, so they are not exact decimals.
- TEXT: A .NET string. Aliases: VARCHAR, STRING.

One column may be PRIMARY KEY, and it is enforced unique and is never NULL. A column is NOT NULL unless its definition says NULL: see the section on NULL. For money, store integer minor units, cents as an INT: it is exact, and it lets the constant-time integer aggregates serve your revenue totals.

```sql
CREATE TABLE sales (
  id     INT PRIMARY KEY,
  region TEXT,
  amount REAL
)
```

##### Inserting, updating and bulk loading

Strings use single quotes, and a quote is escaped by doubling it. Rows go in singly or in batches, with or without a column list.

Every Execute also takes positional ? placeholders. The arguments are quoted and escaped for you, before the statement is parsed. A null argument is the SQL literal NULL (a value in INSERT and UPDATE SET; in a comparison it throws, write IS NULL). A wrong argument count or an unsupported type throws.

A plain INSERT of an existing primary key throws. To insert or replace, use the upsert in the section on atomic change batches.

```sql
INSERT INTO sales VALUES (1, 'EU', 42.50)
```

```sql
INSERT INTO sales (id, region, amount) VALUES (2, 'US', 17.00), (3, 'EU', 61.10)
```

```sql
UPDATE sales SET amount = 0 WHERE region = 'US'
```

```sql
DELETE FROM sales WHERE amount = 0
```

##### NULL

A column holds SQL NULL when it is declared NULL: CREATE TABLE orders (id INT PRIMARY KEY, region TEXT NULL, amount INT NULL, qty INT NOT NULL). Every other column is NOT NULL (the words are accepted and mean the default), and a primary key is never NULL. A NOT NULL column left out of an INSERT still gets its type zero (0, 0.0 or an empty string); a NULL column left out is NULL.

NULL is a value in INSERT, UPDATE ... SET, ON CONFLICT ... SET, ALTER ... DEFAULT, Database.Bind(.., null), RowChange.Upsert (a C# null) and Database.BulkLoad (a mask per column). It is refused, with a message that says to write IS NULL, in = != < > <= >=, IN, BETWEEN, LIKE, NEAREST and a join ON, because a comparison with NULL is never true.

- Three-valued logic: WHERE and HAVING keep a row only when the predicate is true. A comparison, LIKE, IN or BETWEEN on a NULL is unknown; false AND unknown is false, true OR unknown is true, NOT unknown is unknown. x NOT IN (SELECT ...) is never true when the subquery returns a NULL. IS NULL and IS NOT NULL are always true or false.
- Aggregates skip NULL: COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(col), COUNT(DISTINCT col), SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX count and combine the non-NULL values. SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX of a group whose values are all NULL are NULL. Whole-table COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX of an INT column and a one-column GROUP BY with COUNT, SUM and AVG stay maintained answers with NULLs present: no row is read. On an empty selection SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX are NULL and COUNT is 0, as for a NOT NULL column, and an aggregate without GROUP BY always answers one row.
- Groups, order and joins: GROUP BY and DISTINCT make one group of all the NULLs, apart from 0 and the empty string. ORDER BY puts NULL first ascending and last descending. An INNER JOIN never matches a NULL key, not even another NULL. In NEAREST a NULL cell adds nothing to the row's similarity.
- Results: A result that holds a NULL is row-form: read it with Rows or GetValue, where the cell is DBNull.Value, and QueryResult.IsNull(row, col) says so. GetLong, GetDouble and GetText serve a non-NULL cell of the matching type and throw a HoloException on a NULL.
- Where it stops: CREATE INDEX (sorted, text, composite) takes NOT NULL columns only. A Pleroma plane stores the type zero for a NULL and declines, so the engine answers, any statement that touches a plane column holding one; it never answers wrongly. A summary table keeps no rows to fall back on and refuses a NULL, and paged tables do not take NULL columns.
- Speed: A column that has never received a NULL has no null bitmap, and a statement that touches no column holding a NULL and has no IS [NOT] NULL takes the routes it takes for a NOT NULL column. The maintained answers above stay flat with NULLs present. Any other statement on a column that holds NULLs filters with a null-aware compiled predicate and then builds boxed rows, slower than the typed columnar result a NOT NULL column returns. A table that declares a NULL column is not read lock-free, and the live snapshot does not serve a statement that references a declared NULL column, even before it holds a NULL: declare a column NULL only where you need it.
- Older binaries: A log with a NULL in it, or a snapshot of a table with a NULL column, is refused by an older HoloDb binary with a clear error until a newer one has opened it and called Checkpoint(). A database with no NULL column writes the same files as before.

```csharp
using HoloDb;

var db = new HoloDbService(new HoloDbOptions());
db.Execute("CREATE TABLE orders (id INT PRIMARY KEY, region TEXT NULL, amount INT NULL, qty INT NOT NULL)");
db.Execute("INSERT INTO orders VALUES (1, 'north', 10, 1), (2, NULL, 20, 1), (3, 'north', NULL, 2)");
var r = db.Execute("SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(amount), SUM(amount), AVG(amount) FROM orders").Rows[0];
Console.WriteLine($"{r["count(*)"]} rows, {r["count(amount)"]} amounts, sum {r["sum(amount)"]}, avg {r["avg(amount)"]}");
// 3 rows, 2 amounts, sum 30, avg 15
Console.WriteLine(db.Execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE region IS NULL").Rows[0]["count(*)"]);
// 1
Console.WriteLine(db.Execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE region != 'north'").Rows[0]["count(*)"]);
// 0   (the NULL region is neither equal nor different)
foreach (var g in db.Execute("SELECT region, COUNT(*) FROM orders GROUP BY region ORDER BY region").Rows)
    Console.WriteLine($"{(g["region"] is DBNull ? "(null)" : g["region"])}: {g["count(*)"]}");
// (null): 1
// north: 2

// A change feed carries NULLs as C# nulls; BulkLoad takes a mask per column (true = NULL) and a left-out nullable column is NULL.
db.ApplyChanges("orders", new[] { RowChange.Upsert(new Dictionary<string, object?> { ["id"] = 4L, ["region"] = null, ["amount"] = 5L, ["qty"] = 1L }) });
db.BulkLoad("orders", new[] { "id", "amount", "qty" }, new Array[] { new long[] { 5, 6 }, new long[] { 0, 7 }, new long[] { 1, 1 } }, 2,
    new bool[]?[] { null, new[] { true, false }, null });
Console.WriteLine(db.Execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE amount IS NULL").Rows[0]["count(*)"]);
// 2   (id 3 and id 5)
```

Output:

```text
3 rows, 2 amounts, sum 30, avg 15
1
0
(null): 1
north: 2
2
```

##### Parameterized queries

Use ? placeholders instead of building SQL text yourself.

```csharp
using HoloDb;

var db = new HoloDbService(new HoloDbOptions());
db.Execute("CREATE TABLE people (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, age INT)");
db.Execute("INSERT INTO people VALUES (?, ?, ?)", 1, "O'Neil", 41);   // quoted and escaped for you
db.Execute("INSERT INTO people VALUES (?, ?, ?)", 2, "Ada", 36);

var r = db.Execute("SELECT name FROM people WHERE age > ? ORDER BY name", 30);
foreach (var row in r.Rows) Console.WriteLine(row["name"]);
```

Output:

```text
Ada
O'Neil
```

##### Bulk loading

For large loads, skip the SQL parser and hand the engine one typed array per column (long[], double[] or string[]). It is atomic and validates primary-key uniqueness before committing. Load in chunks for very large data sets, as The Analyst does with a large paste.

```csharp
using HoloDb;

var db = new HoloDbService(new HoloDbOptions());
db.Execute("CREATE TABLE sales (id INT PRIMARY KEY, region TEXT, amount REAL)");

// Typed column arrays skip the SQL parser: the fast path for large loads.
var ids = new long[] { 1, 2, 3 };
var regions = new string[] { "EU", "US", "EU" };
var amounts = new double[] { 42.50, 17.00, 61.10 };
db.BulkLoad("sales", new[] { "id", "region", "amount" }, new Array[] { ids, regions, amounts }, count: 3);

var r = db.Execute("SELECT region, COUNT(*), SUM(amount) FROM sales GROUP BY region ORDER BY region");
foreach (var row in r.Rows) Console.WriteLine($"{row["region"]}: {row["count(*)"]} rows, {row["sum(amount)"]}");
```

Output:

```text
EU: 2 rows, 103.6
US: 1 rows, 17
```

##### Querying: the dialect

A SELECT supports aggregates (COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX), a full boolean WHERE (AND, OR, NOT, parentheses, the comparisons = != < > <= >=, LIKE, IN, IN (SELECT ...), BETWEEN ... AND ... and IS [NOT] NULL), GROUP BY with HAVING, ORDER BY with several keys, LIMIT, DISTINCT and INNER JOIN.

Qualify joined columns with the table name, as above. Table aliases are not supported. A join is INNER JOIN only: LEFT, RIGHT, FULL, CROSS and NATURAL joins, USING and comma joins are refused with an error, never answered as an inner join. Several INNER JOINs may share one statement on in-memory tables, and a paged table takes one.

SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX over no rows are NULL, COUNT is 0, and an aggregate without GROUP BY always returns one row. If your code read the SUM or AVG of an empty selection as 0, test QueryResult.IsNull first: GetLong and GetDouble throw on a NULL cell. An INT SUM is exact: it is held in 128 bits, and the statement throws only if the true total leaves 64 bits, on in-memory and paged tables alike. Without ORDER BY the row order, and so which rows a LIMIT keeps, is unspecified.

```sql
SELECT region, COUNT(*), SUM(amount), AVG(amount)
FROM sales
WHERE amount BETWEEN 10 AND 1000
GROUP BY region
HAVING SUM(amount) > 50
ORDER BY sum(amount) DESC
LIMIT 10
```

```sql
SELECT orders.id, customers.name, orders.total
FROM orders
INNER JOIN customers ON orders.customer_id = customers.id
WHERE orders.total > 100
ORDER BY orders.total DESC
```

##### Reading results

Execute returns a QueryResult. The simplest way to read it is row by row as dictionaries keyed by column name, through Rows. Aggregate columns are named by the function applied, in lower case: count(*), sum(amount), avg(amount), min(amount) and max(amount). Columns lists the result's column names in order, and for a write statement Affected is the number of rows changed.

For hot paths QueryResult keeps results columnar and exposes direct accessors (GetLong, GetDouble, GetText and GetValue by row and column), so you can read values without materialising a dictionary per row.

##### Three ways to ask one store

Exact lookup by key, similarity by content and constant-time aggregates all read the same rows. The program below shows each, and the usage meter shows the aggregate scanned no rows.

```csharp
using HoloDb;

var db = Database.Open();   // null path: in memory
db.Execute("CREATE TABLE invoices (id INT PRIMARY KEY, customer TEXT, region TEXT, amount_cents INT)");
db.Execute("INSERT INTO invoices VALUES (1,'Acme','north',1200),(2,'Beta','south',4500),(3,'Cyan','north',1150),(4,'Dune','east',30000),(5,'Echo','north',1300)");

// 1. By key: ordinary SQL, answered from the primary-key index
Console.WriteLine(db.Execute("SELECT customer FROM invoices WHERE id = 3").Rows[0]["customer"]);

// 2. By content: rank rows by resemblance to a partial description; add score to see the ranking
foreach (var r in db.Execute("SELECT id, region, amount_cents FROM invoices NEAREST (region = 'north', amount_cents = 1200) LIMIT 3").Rows)
    Console.WriteLine($"{r["id"]}: {r["region"]} {r["amount_cents"]}");

// 3. By aggregate: read from maintained totals, no scan
foreach (var r in db.Execute("SELECT region, SUM(amount_cents) FROM invoices GROUP BY region ORDER BY region").Rows)
    Console.WriteLine($"{r["region"]}: {r["sum(amount_cents)"]}");
Console.WriteLine($"rows scanned by the aggregate: {Database.LastRowsScanned}");
```

Output:

```text
Cyan
1: north 1200
5: north 1300
3: north 1150
east: 30000
north: 3650
south: 4500
rows scanned by the aggregate: 0
```

##### Similarity search

Each row's columns also feed a holographic vector derived from them, so HoloDb ranks rows by similarity to a partial description, with no separate vector index. Use the NEAREST clause with the fields you know and a LIMIT for how many neighbours you want. Add score to the projection to read the ranking metric.

Similarity is graded: a close number or date, or a near-identical string, ranks ahead of a far or unrelated one. It is an exact scan below 8,000 rows and whenever the query has a WHERE, and above that an approximate sublinear index (locality-sensitive hashing) ranks candidates, so the result can differ from an exact scan. With a WHERE the filter runs first and the survivors are ranked. NEAREST does not combine with GROUP BY, and an UPDATE, DELETE or ALTER TABLE on the table forces the next NEAREST to rebuild its index.

```sql
SELECT id, title
FROM articles
NEAREST (title = 'holographic database')
LIMIT 5
```

##### Transactions

ACID transactions with explicit control: wrap statements in BEGIN and COMMIT, or discard them with ROLLBACK. BEGIN costs the same at any table size, because rows are journaled as they change instead of the table being copied, and ROLLBACK replays the journal. With a WalPath set, a committed transaction is durable.

```csharp
using HoloDb;

var db = new HoloDbService(new HoloDbOptions());
db.Execute("CREATE TABLE accounts (id INT PRIMARY KEY, balance INT)");
db.Execute("INSERT INTO accounts VALUES (1, 500), (2, 100)");

db.Execute("BEGIN");
try
{
    db.Execute("UPDATE accounts SET balance = 400 WHERE id = 1");
    db.Execute("UPDATE accounts SET balance = 200 WHERE id = 2");
    db.Execute("COMMIT");
}
catch
{
    db.Execute("ROLLBACK");
    throw;
}
Console.WriteLine("after commit: " + string.Join(", ", db.Execute("SELECT balance FROM accounts ORDER BY id").Rows.Select(r => r["balance"])));

db.Execute("BEGIN");
db.Execute("UPDATE accounts SET balance = 0 WHERE id = 1");
db.Execute("ROLLBACK");
Console.WriteLine("after rollback: " + string.Join(", ", db.Execute("SELECT balance FROM accounts ORDER BY id").Rows.Select(r => r["balance"])));
```

Output:

```text
after commit: 400, 200
after rollback: 400, 200
```

##### Atomic change batches and upsert

A live replica turns an ordered change feed from another system into one call per batch. ApplyChanges(table, changes) on Database, and ApplyChanges and ApplyChangesAsync on HoloDbService, applies upserts and deletes atomically under one write lock: a reader sees the table before the batch or after it, never part of it, on every read path including the lock-free live metrics. The batch is one write-ahead-log commit group, so on replay it applies whole or not at all, and a table with a Pleroma plane takes the whole batch in one pass.

- RowChange.Upsert(row): Carries a full row: every column, with case-insensitive names. INT takes any integral type, REAL a float or an integer, and TEXT a string. A C# null (or DBNull) is SQL NULL and is accepted only for a column declared NULL; there is no NaN. It inserts a new key or replaces the whole row of an existing one. A missing column throws, because there is no default for an omitted column: it would silently become 0, an empty string or NULL. For a partial update use INSERT ... ON CONFLICT.
- RowChange.Delete(key): Deletes by primary key. A key that is not there is a counted no-op.
- Order and result: Changes count as if applied in order, so the last change to a key wins, and only the net effect runs. ChangeResult reports Inserted, Updated, Deleted and MissingDeletes.
- All or nothing: Everything is validated before anything changes, and a failure leaves the table, its aggregates and its plane as they were. Inside BEGIN and COMMIT the batch commits or rolls back with the transaction.
- What is refused: A paged table refuses ApplyChanges and the SQL upsert with an error that names the table. A text value that contains a line break throws on a database with a write-ahead log, because the log holds one statement per line.
- The log: The log holds the net effect as plain DELETE, UPDATE and INSERT lines, so an older binary can still replay it.

The SQL form is INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (key) DO UPDATE SET column = EXCLUDED.column. The SET list names the columns that change and the others keep their value, which makes it the way to change some columns of a row. It reports Affected as the rows inserted plus the rows updated, and it is allowed inside a transaction. Only EXCLUDED.column of the same column is accepted. DO NOTHING, expressions, a WHERE on the conflict, INSERT OR REPLACE, REPLACE INTO, UPSERT and a conflict target that is not the primary key are each refused with an error that names them. A plain INSERT of an existing primary key still throws.

```csharp
using HoloDb;

var db = new HoloDbService(new HoloDbOptions());
db.Execute("CREATE TABLE orders (id INT PRIMARY KEY, region TEXT, total INT)");

// one atomic batch: readers see the table before it or after it, never part of it
var r = db.ApplyChanges("orders", new[]
{
    RowChange.Upsert(new Dictionary<string, object?> { ["id"] = 1L, ["region"] = "north", ["total"] = 40L }),
    RowChange.Upsert(new Dictionary<string, object?> { ["id"] = 2L, ["region"] = "south", ["total"] = 15L }),
    RowChange.Upsert(new Dictionary<string, object?> { ["id"] = 1L, ["region"] = "north", ["total"] = 45L }),
    RowChange.Delete(2L),
    RowChange.Delete(99L),
});
Console.WriteLine($"{r.Inserted} inserted, {r.Updated} updated, {r.Deleted} deleted, {r.MissingDeletes} missing");

// the SQL form changes only the columns in the SET list and keeps the rest
db.Execute("INSERT INTO orders VALUES (1, 'west', 50), (3, 'east', 7) ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET total = EXCLUDED.total");
foreach (var row in db.Execute("SELECT id, region, total FROM orders ORDER BY id").Rows)
    Console.WriteLine($"{row["id"]} {row["region"]} {row["total"]}");
```

Output:

```text
2 inserted, 1 updated, 1 deleted, 1 missing
1 north 50
3 east 7
```

##### In memory or durable

By default the database lives in memory and is gone when the process ends. To make writes durable, give it a write-ahead log path. Durable state is a compact snapshot of the current data plus a short log of the writes since the last checkpoint. A durable commit flushes to disk before it returns. Recovery is bounded by how much data you hold, not by how long the database has been running: reopening loads a snapshot and replays only the recent tail.

The log is folded into a fresh snapshot automatically once it passes a threshold (CheckpointThresholdBytes, 8 MB by default), and you can force one with Checkpoint, for example before a clean shutdown. In WebAssembly there is no file system, so leave WalPath null and use the in-memory engine. To work with the engine directly, without the async wrapper, call Database.Open with a path, or with null for in memory.

```csharp
using HoloDb;

var wal = Path.Combine(Path.GetTempPath(), "holodb-docs-" + Guid.NewGuid().ToString("N") + ".wal");
try
{
    var db = new HoloDbService(new HoloDbOptions { WalPath = wal });   // writes are durable
    db.Execute("CREATE TABLE notes (id INT PRIMARY KEY, body TEXT)");
    db.Execute("INSERT INTO notes VALUES (1, 'first'), (2, 'second')");
    db.Checkpoint();                                                    // fold the log into a snapshot
    db.Execute("INSERT INTO notes VALUES (3, 'after the checkpoint')");
    db.Database.Close();

    var reopened = new HoloDbService(new HoloDbOptions { WalPath = wal });   // snapshot plus the short tail
    Console.WriteLine(reopened.Execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM notes").Rows[0]["count(*)"]);
    reopened.Database.Close();
}
finally
{
    foreach (var f in Directory.GetFiles(Path.GetTempPath(), Path.GetFileName(wal) + "*")) File.Delete(f);
}
```

Output:

```text
3
```

##### Larger than memory: paged tables

The default engine keeps everything in RAM. When a table needs to outgrow memory, create it as a paged table. It lives on an 8 KB buffer-pool page store with a redo-only write-ahead log, so cold pages spill to disk, and the constant-time aggregates stay maintained on disk. Once created, a paged table is driven through the same Execute call as an in-memory table.

The buffer-pool size (bufferFrames, 8,192 frames of 8 KB by default) bounds how much stays resident. A paged table's primary-key index is built on first use. A key column loaded in increasing order is its own index, searched in place with no RAM. Any other order keeps a dictionary in RAM at about 35 bytes per row, measured at 39 and 34 bytes per entry for 1,000,000 and 10,000,000 entries, and that index, not the buffer pool, then bounds how far a single paged table can grow past memory.

Every 8 KB page carries a CRC-32C, kept in a small side file of 4 bytes per page. A page that fails its checksum is refused with an error that names the page, never read as a different answer. UPDATE and DELETE find their rows through the primary key, a sorted index, a group index that proves a value absent, or the block scan, and they move only the pages that change. A statement may change more pages than the buffer pool holds: the pool spills the open transaction to a scratch file, so a DELETE that moves every later row completes, and a rollback or a power cut still leaves the table exactly as it was. Filtered scans, GROUP BY of any cardinality, top-K and GROUP BY over a join read the needed columns a page run at a time across all cores.

```csharp
using HoloDb;

var dir = Path.Combine(Path.GetTempPath(), "holodb-paged-" + Guid.NewGuid().ToString("N"));
try
{
    var db = new HoloDbService(new HoloDbOptions());
    // a durable, larger-than-memory table backed by a directory
    db.CreatePaged("CREATE TABLE events (id INT PRIMARY KEY, kind TEXT, value INT)", dir);
    var rows = Enumerable.Range(1, 1000).Select(i => (object[])new object[] { (long)i, i % 2 == 0 ? "even" : "odd", (long)i });
    db.PagedBulkLoad("events", rows);
    foreach (var r in db.Execute("SELECT kind, COUNT(*), SUM(value) FROM events GROUP BY kind ORDER BY kind").Rows)
        Console.WriteLine($"{r["kind"]}: {r["count(*)"]} rows, sum {r["sum(value)"]}");
    db.Database.ClosePaged("events");

    var again = new HoloDbService(new HoloDbOptions());
    again.OpenPaged(dir);                                               // reopen it later
    Console.WriteLine(again.Execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM events").Rows[0]["count(*)"]);
    again.Database.ClosePaged("events");
}
finally { if (Directory.Exists(dir)) Directory.Delete(dir, true); }
```

Output:

```text
even: 500 rows, sum 250500
odd: 500 rows, sum 250000
1000
```

##### Indexes, and why aggregates are instant

A sorted index speeds range and lookup queries. You rarely need one for counting: COUNT and SUM over integer columns are served from maintained accumulators in constant time, independent of how many rows the table holds, so the engine does not scan to count. An index needs an INT or TEXT column.

CREATE INDEX also builds the optional aggregate plane, and on a paged table it takes USING SUMMARY, SORTED or KEYED. SHOW INDEXES and EXPLAIN report what exists and what answers a query. Those are described with the plane.

You do not have to declare any of them. With the default SET summaries = auto and SET indexes = auto, the engine builds a summary, a sorted index, an equality index or a keyed summary itself when repeated scans have paid for it, and drops it when the workload moves on. SET summaries = declared or off, and the same for indexes, turn that off. The answers are the same with or without the structure.

```sql
CREATE INDEX ON sales (region)
```

##### Changing a table

ALTER TABLE supports ADD COLUMN only. A NOT NULL column needs a literal DEFAULT, which backfills the rows that exist; a column declared NULL may leave the DEFAULT out, and the existing rows are NULL. There is no DROP, rename or type change.

```sql
ALTER TABLE sales ADD COLUMN note TEXT DEFAULT ''
```

##### Dependency injection and EvalApp

Register HoloDb in a .NET host and inject HoloDbService wherever you need it. HoloDb also runs inside an EvalApp harness: WithHoloDb attaches a service to a pipeline, so heavy queries execute as compiled, resource-gated, self-tuning pipeline steps and any step can reach the service.

```csharp
using HoloDb;
using Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection;

var services = new ServiceCollection();
services.AddHoloDb(options => { options.WalPath = null; });   // singleton HoloDbService

using var provider = services.BuildServiceProvider();
var db = provider.GetRequiredService<HoloDbService>();
db.Execute("CREATE TABLE sales (id INT PRIMARY KEY, region TEXT, amount INT)");
db.Execute("INSERT INTO sales VALUES (1, 'EU', 10), (2, 'US', 5), (3, 'EU', 7)");
var totals = await db.ExecuteAsync("SELECT region, SUM(amount) FROM sales GROUP BY region ORDER BY region");
foreach (var r in totals.Rows) Console.WriteLine($"{r["region"]}: {r["sum(amount)"]}");
```

Output:

```text
EU: 17
US: 5
```

##### The usage meter

After each query, static per-thread readings report what the engine actually processed: LastRowsScanned, LastTableRows, LastRowBytes and LastLogicalBytes. An aggregate served from a maintained total reports zero rows scanned, which is the figure a metered API bills on.

##### In the browser, and over the network

HoloDb is plain managed .NET with no native dependencies, so it compiles to WebAssembly and runs client-side with no server and nothing leaving the device. The Analyst is exactly that: a real HoloDb in your browser tab, profiling and querying whatever you paste in.

The same engine runs as a server, and a typed client talks to it over TLS with the same surface as the in-process engine.

#### HoloDb is built with Pleroma (https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/holodb/pleroma/)

Ask a table a question without reading the table.

Switch on the plane for a table and HoloDb answers filters, group-bys, distinct counts and joins from a small exact summary instead of scanning rows. It is optional, off until you ask, and every answer matches the engine's.

- About 600 times: faster for an overdue-invoices rollup on 10,000,000 rows with the plane on: 5.93 ms down to 0.01 ms
- 121 times: median speed-up over the engine on nine ad-hoc filters across a 10,000,000-event dashboard
- 343 to 385 microseconds: for one insert and one group-by with the plane on, from 100,000 to 1,000,000 rows. The engine alone climbs from 1.03 to 3.54 ms

HoloDb is built with Pleroma, the exact count-and-sum structure in the Phasor package. Three parts of HoloDb are Pleroma parts. This page says what each gives you and what it costs. The first two are optional and off until you ask for them.

##### Engine results and plane results

The 10,000,000-invoice comparison against engines as they ship ran on the HoloDb engine alone, with no plane attached, and the 100,000,000-invoice comparison uses summaries that are declared or built by the planner. The plane is a separate, opt-in feature, measured in its own runs in the deep dive, where its costs sit beside its wins.

##### The aggregate plane: exact answers from a derived summary

You name a few small-domain columns (dimensions, INT or TEXT) and the INT columns to sum (measures). HoloDb keeps a Pleroma summary of them, updated by every write, and answers filters, multi-column GROUP BY, COUNT(DISTINCT), MIN and MAX of a dimension, and equi-join COUNT and SUM from it, without scanning the table.

- Exact and derived: The columns stay the source of truth, and the plane is rebuilt from them. PleromaVerify rebuilds it and compares, and returns nothing when they agree. Sums are held exactly past 64 bits: the plane raises an error rather than wrap, and PleromaSumExact returns the exact 128-bit total.
- It declines safely: Anything the plane does not hold (AVG, a column that is not a dimension or measure, a dimension over its cap of distinct values, a join over 4,095 keys) goes to the engine, so a query returns the same rows with the plane on or off. The default routing, PleromaMode.Auto, also leaves to the engine the shapes where it already reads a maintained total (whole-table counts and sums, single-column GROUP BY) and GROUP BY with a WHERE below 140,000 rows, because the engine is faster there.
- Batches: ApplyChanges hands the plane a whole batch of upserts and deletes in one pass, as one commit group. The evidence page shows how the cost of a batch grows with its size, and that one insert followed by a group-by costs about the same at 100,000 rows as at 1,000,000.
- What it costs: On a 1,000,000-row table the plane is slower than the engine alone on whole-table COUNT, whole-table SUM, single-column GROUP BY and MIN and MAX, because the engine reads a maintained total in microseconds there. It adds to single-row INSERT and UPDATE, and to bulk load a little. Every cost is in the evidence record beside the wins.
- Automatic by default: With no declaration at all, the engine watches which aggregate statements keep scanning, and when the scanning has cost as much as a summary would cost to build it builds that summary itself (inline for tables up to a million rows, in the background above that while writes continue), names it auto_<table>_summary, and drops it again if the workload moves on. SET summaries = auto | declared | off and SHOW SUMMARIES control and show it, and EXPLAIN says which summary answered and why it was built. The answers are the same with or without it.
- On paged tables too: The same rule builds the summary in the background from a paged table's pages, keeps it exact through appends, updates, deletes and transactions, and saves it beside the table, checksummed and valid only for the state it was saved from. A fresh paged table scans its first calls; after three repeats and enough scan time to pay for the build, the same statements are answered from the summary.
- A sorted index for the big scan: A paged table can keep a sorted index on an INT column (16 bytes per row, read from disk in checksummed blocks). A range count, MIN and MAX, and the 20 largest are answered from the index whatever the table size: at 30,000,000 rows, warm, 0.002 ms against 2.7 ms for the scan. It stays exact through appends, updates and deletes, is saved with the data, and the planner builds one by itself when the scans have paid for it.
- A keyed summary for the high-cardinality joins: For every customer id the exact count and sum, so top customers and revenue by segment are answered from the 600,000 keys instead of the 30,000,000 rows (12 ms and 13 to 30 ms cold after a restore; the scans took 120 to 1,170 ms). Joins with a dimension are kept as exact pre-grouped totals that every appended row and every new customer updates as it arrives, and a customer who changes segment moves their totals. At 100,000,000 invoices the four dimension joins answer in 0.19 to 0.25 ms warm and top customers in 0.58 ms warm (medians of three, one run, structures declared and loaded from their saved files). The planner builds the summary when the scans have paid for it, counting the writes the table has seen: a table that is mostly written to does not get one. The comparison with tuned DuckDB and tuned SQL Server is on the evidence page, with the queries HoloDb loses.
- Restored from a backup, nothing to rebuild: Declare the summary on a paged table (CREATE INDEX ... USING SUMMARY) and it is saved beside the data with the table's group indexes and sorted key, each checksummed and trusted only for the exact table state it was saved from. A database restored from a backup opens with all of it present, and the first query is answered from the summary with no pass over the data. A stale or damaged file is discarded or rebuilt from its saved definition, and SHOW SUMMARIES says why.
- Limits: A plane attached with EnablePleroma is for memory-resident tables and is not persisted, so call it again after Open. A plane created with SQL, or built automatically, is logged and saved with the snapshot, so Open does not rebuild it, and it survives Checkpoint. On a paged table CREATE INDEX takes USING SUMMARY, SORTED or KEYED, and the planner builds the same structures by itself. A plane serves a dimension only up to its cap of distinct values and a join of at most 4,095 keys, and declines anything else to the engine.

##### Index SQL and EXPLAIN: build it and see why

The plane has a SQL form, so a remote client can build it through the server like any statement. SHOW INDEXES reports its size and how many queries it served and declined, and EXPLAIN reports why a query was served or declined, without running it.

EXPLAIN runs the engine's own routing code in a mode that stops before the heavy work, so what it reports is the decision the real statement takes. It does not run an IN (SELECT ...) subquery, which it shows unresolved. A binary older than the release that added this SQL cannot open a log or snapshot that contains it.

```csharp
using HoloDb;

var db = Database.Open();
db.Execute("CREATE TABLE sales (id INT PRIMARY KEY, region TEXT, tier INT, qty INT)");
db.Execute("INSERT INTO sales (id, region, tier, qty) VALUES (1,'north',1,10),(2,'north',2,-4),(3,'south',1,7),(4,'east',3,5),(5,'south',2,9)");

// build the plane from SQL: key columns are dimensions, INCLUDE columns are measures
db.Execute("CREATE INDEX by_region ON sales (region, tier) INCLUDE (qty) USING SUMMARY");
db.PleromaMode = PleromaMode.Always;

Console.WriteLine(db.Execute("SELECT SUM(qty) FROM sales WHERE region = 'north' OR tier = 3").Rows[0]["sum(qty)"]);

// why was it served, or declined?
foreach (var r in db.Execute("EXPLAIN SELECT region, SUM(qty) FROM sales WHERE region = 'north' GROUP BY region").Rows)
    Console.WriteLine($"{r["kind"]}: {r["route"]}");
foreach (var r in db.Execute("EXPLAIN SELECT COUNT(*) FROM sales WHERE qty > 5").Rows)
    Console.WriteLine($"{r["kind"]}: {r["route"]}");

Console.WriteLine(db.PleromaVerify("sales") ?? "plane equals a rebuild from the columns");
Console.WriteLine(db.PleromaSumExact("SELECT SUM(qty) FROM sales"));
```

Output:

```text
11
route: Pleroma plane (exact aggregate from the derived plane)
plan: Aggregate by region: sum(qty)
plan:   Filter region[FilterEq]
plan:     Scan sales
summary: declared summary by_region
index: no index: 5 rows is below the 100,000-row floor where a scan is a few milliseconds
decline: WHERE uses a column that is not a plane dimension, a dimension over its cap, a column-to-column comparison or a subquery
access: block-wise mask scan
route: predicate count (block-wise byte-mask, no position list)
plan: Aggregate count(*)
plan:   Filter qty[FilterRange]
plan:     Scan sales
summary: declared summary by_region
index: no index: 5 rows is below the 100,000-row floor where a scan is a few milliseconds
plane equals a rebuild from the columns
27
```

##### The Pleroma page store: durable, checksummed pages

PleromaPageStore holds many exact Pleroma pages as the data itself, durably and larger than memory, with no columns behind them. PleromaSparsePageStore does the same for sparse pages over a large vocabulary.

- Checksummed pages: Every page carries a check prime, a mirror of its cells in a second prime, and a header hash. Verify proves every record and parity group intact. VerifyOnLoad does the same on every load and is off by default (about 100 microseconds for a 110-key page).
- Parity repair: Records are grouped (8 by default) with one exact-sum parity record per group, and the members of a group sit on different 8 KB pager pages. Any one lost pager page, or any one damaged record per group, is rebuilt by Repair. A rebuilt page must pass its own check before it is written, and a page whose group parity is also damaged is reported as unrecoverable, never rebuilt wrong.
- Restore points: Checkpoint returns a restore point, and RestoreTo returns the store to exactly that state with no recount. It is copy-on-write, so a restore point costs one before-image per page changed since, not a copy of the data. Eight are kept by default.
- Exactly-once replay: Every AddBatch is journaled (fsynced by default) before it is applied, and each page remembers the last batch applied to it, so crash recovery applies a logged add exactly once, even over pages already flushed. A torn journal tail is discarded, so a batch survives whole or not at all.

Limits: one shape per store, and it must be CompleteKeys and admissible for a check prime. Shapes with a continuous component or a relation face cannot be saved. One process opens a store at a time and one writer works at a time. A batch is applied page by page, so a reader sees every page whole but may see a batch on some pages and not on others. The sparse store has no parity groups, restore points or event journal. Page-store throughput is not reported.

```csharp
using HoloDb;
using Phasor;

var shape = new HologramShape { KeyCapacity = 2, KeyCycle = 110, CompleteKeys = true };
var dir = Path.Combine(Path.GetTempPath(), "plrstore-restore");
if (Directory.Exists(dir)) Directory.Delete(dir, true);

using (var store = PleromaPageStore.Open(dir, shape))
{
    store.AddBatch(new[] { new PageAdd(42, 5, 3) });
    var point = store.Checkpoint();                       // a restore point: id and journal position
    store.AddBatch(new[] { new PageAdd(42, 5, 10), new PageAdd(9, 1, 1) });
    Console.WriteLine($"{store.Counts(42)[5]} {store.Contains(9)}");

    store.RestoreTo(point.Id);                            // back to the point, no recount
    Console.WriteLine($"{store.Counts(42)[5]} {store.Contains(9)}");

    Console.WriteLine(store.Verify().Clean);
    Console.WriteLine(store.Repair().Unrecoverable.Count);
}
Directory.Delete(dir, true);
```

Output:

```text
13 True
3 False
True
0
```

##### Exactness

The plane returns row-for-row the same answers as the engine and SQLite across its parity suite, including a random insert, update, delete, rollback and reopen log, and sums past 64 bits, and the page store passes its fault suite. The checks, and the deliberate mutations that turned them red, are listed with the figures.

#### HoloDb over the network: the client and the wire protocol (https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/holodb/client/)

HoloDb.Client connects your .NET app to a HoloDb server over TCP with mandatory TLS and token authentication. HoloDb.Protocol is the columnar wire protocol between the two.

##### The client

Run SQL queries and bulk-load data with the same API as the embedded, in-process HoloDbService, so you can move from embedded to networked by changing only how you create the handle. Building a data-driven app usually means choosing between speed (embed the database) and scale (run it on its own server), with two APIs that behave differently. The client gives you one code path for both.

Install it with dotnet add package EvaluatedApplications.HoloDb.Client, or pin it in a project file with the version range 1.5.*. It targets .NET 8 and .NET 10 and needs a HoloDb server it can reach over TLS.

- Same API, embedded or networked: Execute, ExecuteAsync, BulkLoadAsync, GetStatsAsync and PingAsync have the same surface whether you talk to the in-process service or a remote server.
- Columnar over the wire: Results are typed column arrays that match the in-process engine's QueryResult. There is no row buffering and no JSON serialization.
- Secure by default: TLS is on. Trust a self-signed server by pinning its certificate thumbprint, or skip it in development only.
- Resilience when you opt in: Exponential backoff with full jitter, a circuit breaker and a per-operation deadline budget across retries.
- SQL NULL: A NULL cell arrives as DBNull.Value, and IsNull(row, col) tells you which cells are NULL.
- Built for concurrency: One client per concurrent worker, or pool clients up front with HoloDbClientPool.

##### Connect and query

These examples are compiled against the published package. Running them needs a HoloDb server.

```csharp
using HoloDb.Client;

// Connect to a server (compile-checked here: running it needs a HoloDb server)
var client = await HoloDbClient.ConnectAsync("db.example.com", 5433);
try
{
    // The same surface as the in-process HoloDbService; a NULL value is DBNull.Value
    var result = await client.ExecuteAsync("SELECT id, value FROM data LIMIT 10");
    foreach (var row in result.Rows)
        Console.WriteLine($"id={row["id"]}, value={row["value"]}");
}
finally
{
    await client.DisposeAsync();
}
```

```csharp
using HoloDb.Client;

// Wraps the client with exponential backoff and a circuit breaker (compile-checked)
var resilient = await ResilientHoloDbClient.ConnectAsync(
    "db.example.com", 5433,
    retryDelay: TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(200),
    maxAttempts: 3,
    breakerFailureThreshold: 5);

// Retries transport failures; SQL and authentication errors are not retried
var result = await resilient.ExecuteAsync("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM data");
Console.WriteLine(result.RowCount);
```

```csharp
using HoloDb.Client;

// Pin the server certificate by thumbprint, for a self-hosted server (compile-checked)
var options = new HoloDbClientOptions
{
    AuthToken = "your-token",
    UseTls = true,
    PinnedThumbprint = "ABC123DEF456",
};
var client = await HoloDbClient.ConnectAsync("localhost", 5433, options);
await client.DisposeAsync();
```

##### Things to know

- One client is one session: Requests serialize through an internal queue, and concurrent callers share the same TCP connection. Use one client per worker, or a pool.
- No automatic reconnect: A dropped socket raises an exception, and you reconnect explicitly. ResilientHoloDbClient does this for you when you use it.
- Transient and application errors differ: HoloRemoteException (SQL errors, authentication failures) is not retried. The resilient client retries only transport failures such as IOException and SocketException.
- NULL: Write NULL as the literal NULL in the SQL text. Read it with IsNull(row, col) or GetValue(row, col). A result that holds a NULL is row-form, so the typed GetLong and GetText accessors are for columnar results only. Bulk loads are dense arrays and carry no NULL.
- No parameterised Execute: The client takes SQL text. Use HoloDb.Database.Bind(sql, args) to build the text from values.
- Timeouts: ConnectAsync takes a TimeSpan for the connection only. The resilient client adds an operation timeout to every method, a budget across all its retries.

##### The wire protocol

HoloDb.Protocol defines how the server and client communicate. Instead of sending results as JSON or row objects it keeps the columnar shape: a long[], double[] or string[] travels as a typed array. That keeps the engine's columnar advantage intact when data moves between processes. You normally get the package through HoloDb.Client (version range 1.5.*). Depend on it directly, as EvaluatedApplications.HoloDb.Protocol with the version range 1.1.*, only to implement a server.

The wire format is stable: opcode byte values never change, and field order and types are fixed. Clients and servers from different builds negotiate a version and fail cleanly when incompatible.

- SQL NULL: A NULL cell travels as its own tag and reaches the client as DBNull.Value (QueryResult.IsNull), never as an empty string.
- Length-prefixed TCP framing: Safe message boundaries, with frame size limits and count bounds checks that stop a hostile length prefix from forcing a huge allocation.
- Binary columnar codec: Typed long, double and string arrays in little-endian format. Non-columnar results (joins, GROUP BY) are packed in a compact binary row format.
- Request and response dispatch: Opcodes for Hello (handshake), Exec (SQL), BulkLoad, Stats and Ping.
- Error semantics: Protocol errors (corrupt or malformed bytes) are distinct from query errors (bad SQL, a constraint violation), so a caller knows whether to retry.
- Transport-agnostic: It works over TCP, TLS or any duplex Stream. The protocol provides no encryption: TLS is the transport layer's job, and the authentication token travels in the Hello handshake as UTF-8, so run it over TLS.

A columnar query returns column arrays, not rows. If you expect row-by-row iteration, read the columns by position as above, or use Rows to materialise dictionaries.

```csharp
using HoloDb.Client;

// Reading a columnar result without row unpacking (compile-checked here; it needs a server to run)
await using var client = await HoloDbClient.ConnectAsync("localhost", 5433, new HoloDbClientOptions { AuthToken = "mytoken" });
var result = await client.ExecuteAsync("SELECT id, price FROM prices");

if (result.IsColumnar)
{
    // column 0 is a long, column 1 is a double
    for (int r = 0; r < result.RowCount; r++)
        Console.WriteLine($"ID {result.GetLong(r, 0)}: price {result.GetDouble(r, 1)}");
}
```

```csharp
using HoloDb;
using HoloDb.Protocol;

// A server loop built on the wire protocol (compile-checked here; it needs a connected stream to run)
async Task HandleOneRequest(Stream networkStream, HoloDbService engine, CancellationToken ct)
{
    var payload = await Wire.ReadFrameAsync(networkStream, ct);
    var request = HoloProtocol.DecodeRequest(payload);

    if (request.Op == WireOp.Exec)
    {
        var result = await engine.ExecuteAsync(request.Sql);
        var response = HoloProtocol.Result(result);
        await Wire.WriteFrameAsync(networkStream, response, ct);
    }
}
Console.WriteLine(nameof(HandleOneRequest));
```
