### AlgFormer: a transformer engine for .NET

Train and run language models in plain C#. The holographic attention core reads long prompts in a fraction of the time.

Page: https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/algformer/
- Package EvaluatedApplications.AlgFormer, release 3.3.0: `dotnet add package EvaluatedApplications.AlgFormer`
- Package EvaluatedApplications.AlgFormer.Gpu, release 1.12.0: `dotnet add package EvaluatedApplications.AlgFormer.Gpu`
- Builds on: EvalApp, Phasor
- Used by: Prism, Prose
- Tools: Prism, Prose

Train a language model in plain C#. Nothing else to install.

Define, train and run transformer models with no Python, no GPU and no native runtime. Pick classic attention, or the holographic core that reads long prompts in a fraction of the time.

- 26 times: less time to read a 1,984-token prompt with holographic attention
- 50 times: less time for each further token, which stays flat as the context grows
- 663 times: smaller serve cache, constant in the length of the context

AlgFormer is a .NET library for defining, training and running transformer-style language models. Give it a vocabulary and a shape, train it on your own token sequences through a data-parallel pipeline, and run inference as a single prediction, as full logits or as streaming generation with a cache.

It is a real, gradient-trained architecture written entirely in C# on double arrays with SIMD. It runs anywhere .NET runs, with no GPU, no Python and no native binary to ship. Most transformer tooling means binding into a native runtime such as ONNX, PyTorch or CUDA, or hand-rolling matrix code with no attention research behind it. AlgFormer sits between the two.

It also lets you compare two ideas of what attention should cost. Softmax attention scores every token against every other token, which is quadratic in the length. The holographic core composes context by binding, bundling and unbinding instead. The two cores are parameter for parameter comparable, so you can train the same shape on the same data with either.

Why use it:
- Two real cores, not a toy. AlgFormer (softmax dot-product attention, the well-understood baseline) and HoloFormer (holographic attention) share a model shape, a training loop, a checkpoint format and a serving API. You swap the core, not the workflow.
- No external ML runtime. Everything is plain double arrays and SIMD, compiled into your app. There is no ONNX Runtime, no libtorch, no CUDA toolkit and no Python interop.
- Attention that scales differently. HoloFormer reads a prompt in time that grows with its length rather than its square, and serves each further token at a constant cost through an incremental cache. That matters when context windows get long. The chart above measures both cores.
- Everything needed to use it. A subword tokenizer, a data-parallel trainer, streaming generation with a cache, checkpoints with format versioning, and helpers that grow a trained model to a longer context or a bigger vocabulary without retraining from scratch.
- Built for swarm training. Relay components let several machines train one shared model over MQTT, exchanging either full batches or lightweight position manifests.

Capabilities:
- Two comparable attention cores. AlgFormer (softmax) and HoloFormer (holographic resonance), built from the same shape parameters.
- Pure managed implementation. double arrays and SIMD, with no external ML runtime, no native dependency and no GPU required.
- Data-parallel training. A resource-gated, adaptively tuned pipeline for full epochs over your data, built on EvalApp.
- Streaming inference. An incremental cache for low-latency generation. HoloFormer's cache holds one running holographic memory per layer, so each token costs the same however long the context is.
- Checkpoints that keep loading. Save and load with backward-compatible format versioning, so old checkpoints keep loading as the format evolves.
- Growth in place. Extend the context length, the attention shifts or the vocabulary of a trained model without starting again.
- Sizing from a measured law. HoloShape chooses model dimensions from measured trade-offs. HoloShape.Derive turns a single width into a starting set of shifts, context length and layers.
- Tokenizer and data sources. A built-in subword tokenizer and ready-made adapters for raw corpus windows, prompt and answer pairs and source mixing.
- Distributed training. Relay components over MQTT, from full-model relay to a data-free relay of position manifests.
- Preference training. Direct preference optimisation on the CPU HoloFormer: sequence log-probability over a chosen span, an exact clone for the frozen reference model, a signed per-sequence weighted all-positions step and a helper that returns the loss and the two weights.
- Gradient-check oracles. Built-in checks let you verify the training maths instead of assuming it is right.
- ADAM and EVE. An opt-in, per-layer Adam gate for HoloFormer that nudges a layer's update toward a norm range derived from the codebook. It is off unless you enable it through HoloFormer.EveOptions.

Quick start:

```csharp
using PrismFormer;

// Define a model. Tokens are ints; bring your own tokenizer or encoding.
var model = new AlgFormer(vocab: 16, shifts: 4, layers: 2, maxContext: 6, dModel: 32, frozenPrefix: 0);

// Train on (context tokens, target token) pairs.
var data = new List<(int[] Ctx, int Target)>
{
    (new[] { 1, 2, 3 }, 4),
    (new[] { 2, 3, 4 }, 5),
};
var trainer = new PrismTrainer(model);                 // data-parallel, run through EvalApp
double loss = trainer.TrainEpoch(data, batchSize: 2, lr: 5e-2, shuffleSeed: 1);

// Run inference.
var context = new[] { 1, 2, 3 };
int next        = model.Predict(context);                                    // argmax next token
double[] logits = model.LogitsFor(context);                                  // full logits
int[] generated = model.Generate(context, maxNewTokens: 5, temperature: 0.8, seed: 1);

Console.WriteLine($"loss={loss:F3} next={next} logits.Length={logits.Length} generated=[{string.Join(",", generated)}]");
```

Output:

```text
loss=2.776 next=4 logits.Length=16 generated=[3,1,7,12,10]
```

Limits:
- The two cores share an API, not a behaviour. HoloFormer's capacity is set by its shape: a bundle holds a limited number of items cleanly, and HoloShape reports how many. A context longer than that reads back less cleanly.
- A shift count of 1 collapses the relation bank to a per-position diagonal and attention breaks. Keep at least two shifts and shrink the width or the layer count instead.
- A single model instance is not safe for concurrent training steps. Serving is read-only and safe to call from several threads on a model that is not changing, but a cache belongs to one generation on one thread.
- HoloFormer's serve-time knobs (Iters, IterAlphaServe, IterClean and IterTau) are not saved in a checkpoint. Set them again after loading.
- Step returns false when it drops a batch because the gradient was not finite. Check the result, or watch SkippedSteps, in a long training run.
- The ADAM and EVE gate is exercised in training only through AlgFormer.Gpu. On the CPU trainer it is covered by checks and has not been run as a training loop.
- The package ships as a binary with no source. It depends on Phasor and EvalApp, and the swarm relay uses MQTTnet.

#### How HoloFormer works (https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/algformer/holoformer/)

Attention that stays fast as the context grows.

HoloFormer folds everything it has read into one running memory per layer. Reading a prompt grows with its length instead of its square, and each new word costs the same however long the context is.

- 26 times: less time to read a 1,984-token prompt with holographic attention
- 50 times: less time for each further token, which stays flat as the context grows
- 663 times: smaller serve cache, constant in the length of the context

HoloFormer is the holographic attention core in AlgFormer. This page explains it in plain terms: how a token is stored, how ideas are combined, how the model thinks longer and how it remembers a whole context in one place. Each idea ends by naming the part of the model it describes.

##### A token is a chord

Give the model a letter, a word or a number and it writes it down as a chord: a particular stack of pure tones played together. Each tone is one channel of a complex-valued vector, and the chord is the whole vector. One word is one chord and another word is another.

How many tones can a chord stack? That is the size of the instrument. A small instrument has few strings, so chords blur into one another and the model cannot tell things apart. A bigger instrument keeps chords crisp and distinct.

- In the model: The tones are the channels, set by dModel when you construct the model. More channels keep meanings distinct.

##### Combining is playing together

The model has essentially one core move. To join two things it plays their chords together, and they merge into a single new chord. That is how a word is tied to its role, or a question to its subject.

Numbers are chords tuned so that playing two of them together adds their values. The chord for 5 played with the chord for 3 decodes as 8. The arithmetic is in the sound itself, so the model does not have to memorise a times table the way an ordinary transformer would. The program below is the Phasor codec that supplies the chords.

```csharp
using Phasor;

// Encode a number and some symbols
double[] five = PhasorCodec.Encode("5");
double[] three = PhasorCodec.Encode("3");
double[] age = PhasorCodec.Encode("age");
double[] name = PhasorCodec.Encode("name");
double[] hello = PhasorCodec.Encode("hello");

// Bind two numbers: adds them on the linear band
double[] fivePlusThree = PhasorCodec.Bind(five, three);
Console.WriteLine($"5 + 3 = {PhasorCodec.DecodeSum(fivePlusThree, max: 10)}");

// Bind each value to a role, bundle the pairs into one record, then unbind a role to read its value back
double[] record = PhasorCodec.Bundle(PhasorCodec.Bind(age, five), PhasorCodec.Bind(name, hello));
double[] ageField = PhasorCodec.Unbind(record, age);
Console.WriteLine($"age field matches 5 better than 3: {PhasorCodec.Correlate(ageField, five) > PhasorCodec.Correlate(ageField, three)}");

// For larger workloads and similarity search, HoloCodec is SIMD and configurable in width
var codec = new HoloCodec(dim: 1024);
double[] encoded = codec.Encode("hello");
Console.WriteLine($"HoloCodec self-similarity is positive: {HoloCodec.Dot(encoded, codec.Encode("hello")) > 0}");
```

Output:

```text
5 + 3 = 8
age field matches 5 better than 3: True
HoloCodec self-similarity is positive: True
```

##### Chord moves

Stacking chords is not enough. The model also has to transform them, steering a question toward its answer. It does this with a small set of learned moves, each of which blends in tones from elsewhere on the instrument.

More moves let it express richer relationships. The moves are spread across the instrument rather than only nudging neighbouring strings, so it can connect distant ideas and not only adjacent notes. At least two are needed: with one move every tone only ever reads itself, and nothing can route between tones.

- In the model: The moves are the shifts of the relation bank, spread by golden-ratio spacing so a few of them cover the whole range. HoloShape.ShiftsFor chooses how many a given context needs.

##### A chain of arrangers

The sound is not shaped all at once. It flows through several stages in a row, and each stage restyles it with its own set of moves before handing it on, the way a melody passes through a chain of arrangers.

- In the model: The stages are the layers. Depth is how many times the sound is reworked.

##### Play it through twice

Thinking, for this model, is replaying. Each stage can play its part again over what it just laid down, and only then hand the sound on. The first pass sketches and the second develops the sketch.

Replaying costs no extra parameters, because the same stage is simply applied again. The model can think harder about a short input by playing it through more times, and a newly added stage can be eased in by letting its replay weight start at zero and ramp up.

- In the model: The repeats are the K weight-tied iterations of each layer (the StackIter family), with a per-layer alpha that ramps a new layer in.

##### One shared sound you tune into

This is where HoloFormer parts company with an ordinary transformer. A transformer makes every position compare itself with every earlier position: a crowded room in which everyone talks to everyone, and the effort grows with the square of the conversation.

HoloFormer folds everything it has heard into one running sound per layer. Each position binds its key to its value and adds the result to the bundle. To recall something, the query is unbound from the bundle: the matching part rings out and the rest averages toward silence, like finding one station on a radio dial.

One bundle holds the whole context, so reading a prompt grows with its length rather than its square, and each new token costs the same however long the context has become. The chart on the overview page measures both cores. The held memory can also be listened to: the inspectors read off what the final query resonated with and decode it to tokens.

- In the model: This is holographic memory: retrieval by resonance instead of every-position-to-every-position comparison. The incremental cache of this core is one running bundle per layer.

##### How much one sound can hold

Many bound pairs summed into one vector crosstalk: each read comes back with a little noise from all the others. A bundle can therefore hold a limited number of items cleanly. HoloShape reports two numbers for a shape. The crosstalk edge is the number of shifts times the width, halved. The clean capacity is the number of tokens that read back at least 90 percent clean, which is about 12 percent of the edge.

Models are sized so that the context sits at a chosen fraction of the edge, and the default is a quarter. At a width of 128, HoloShape derives a context of 2,048 tokens. The crosstalk edge there is 8,192 tokens and 983 tokens read back clean. The constants behind the derived shapes are single measurements, so treat the shape as a starting point.

```csharp
using PrismFormer;

int ctx = 64, dim = 32;
int shifts = HoloShape.ShiftsFor(ctx, dim);                       // the normal way to choose Shifts
bool collides = HoloShape.ShiftsCollide(shifts, dim, golden: true);
Console.WriteLine($"ShiftsFor({ctx},{dim}) = {shifts}, collides = {collides}");
Console.WriteLine($"bind rank {HoloShape.BindRank(shifts, dim)}, reads back clean {HoloShape.CleanCapacity(shifts, dim)}");

// A starting shape from a width alone. Treat it as a place to begin, not a guarantee.
foreach (var width in new[] { 64, 128, 256 })
{
    var s = HoloShape.Derive(width, stackK: 2);
    Console.WriteLine($"Derive({width}): shifts {s.Shifts}, context {s.Context}, layers {s.Layers}");
}
```

Output:

```text
ShiftsFor(64,32) = 16, collides = False
bind rank 256, reads back clean 30
Derive(64): shifts 64, context 512, layers 3
Derive(128): shifts 128, context 2048, layers 6
Derive(256): shifts 256, context 8192, layers 8
```

##### Side by side with an ordinary transformer

An ordinary transformer memorises the music. This one plays it.

##### Try it

The holographic core takes the same constructor as the softmax core. This program trains one, serves it through the incremental cache and reads what its final query resonated with.

```csharp
using PrismFormer;

// The holographic core has the same constructor shape. Swap the type, keep the workflow.
var holo = new HoloFormer(vocab: 16, shifts: 4, layers: 2, maxContext: 6, dModel: 32, frozenPrefix: 0);

var data = new List<(int[] Ctx, int Target)>
{
    (new[] { 1, 2, 3 }, 4),
    (new[] { 2, 3, 4 }, 5),
};
double loss = holo.TrainEpoch(data, batchSize: 2, lr: 5e-2, shuffleSeed: 1);

// Serve with the incremental cache: one running holographic memory per layer, so each token costs the same
// however long the context has become.
var cache = holo.NewCache();
double[] afterPrompt = holo.Prime(cache, new[] { 1, 2, 3 });
double[] afterNext = holo.Step(cache, 4);

// Read the model's mind: the resonance of the final query against every earlier position, and what it retrieved.
var alpha = new double[holo.Layers]; Array.Fill(alpha, 1.0);
int[] toks = { 1, 2, 3 };
double[][] resonance = holo.InspectAttention(toks, K: 2, alpha);
double[] retrieved = holo.InspectRetrieval(toks, K: 2, alpha);
double[] decoded = holo.DecodeFace(retrieved);          // per-token logits for what the query pulled out

Console.WriteLine($"loss={loss:F3} cache length={cache.Length} logits lengths {afterPrompt.Length},{afterNext.Length}");
Console.WriteLine($"resonance rows={resonance.Length}, positions per row={resonance[0].Length}, decoded logits={decoded.Length}");
```

Output:

```text
loss=2.777 cache length=4 logits lengths 16,16
resonance rows=4, positions per row=3, decoded logits=16
```
