### Prism: decode gate, lineage journal and growth for AlgFormer models

A model that remembers how it grew. A confidence-gated decoder and a journal of every change, behind the Prism chat tool.

Page: https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/prism/
- Package EvaluatedApplications.Prism, release 1.3.4: `dotnet add package EvaluatedApplications.Prism`
- Builds on: AlgFormer
- Tools: Prism

A model that remembers how it grew.

Prism picks each next word by how confident the model is, records every time you grow the model, and works out how it stood at any past round. It is the code behind the Prism chat in your browser.

- 30,400: checks that the decode gate matches the hand-written code it replaced, with zero mismatches
- 19.5 ms: to open a journal of 50,000 events, far more than a real model records

Prism is the NuGet package that the Prism chat tool runs on. It holds three things for a model built on AlgFormer: the decode policy that chooses each next token, a lineage journal that records how the model grew, and a growth surface that changes the model and writes that record for you.

Why use it:
- One decode policy. Commit greedily when the model is confident, otherwise sample only from what clears the floor. The gate is one tested policy with an explicit floor mode: a resonance floor for the holographic core, no floor, or nucleus sampling.
- Facts about the past stay facts. Every structural change is stamped with the parameters a later calculation needs, when it happens. Questions such as how ramped a layer is, or when the model last grew, are answered from that history and never from whatever a live constant holds today.
- Growth that records itself. Growing context, layers, shifts or vocabulary through the growth surface stamps the journal automatically, so a model cannot grow without the record.

Capabilities:
- Lineage journal. Idempotent append, so a resumed process stamping the same event again is a no-op. Derivations AlphaAt, DepthAt, LastGrowthRound and AddRoundOf resolve against the stamped history, including layers inserted at the front.
- Storage seam. A file-backed JSONL store with durable append, and a pure in-memory store for browser and WebAssembly hosts that have no file system.
- Growth surface. Grow a HoloFormer's context, layers, shifts or vocabulary, correct by construction, with the lineage stamped for you.
- Decode policy and gate. DecodePolicy, Gate and GateDecision implement the confidence-gated decode with an explicit FloorMode.
- Degeneration guard. DegenGuard fires on a run of repeated tokens or a run of non-greedy picks, the two signs that decoding has collapsed.

Licence: Commercial licence for commercial use. Evaluation and non-commercial use are permitted. Terms at https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/licence/

### Prose: a grammar-driven corpus generator for .NET

Three novels in, nearly two thousand checked new sentences out. Mines grammar into HoloDb and recombines it into text and question and answer pairs.

Page: https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/prose/
- Package EvaluatedApplications.Prose, release 1.4.0: `dotnet add package EvaluatedApplications.Prose`
- Builds on: EvalApp, HoloDb, AlgFormer
- Tools: Prose

Three novels in. Nearly two thousand checked new sentences out.

Prose reads your text through the rules of grammar, keeps what it learns in HoloDb and recombines it into new sentences and question and answer pairs. Every sentence is re-parsed before you get it.

- 8,232: sentences mined from three public-domain novels
- 1,966: different sentences from one call that asked for 2,000
- 1,966 of 1,966: passed the grammar gate on a fresh parse: a real subject, a finite verb and agreement
- 1,966 of 1,966: used only words the corpus contains. Nothing imaginary

Prose reads plain text through the rules of grammar, keeps what it learns in a HoloDb database, and recombines that knowledge into new sentences that are grammatical, use words suited to their slots and read plausibly. It exists to grow a training corpus. Mine the grammatical knowledge already in your text, which nouns, verbs and adjectives go together and how, then generate more of it, along with question and answer pairs for reading-comprehension training data.

Language models need volume and variety of grammatically correct text. Writing or scraping more does not scale, and most data augmentation either pastes fragments together ungrammatically or needs a large model of its own. Prose takes a different route. It parses real text into its grammatical structure with deterministic rules, stores what nouns, verbs and adjectives actually go with, and recombines those observed pieces into fresh sentences that are checked to parse correctly before they are written out.

Why use it:
- Rules first, not model first. Parsing, mining and generation all run on deterministic grammar rules with no training. An optional small language model can rank candidates by plausibility, but Prose falls back to pure rules and never depends on a model to produce correct output.
- No word is locked to one role. The same surface form resolves to a noun or a verb by context, the way a reader who has learned grammar reads it. In the classic example, the panda eats shoots and leaves parses as one verb with two objects, while the panda eats, shoots, and leaves parses as three verbs. Same words: the punctuation and structure alone flip the reading.
- Nothing imaginary. Every open-class word Prose emits is a form it observed in the source text, and it never invents an inflection. Generated sentences are re-parsed and checked by a validity gate (a real subject, a finite verb, subject and verb agreement, article and noun agreement) before they are kept. Question and answer pairs are checked the same way on both sides.
- Real grammatical structure. Beyond simple subject, verb and object sentences, Prose mines and generates indirect objects (gave him a book), relative clauses (the panda that eats bamboo) and multi-sentence passages in which later sentences refer back to earlier ones by name or pronoun, the long-context structure comprehension training needs.

Capabilities:
- Parse. Sentence splitting, part-of-speech tagging, phrase chunking and role assignment (subject, verb, objects, indirect object, predicate, relative clauses) with zero training and no external model.
- Mine. Scans a corpus and builds a lexicon plus selectional tables: which subjects go with which verbs, which verbs take which objects and which adjectives modify which nouns. They are stored in a HoloDb database.
- Generate. Samples a sentence shape from the mined patterns (simple, transitive, ditransitive, copular, with optional relative clauses), fills each slot with an observed, agreement-correct word, and keeps only sentences that re-parse validly.
- Plausibility scoring. Optional. A small language model ranks generated candidates so the output reads more sensibly, without weakening the grammatical guarantee.
- Question and answer generation. Turns generated sentences into context, question and answer triples, including multi-sentence passages with coreference and self-referential two-turn dialogues.
- Corpus and TSV export. Write generated sentences straight to text files, or question and answer pairs to a prompt and target TSV, ready for a language model's training data.

Quick start:

```csharp
using Prose;

var prose = new ProseEngine();
prose.MineText("The wise king rules the peaceful kingdom. The kingdom is calm. " +
               "The king gives the poor man a book. The man reads the book. " +
               "The dog chases the red ball. The dog barks. The sky is blue. " +
               "The queen sends the man a letter. The queen is kind.");

foreach (var sentence in prose.Generate(5, seed: 1))
    Console.WriteLine(sentence);
```

Output:

```text
A king rules the peaceful kingdom.
The peaceful ball barks.
A queen sends the letter.
A book chases the ball.
The peaceful kingdom rules the wise kingdom.
```

Limits:
- A small corpus recombines freely. Below 500 mined sentences generation falls back to the whole part-of-speech pool, so pairings need not have been seen. From 500 sentences on it draws only from pairings the tables contain.
- Grammatical is not the same as meaningful. The output is built from observed pairings and checked for form, and it can still say odd things. The optional scorer ranks candidates, and correct output never depends on it.
- Relative clauses are handled for subject relatives. Object relatives and non-restrictive relatives are not.
- Generation is deterministic for a seed. Parallel generation uses a fixed number of shards, so it is also deterministic across machines, but it draws a different sequence from the sequential path.
- It depends on HoloDb, which holds the mined tables, and on AlgFormer, which supplies the optional scorer. Installing the package brings both in.
- The package ships as a binary with no source.

Licence: Commercial licence for commercial use. Evaluation and non-commercial use are permitted. Terms at https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/licence/

### HoloGenome: DNA as a hologram of measured helix physics for .NET

Turn DNA into a vector that winds like the real helix, then check it against laboratory measurements it never saw. The wins and the losses are published.

Page: https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/hologenome/
- Package EvaluatedApplications.HoloGenome, release 0.1.1: `dotnet add package EvaluatedApplications.HoloGenome`
- Builds on: Phasor, HoloDb
- Tools: The Helix

Turn DNA into a vector that winds like the real helix.

HoloGenome reads a stretch of A, C, G and T and gives you one fixed-width vector. Its phase turns by the measured twist of each base pair step, so the order along the helix is in the vector. Then it is graded against laboratory measurements it never saw, with the losses published beside the wins.

- 10.48 to 10.51: bases per turn found by a small model that was never told the helical period, on four independent libraries (the crystallographic value is 10.534)
- 0.529 vs 0.483: correlation with held-out bendability using the measured twist of each base pair step, against one constant twist
- 0.600: correlation with held-out bendability once the local-shape layer is added, against 0.253 for counts of short words
- 0.28 to 0.39: behind the best trained network, DNAcycP, on every library where it has published scores (0.93, 0.77 and 0.89 against 0.54, 0.50 and 0.60)

A stretch of DNA becomes one list of phase angles. Each base is a Phasor symbol. As you move along the sequence a carrier phase advances by the measured twist of each pair of neighbouring bases (the published table of Olson et al. 1998), so the vector records how the real double helix winds, not just which letters are present.

An optional second layer adds local shape (minor-groove width, propeller twist, roll, helix twist) from a pentamer table you supply, weighted in as extra signal beside the helical phase. Everything is bound and summed into a single fixed-width vector.

Why use it:
- Each base is a Phasor symbol. The encoder uses the Phasor codec, so a window is one vector you can bind, sum, store and compare by dot product like any other Phasor value.
- The carrier follows the measured twist. The phase advances by the measured twist of each pair of neighbouring bases, taken from a published table that is built in. The vector records how the helix winds along the window.
- Shape is optional and yours. Supply a pentamer table and its minor-groove, propeller-twist, roll and helix-twist values are weighted in beside the helical phase. No third-party shape data ships in the package.
- Nothing in the encoding is invented. Each number comes from a cited measurement. The one constant twist of {constantDegrees} degrees exists only as the sequence-blind control.

Capabilities:
- GenomeEncoder. Encode(window) gives the fixed-width vector, EncodeWindow(sequence, start, length) encodes a window and uses the bases outside it only as shape context, and HelixPhases(window) returns the cumulative helix angle along the window.
- Twist models. OlsonTwist is the measured table, with all six step parameters per pair of bases. ConstantTwist is the sequence-blind control. Setting no twist model turns the helix off.
- Local-shape layer. PentamerShapeTable loads or parses a table you supply, falls back to the reverse complement when a pentamer is missing, and counts the misses. Nothing from a third-party shape table is in the package.
- Window store. GenomeWindowStore keeps windows in a HoloDb table with ordinary SQL columns beside the hologram: bulk and atomic puts, reads by id, and float32 packing.
- Strict input. Dna.Normalise accepts A, C, G and T and throws on anything else. Reverse complement and complement helpers are included.

Quick start:

```csharp
using HoloDb;
using HoloGenome;

var encoder = new GenomeEncoder(new GenomeEncoderOptions { Dim = 512, Twist = OlsonTwist.Instance });
string seq = "ATGCGTACGTTAGCAAAAATTTTTGCGCGATCGATCGTAGCTAGCTAGCA";
double[] h = encoder.Encode(seq);

// How many turns does the helix make along this sequence?
Console.WriteLine($"{h.Length} reals; helix turns: {encoder.HelixPhases(seq)[^1] / (2 * Math.PI):F2}");

// The mean measured twist gives the helical repeat.
double sum = 0;
foreach (char a in "ACGT") foreach (char b in "ACGT") sum += OlsonTwist.Instance.TwistDegrees(a, b);
Console.WriteLine($"{360 / (sum / 16):F4} bases per turn");

// Store the window beside ordinary SQL columns and read it back.
var store = new GenomeWindowStore(new HoloDbService(new HoloDbOptions()));
store.Put([new GenomeWindow(1, "demo", 0, seq, h)]);
Console.WriteLine(store.Get(1)!.Sequence == seq);
```

Output:

```text
512 reals; helix turns: 4.68
10.5340 bases per turn
True
```

When another tool fits better:
- You need the most accurate bendability predictor. Use DNAcycP, which is trained for exactly that and scores far higher on Loop-seq.
- You need shape tracks for a whole genome. Use a dedicated shape predictor such as DNAshapeR; HoloGenome only reads a table of shape values you load.
- You need alignment, variant calling or annotation. HoloGenome is not an aligner or a caller. It encodes windows of sequence for physical comparison.
- You need clinical or consumer results. It makes no health, disease-risk, drug-response or ancestry claims.

Limits:
- Sequences must be A, C, G and T. Anything else is rejected, not guessed.
- The hologram is an unnormalised sum, so compare windows of equal length.
- The encoding is strand-specific: a sequence and its reverse complement give different vectors (cosine 0.23 for the example above).
- Stored holograms are float32, exact to about 6e-8 relative error.
- All grading so far uses one kind of measurement (Loop-seq bendability in yeast-derived and random sequence). Nothing is claimed for other organisms, other assays or chromatin in the living cell.
- The graded scores on this page (the linear readout, the zero-parameter helical score and the fitted phasor models) come from a research harness and are not in the shipped package. The package ships the encoder, the twist tables and the window store.
- The shape layer was graded with a pentamer table from the DNAshapeR project. That table is not shipped because its licence does not allow it, so you load your own.
- The Loop-seq data is not redistributed with the package.
- Early-stage package: the public surface may change.

Licence: Commercial licence for commercial use. Evaluation and non-commercial use are permitted. Terms at https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/licence/

### Tracer: pathfinding and game AI for .NET

Send a whole crowd to one exit with a single search. Navmesh pathfinding with dynamic obstacles, line of sight and combat.

Page: https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/tracer/
- Package EvaluatedApplications.Tracer, release 2.0.2: `dotnet add package EvaluatedApplications.Tracer`
- Builds on: EvalApp
- Tools: Doctrine, Prism

Send a whole crowd to one exit with a single search.

Bake a navmesh, route single agents or whole swarms across it, close a doorway mid-game and watch the crowd find another way. Line of sight, fog of war and combat are in the same package.

- 14 of 14: agents given a path in one swarm tick on the recorded level
- 14 of 14: still given a path after a doorway is closed
- 12 of 14: agents that took a new route around the closed doorway
- 2: goals for 14 agents. Agents that share a goal share one solve

Tracer is a pathfinding and game-AI SDK for real-time simulations with many moving agents: crowds, RTS-style unit groups and tactical squads. It bakes triangle navmeshes, routes single agents and whole swarms across them, reacts to obstacles that appear or vanish mid-game, and adds the game-AI toolkit around pathfinding: line of sight, fog of war, influence maps and combat engagement.

Why use it:
- A swarm that shares a goal shares the work. Agents that share a goal share one guidance solve. In a measured 500-agent tick on a 1,152-triangle mesh, a shared goal with a bounded conflict radius took about 3.8 ms against about 22 ms for 500 distinct goals. Adaptive path budgeting keeps large swarms inside a frame-time budget under pressure.
- Obstacles change without a re-bake. Block and unblock regions of a baked mesh while the game runs. The mesh handle is immutable, so you swap the new one in between ticks.
- Everything around the path. Line of sight, fog of war, influence maps, congestion analysis, steering behaviors and combat resolution ship in the same SDK, on the same pipeline runtime.

Capabilities:
- Navmesh baking. Turn triangle geometry into a queryable navmesh, with obstacle-polygon exclusion and an optional hierarchical bake for large levels, or layered meshes for ground, air and water.
- Single and multi-agent paths. One-shot smoothed paths, batches in parallel, or a swarm tick where agents with the same goal reuse one solve.
- Dynamic obstacles. Block and unblock circular zones of a baked mesh at runtime without a full bake.
- Line of sight, fog of war, influence maps. Visibility and area-control queries for perception and decision-making, with congestion analysis alongside.
- Combat engagement. Spatially hashed attacker and defender resolution with pluggable damage, dodge and block formulas.
- Steering behaviors. Seek, Wander, Patrol, Flee, Queue and FlowLane, composed through a fluent navigator builder.
- Grid tactics. A separate bake-free lane for tile games: line of sight, movement range, cover and target selection over any tilemap.
- Adaptive budgeting and populations. Cluster large agent counts and path only representatives when the frame budget is tight, or run several named populations under one shared budget.

Quick start:

```csharp
using System.Numerics;
using Tracer;
using Tracer.Models;

var world = new PathfindingWorld();

// A 6x4 room with a wall down the middle and a doorway in it.
// Two triangles per walkable cell; vertices sit on the integer lattice.
var vertices = new List<Vector2>();
var triangles = new List<(int A, int B, int C)>();
var lattice = new Dictionary<(int, int), int>();
int V(int x, int y)
{
    if (!lattice.TryGetValue((x, y), out var i)) { i = vertices.Count; lattice[(x, y)] = i; vertices.Add(new(x, y)); }
    return i;
}
for (int y = 0; y < 4; y++)
    for (int x = 0; x < 6; x++)
    {
        bool wall = x == 3 && y != 1;           // the doorway is the cell (3, 1)
        if (wall) continue;
        triangles.Add((V(x, y), V(x + 1, y), V(x + 1, y + 1)));
        triangles.Add((V(x, y), V(x + 1, y + 1), V(x, y + 1)));
    }

var mesh = await world.CreateNavMeshBakerService().BakeAsync(vertices, triangles);
Console.WriteLine($"triangles: {mesh.TriangleCount}");

// One smoothed path.
var path = await world.CreateSingleAgentService()
    .QueryPathAsync(mesh, new Vector2(0.5f, 3.5f), new Vector2(5.5f, 3.5f));
Console.WriteLine($"single path: {path.Count} waypoints, ends at {path[^1]}");

// A swarm sharing one goal is solved once.
var goal = new Vector2(5.5f, 0.5f);
var agents = Enumerable.Range(1, 3)
    .Select(i => new AgentDto(Id: i, Position: new Vector2(0.5f, i - 0.5f), Goal: goal, GoalChanged: true))
    .ToList();
var tick = await world.CreateMultiAgentService().TickAsync(agents, mesh, tickNumber: 0);
Console.WriteLine($"swarm: {tick.Paths.Count(p => p.PathFound)} of {agents.Count} agents have a path");

// Close the doorway at runtime. No re-bake.
var blocked = await world.CreateDynamicObstacleService()
    .UpdateAsync(mesh, new[] { new NavMeshBlockedZone(Center: new Vector2(3.5f, 1.5f), Radius: 0.6f) });
var after = await world.CreateSingleAgentService("after")
    .QueryPathAsync(blocked, new Vector2(0.5f, 3.5f), new Vector2(5.5f, 3.5f));
Console.WriteLine($"doorway closed: path found = {after.Count > 0}");
```

Output:

```text
triangles: 42
single path: 4 waypoints, ends at <5.5, 3.5>
swarm: 3 of 3 agents have a path
doorway closed: path found = False
```

Limits:
- The navmesh is made of triangles, not tiles. A tile game bakes two triangles per walkable cell, or uses the bake-free tile lane.
- An unreachable or off-mesh goal never throws. A single query returns an empty list, and a swarm result reports that no path was found.
- Blocking a zone at runtime isolates triangles in place, so the triangle count does not change. Baking with blocked zones excludes them instead.
- Pressure is a meaningful signal only when a frame-time target is set.
- Swarm waypoints are shared guidance. On the level in the diagram they cut doorway corners by up to 0.50 of a cell; single-agent queries stay within 0.11 of a cell. Use single queries where exact corner clearance matters.
- Mesh handles are immutable and safe to read from any thread. Services that persist tuner state should not be driven concurrently under one service key.

Licence: Commercial licence for commercial use. Evaluation and non-commercial use are permitted. Terms at https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/licence/

### HoloVoxel: a level-of-detail-native voxel engine for .NET

Voxel worlds that stay crisp up close and cost almost nothing far away, with no mesh tiers and no popping.

Page: https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/holovoxel/
- Package EvaluatedApplications.HoloVoxel, release 1.5.2: `dotnet add package EvaluatedApplications.HoloVoxel`
- Builds on: Phasor

Crisp up close, cheap far away, and nothing ever pops.

Store each chunk of a voxel world once. Read it with a big budget near the viewer and a tiny one in the distance, and the detail fades smoothly. No mesh tiers to build, store or stitch.

- 98.4%: of cells decoded correctly with all 8,192 components
- 341 times: less hologram read at 24 components than at the full budget
- 189 times: less decode time at the smallest budget than at the full one

Most voxel engines store a world as arrays of blocks and fake distant detail with mesh simplification, mipmaps or detail popping. HoloVoxel stores a chunk of the world as one holographic superposition instead. Every voxel is bound as position and content and summed into a single vector, using the Phasor codec.

Reading a voxel back is a correlation against that vector, and correlating with fewer components gives a cheaper, fuzzier answer. Near the viewer, with the full budget, the correlation collapses to one crisp block. Far away, with a handful of components, the interference of every candidate block blends into a soft, continuous colour. The result is crisp near and soft far, with no discrete tiers of detail and no popping between them.

The engine also exposes a rendering signal. Decoded confidence, how unambiguous a read is, maps naturally to visual solidity, so a renderer can make distant, low-confidence terrain read as hazy while confident terrain stays solid. The number is computed here. Drawing it is up to your renderer.

Why use it:
- Level of detail is free. There is no simplified mesh to generate, store or stitch. The same hologram answers a near read and a far read, at whatever cost you choose to pay for that read.
- Memory follows perceived detail. A chunk stores only as many components as its level of detail will ever read back, and the first k components of a truncated hologram are bit-identical to reading the same chunk in full. Storage tracks the budget you plan to read at, not the size of the world.
- The blur is the data. Distant terrain looks soft because the engine has less information at that budget, not because a texture was downsampled. The same signal that saves compute drives the look.
- Plug into anything. No rendering or graphics dependency, and it is verified headless. You bring the renderer, the block palette and the world source, or use the built-in procedural generator.

Capabilities:
- Holographic chunk storage. HoloWorld and Chunk encode a chunk once and decode it at any component budget, as a colour field or as a triangulated surface mesh with analytic per-vertex normals.
- Continuous, meshless level of detail. The same stored hologram serves a crisp near view and a soft far view. Lod.Components maps a distance to a budget as a starting point.
- Field confidence for adaptive detail. FieldConfidence reports how unambiguous each decoded point is, the softmax margin between the winning material and its runner-up. Lod.AverageConfidence and Lod.AdaptiveComponents turn that into a budget that spends more only where the world is genuinely ambiguous.
- Spatial coarsening at distance. Far reads average over a footprint of the underlying world data, for terrain height and material, instead of sampling one noisy point. That keeps far terrain reading as smooth, coherent shapes. It is a separate knob from the component budget, and the two compound.
- Truncated holograms. Storage cost tracks the level of detail you plan to read at, not the size of the world.
- Fused SIMD bind and correlate. Generation and decode are allocation-free on the hot path.
- Entities too. HoloModel stores a creature or a prop the same holographic way, with the same level of detail and confidence, independent of the terrain grid.
- A built-in world generator. WorldGen offers biomes, height fields and an optional maze layout. Supply your own IWorldSource to skip it entirely.
- Ringworld warp. Ring is a pure flat-to-cylinder coordinate transform for cylindrical spaces, on top of the same flat chunk storage.

Quick start:

```csharp
using HoloVoxel.Core;

var world = new HoloWorld(seed: 2024);

// A near chunk at the full budget: crisp, one cell per surface column of a 16 by 16 chunk.
var near = world.GetChunk(0, 0).DecodeField(step: 1, components: world.Comps);
Console.WriteLine($"near: {near.Count} cells from {world.Comps} components, each {near[0].Size} wide");

// A distant chunk, decoded cheaply and fuzzily: coarse cells and a small budget.
var far = world.GetChunk(40, 0).DecodeField(step: 8, components: 40);
Console.WriteLine($"far: {far.Count} cells from 40 components, each {far[0].Size} wide");
```

Output:

```text
near: 256 cells from 8192 components, each 1 wide
far: 4 cells from 40 components, each 8 wide
```

Limits:
- This is the engine, not the renderer. It hands you decoded colour fields, meshes and confidence values. Shaders, GPU decode and a game-engine binding belong to your front end. A reference shading recipe (lighting from the mesh normals, ambient occlusion from the height field, confidence-driven haze) is a reference outside the package.
- Chunks are 16 columns on a side and that size is fixed. A full build stores four buried layers per column.
- Chunks only ever get finer. A chunk built coarse can be refined but never coarsened, and decoding at a step finer than the build is invalid.
- Call Prewarm once, on one thread, before any concurrent chunk work. After that, parallel generation and decode are lock-free.
- Accuracy checks and the argmax decode need a full build. Confidence is empty for a chunk whose first build was coarse and for a wall chunk.
- A read asking for fewer than eight components still reads eight.
- Entity voxels must stay inside 16 by 16 columns and 12 layers, or they alias another position.

Licence: Commercial licence for commercial use. Evaluation and non-commercial use are permitted. Terms at https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/licence/

### Blazier: lazy Blazor WebAssembly for static hosts

Blazor pages that read at once and download .NET only when a visitor presses Start, with long C# jobs in a Web Worker.

Page: https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/blazier/
- Package EvaluatedApplications.Blazier, release 1.1.0: `dotnet add package EvaluatedApplications.Blazier`
- Tools: Umbrarium, preset demo, Doctrine, The Helix, The Analyst, Prism, Prose, Council Spending Scanner

Show the page now. Download .NET when they press Start.

Blazier turns your Blazor WebAssembly pages into real HTML at publish time. Visitors read at once, and the .NET runtime downloads only when someone presses the button that needs it. Long C# jobs run in a Web Worker behind an ordinary interface.

- 6.8 KB: downloaded before the visitor does anything, against 2.8 MB when the same app boots the usual way
- 416 to 484 ms: until real content is on screen on the phone profile, against 13.2 to 15.5 s booting the usual way
- 14 to 19 ms: worst gap on the page's timers while a worker ran a long job, with 0 long tasks
- 0.49 to 0.57 ms: for one call to a worker service, round trip

Blazier is a publish step, a small loader and a worker bridge in one package. It hosts any Blazor WebAssembly app and needs no other Evaluated Applications package.

Why use it:
- Publish renders your pages. After dotnet publish, a small tool renders every BlazierPage component with Blazor's HtmlRenderer and writes it into your own index.html as path/index.html. Components see IBuildTime.IsPrerender as true while this happens.
- A tiny loader waits for intent. blazier.js is a classic script with no dependencies. On click (anywhere in the page or only on one chosen control), visibility, idle or immediately, it starts Blazor and mounts the component over the shell, keeping the shell on screen until the live one has rendered. A handshake from Blazor ties runtime start and mounting together, so mounting does not race the runtime.
- Islands are named components. Register them in UseBlazier; mark them in Razor with Island or in plain HTML with data-blazier-island. Each element reports its state (idle, booting, mounting, live, failed) for styling, and the page raises blazier events with byte and timing figures.
- Lazy assemblies are named in the project file. LazyIsland("chart", "Charts.PrimeChart, Charts", "Charts") mounts a component from an assembly that downloads on demand. After each build a guard walks the code reachable from startup and fails the build, naming the path, if it reaches a lazy-assembly type.
- The worker bridge is generated. A source generator turns a WorkerService interface into a page-side proxy and a worker-side dispatcher. The worker starts a second runtime from the files the page already downloaded. Calls, progress and streamed items are messages; arguments and results travel as JSON. A cancellation token cancels cooperatively. A job that never yields is stopped by terminating and restarting the worker after a grace period, and only that worker's calls fail.

Capabilities:
- Per-page head tags. Title and Description on the BlazierPage attribute replace the template's title and meta description in each shell. Set the BlazierSiteUrl property and every shell also gets a canonical link and Open Graph tags.
- On-intent loader. Boots Blazor on click, visibility, idle or immediately, keeps the static shell visible until the component has rendered, and mounts islands on a ready handshake from the runtime.
- Start on one control. Give a Click page a ClickTarget selector and only a click on that control starts the runtime, so a phone visitor who scrolls or taps text never downloads it.
- Islands. Several named components on one static page, each booting the one shared runtime on its own trigger. Island marks them in Razor, and data-blazier-island works in plain HTML.
- Build-time shells for pages that fetch. Inject IBuildTime and skip fetching when IsPrerender is true, or wrap the live part in NotAtBuildTime with a skeleton. A page that still tries to fetch fails the publish with BLZ102 instead of shipping an error message as static HTML.
- Lazy assemblies with a guard. LazyIsland mounts a component whose assembly downloads only on demand. After every build a guard fails with BLZ001, naming the path, if startup code reaches a lazy-assembly type.
- Typed worker bridge. Calls are awaitable, IProgress streams progress, IAsyncEnumerable streams results with backpressure, and a CancellationToken cancels cooperatively. A job that never yields is stopped by terminating and restarting the worker after a grace period.
- Same protocol in-process. BlazierWorker.StartInProcessAsync runs your services on a dedicated thread with the same messages, for unit tests and non-browser hosts.

Quick start:

Start from a Blazor WebAssembly project and turn on scaffolding in the project file.

```xml
<PropertyGroup>
  <BlazierScaffold>true</BlazierScaffold>
</PropertyGroup>
```

Load the loader in wwwroot/index.html instead of starting Blazor yourself. Keep the import map line.

```html
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="utf-8" />
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0" />
    <title>Hello</title>
    <base href="/" />
    <script type="importmap"></script>
</head>
<body>
    <div id="app" data-blazier-island="app" data-blazier-start="immediate">Loading...</div>
    <script src="_content/EvaluatedApplications.Blazier/blazier.js" defer></script>
</body>
</html>
```

Register your root component. HelloApp stands for your project's root namespace.

```csharp
using Blazier;
using HelloApp;
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.WebAssembly.Hosting;

var builder = WebAssemblyHostBuilder.CreateDefault(args);
builder.UseBlazier(b => b.App<App>());
await builder.Build().RunAsync();
```

Mark the page. The button is the only thing that starts the runtime.

```razor
@page "/hello"
@using Blazier
@attribute [BlazierPage("hello", Start = StartOn.Click, ClickTarget = "[data-blazier-go]",
    Title = "Hello", Description = "A page that is readable before any .NET code runs.")]
@inject IBuildTime Build

<h1>Hello</h1>
<p>This text is plain HTML. Reading it downloads no .NET runtime.</p>
<button type="button" data-blazier-go>Start</button>
@if (!Build.IsPrerender)
{
    <p>The runtime is running now.</p>
}
```

dotnet publish writes hello/index.html with the heading, text and button already in it. The runtime downloads when the button is pressed, then the live component replaces the shell.

```html
<div id="app" data-blazier-island="app" data-blazier-start="click" data-blazier-click-target="[data-blazier-go]"><h1>Hello</h1>
<p>This text is plain HTML. Reading it downloads no .NET runtime.</p>
<button type="button" data-blazier-go>Start</button></div>
<script src="_content/EvaluatedApplications.Blazier/blazier.js" defer></script>
```

A long job in a worker, behind an ordinary interface. The page awaits the call, shows progress and can cancel.

```csharp
using Blazier.Workers;

[WorkerService]
public interface IPrimes
{
    Task<int> CountAsync(int limit, IProgress<double> progress, CancellationToken cancellationToken);
}

public sealed class Primes : IPrimes
{
    public async Task<int> CountAsync(int limit, IProgress<double> progress, CancellationToken cancellationToken)
    {
        var slice = new CooperativeSlice();   // yields about every 12 ms so a cancel message can be read
        int count = 0;
        for (int n = 2; n <= limit; n++)
        {
            bool prime = true;
            for (int d = 2; d * d <= n; d++) if (n % d == 0) { prime = false; break; }
            if (prime) count++;
            if (slice.IsDue)
            {
                progress.Report((double)n / limit);
                await slice.YieldIfDueAsync(cancellationToken);
            }
        }
        return count;
    }
}

public static class PrimeDemo
{
    // Call from a button handler: the work runs in a Web Worker and the page stays responsive.
    public static async Task<int> RunAsync(Action<double> onProgress, CancellationToken cancellationToken)
    {
        await using var worker = await BlazierWorker.StartAsync();
        return await worker.Get<IPrimes>().CountAsync(5_000_000, new Progress<double>(onProgress), cancellationToken);
    }
}
```

The page project and the worker program both build against the published package. The block under hello/index.html is the body that dotnet publish wrote for this page. Running the worker needs a browser.

Every tool on this site is a Blazier page. Open any tool. Its page reads at once, and its roughly 11 MB runtime downloads only when you press Start. Scrolling, tapping text or following a link downloads nothing.

What exists today:
- Typed Web Worker bridge (built). Awaitable calls, IProgress, IAsyncEnumerable with backpressure, cooperative and hard cancellation, restart, and an in-process mode that speaks the same protocol for unit tests. It has been run in headless Edge against the sample app. It has not been run in Firefox or Safari, and its phone memory and battery cost are not measured. Arguments are JSON text; there is no binary or zero-copy message.
- EvalApp host seam (not built). Blazier has no EvalApp dependency and no EvalApp-specific code. Nothing fans an EvalApp pipeline out across several worker runtimes. You can run a whole pipeline inside one worker service today by writing that service yourself; a built-in pool of workers behind EvalApp does not exist.

When another tool fits better:
- A page that always needs the runtime, a dashboard behind a login for example, gains little from a static shell. Plain Blazor WebAssembly is simpler.
- Content that needs no .NET in the browser at all is better served by a static site generator.
- Server-rendered interactivity (Blazor Server or Blazor Web App) suits apps that can run a server. Blazier is for hosts with none, such as GitHub Pages.
- Parallel speed-ups across cores. Workers free the page; they do not share memory. Each worker is its own runtime with its own copy of your data.

Limits:
- The first interaction starts the runtime but is not replayed: the visitor presses again once the page is live.
- Moving between two static pages is a full page load, so in-memory state does not carry over. Mount the routed app (App<TApp>()) to keep one runtime across tools.
- The lazy guard is conservative: it follows startup code, routable pages and component render code, not lambdas that run later (event handlers, DI factories).
- Lazy assemblies save little in an ahead-of-time compiled build, because that native code lives in the main runtime file either way. They pay off with the interpreter build.
- A worker runtime starts at about 32 MiB of memory; on phones, memory is the budget. The worker bridge was measured with a shared bundle on the interpreter build. A separate worker bundle exists but has not been run in a browser.
- Requires .NET 10 and the Blazor WebAssembly package matching the installed browser-wasm runtime pack. The publish step runs a small tool that needs the ASP.NET Core runtime.

Licence: Commercial licence for commercial use. Evaluation and non-commercial use are permitted. Terms at https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/licence/

## Tools

### Umbrarium, preset demo

The real Umbrarium dashboard computing exact answers over up to three million generated rows, entirely inside your browser tab. Click a chart to slice the rest, or run your own SQL.

Page: https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/umbrarium/
Powered by HoloDb.

### Doctrine

Send soldiers down three lanes toward the enemy castle. The battle runs on a navigation mesh and pauses every 30 seconds so you can choose what to send next. Play the computer, or another person through a public relay, with no accounts.

Page: https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/tools/doctrine/
Powered by Phasor, Tracer and EvalApp.

### The Helix

Paste DNA sequences and a column of measurements and see the double helix in the numbers: a score graded in your browser, with the controls that would expose a false win shown beside it.

Page: https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/tools/helix/
Powered by HoloGenome.

### The Analyst

Paste any data and profile it with a real SQL database in your browser: types, distributions, anomalies and hidden entities, then query it at a live SQL prompt.

Page: https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/tools/analyst/
Powered by HoloDb.

### Prism

A tiny language model that runs entirely in your browser: chat with it, have it write a story, watch one of its decisions on a map, then train your own copy on a foraging task or a price tape.

Page: https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/tools/prism/
Powered by AlgFormer, Prism and Tracer.

### Prose

Paste in a body of text, mine its grammar in your browser, and recombine it into sentences and question and answer pairs for a training corpus.

Page: https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/tools/prose/
Powered by Prose, HoloDb and AlgFormer.

### Council Spending Scanner

English councils' published spending data, prepared ahead of time and opened one month at a time, with the same mechanical checks for every council.

Page: https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/tools/council-spending/


## Games

### Doctrine

Send your soldiers down the lanes and take their castle.

A lane battle between two castles. Every soldier is its own body on a navigation mesh, and every 30 seconds the battle pauses so you can choose what to send and how to order it. Play the computer, or another person online.

Each side's soldiers are items in one store, and the same choices in the same order always play out the same match, so a match can be checked by a short fingerprint at each pause.

Page: https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/games/doctrine/
Play: https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/tools/doctrine/
Modes: Solo and Two players.
Powered by Phasor, Tracer and EvalApp.
Laid out for a phone screen: one column, 44 px tap targets.

#### How a match goes

Two castles face each other across three lanes. The battle runs for 30 seconds, then pauses. While it is paused you can see the whole board: every soldier, every lane, both castles. You spend a small budget of points on packs of soldiers, place each pack in a lane, and give a lane an order. Press Ready, or let the 30 seconds run out, and the next 30 seconds of battle play.

Destroy the enemy castle to win. If neither castle has fallen after 20 phases, it is a draw. The same seed raises the same match, so you can play it again and try something different.

#### Play another person

Choose Play another person on the start screen. Create a room to get a six-character code to give to a friend, join with a code, or pick a room from the list of open ones. Both browsers run the same match from the same starting point. At each pause each player commits to their plan, then both plans are revealed together and applied, and a short fingerprint of the whole board is compared, so neither side can change a plan after seeing the other one.

The connection goes through a public relay. Anyone who has a room code can see that room and its plans, the list of open rooms is visible to everyone, and there are no accounts, so use a made-up name. A player who stops answering for three pauses in a row, or who leaves, gives the match to the one who stayed.

#### The soldiers

Eight kinds of soldier can be sent: Spearmen, Shieldwall, Riders, Archers, Priests, Wights, Wolves and Catapults. Each has its own strength, speed and reach, and each stands better against some kinds than others. Spearmen stand against riders, riders ride down archers, archers shoot through shieldwall, and shieldwall holds against spearmen. Priests answer the cursed. Look at what the other side has sent before you choose.

#### Orders

A lane can be given one order: Advance, Hold, Fall back, Hunt or Guard. A lane told to hold digs in, and a line that holds its ground without being hit for a few ticks strikes harder until it is hit or moves. Your orders land together with the other side's at the end of the pause.

#### The battle

The ground is a baked Tracer navigation mesh, with walls that block sight and cover that protects. Every soldier is a separate agent that finds its path, takes cover and strikes on it, so a crowd really does funnel through a gap.

A match is a set of choices played out by a fixed set of rules. Two players who make the same choices in the same order get the same match, every time. That is also how a match can be checked: each pause carries a short fingerprint of the whole board.

#### What powers it

Each side's soldiers are items in a Pleroma store from the Phasor package. The battle runs on Tracer, and each step of the battle runs as an EvalApp pipeline. The whole game runs in your browser tab, and an online match sends only your choices through a public relay. Read more on the Pleroma page.

## Evidence

### What attention costs

At the same shape and the same parameter count, reading a 1,984-token prompt takes 182 ms with softmax attention and 7.08 ms with holographic attention. Each further token takes 181 µs against 3.60 µs, and the serve cache holds 2,253 KB against 3.40 KB. Softmax reading grows with the square of the length (exponent 1.9) and holographic reading grows in step with it (1.0).

Page: https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/algformer/evidence/

Method:
- Workload: Both cores are built at 32 channels, 8 shifts and 2 layers, which gives them the same parameter count, and driven with the same random tokens. For each context length the run reads the prompt through the serve cache, then produces 16 more tokens and averages them. Cache memory is the managed memory kept alive by the primed cache.
- Engines: AlgFormer (softmax attention); HoloFormer (holographic attention)
- Check: Both cores are warmed at every length before timing, so compilation has settled. The two have identical parameter counts.
- Statistic: Median of 7 runs per length, on one thread.
- Machine: 16 logical processors; the run used one thread.
- Ties: This measures cost only. It says nothing about which core predicts better.

Where it loses:
- Holographic attention holds a limited number of items cleanly in one bundle, and HoloShape reports how many for a shape (the capacity table). Softmax attention has no such bound, at the cost of everything above.

#### Results

Time and memory by context length

| Tokens in context | Read the prompt, softmax (ms) | Read the prompt, holographic (ms) | One more token, softmax (µs) | One more token, holographic (µs) | Cache, softmax (KB) | Cache, holographic (KB) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 64 | 0.35 | 0.21 | 7.60 | 3.20 | 90.6 | 3.40 |
| 128 | 1.01 | 0.45 | 12.5 | 3.50 | 163 | 3.40 |
| 256 | 3.37 | 0.99 | 22.4 | 3.80 | 307 | 3.40 |
| 512 | 12.2 | 2.44 | 45.6 | 4.10 | 595 | 3.40 |
| 1,024 | 44.2 | 4.16 | 97.2 | 3.90 | 1,171 | 3.40 |
| 1,984 | 182 | 7.08 | 181 | 3.60 | 2,253 | 3.40 |

The shape HoloShape derives from a width, and the capacity of a holographic bundle at that shape

| Width | Shifts | Layers | Derived context (tokens) | Crosstalk edge (tokens) | Reads back 90% clean (tokens) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 32 | 32 | 1 | 128 | 512 | 61 |
| 64 | 64 | 3 | 512 | 2,048 | 245 |
| 128 | 128 | 6 | 2,048 | 8,192 | 983 |
| 256 | 256 | 8 | 8,192 | 32,768 | 3,932 |
| 512 | 512 | 11 | 32,768 | 131,072 | 15,728 |

Limits:
- Absolute times depend on the machine. The way each cost grows with the context length is the finding.
- One shape and one random token stream. The growth exponents are fitted between the 128-token and the longest measurement.
- Cost only, not quality.

### What a visitor waits for

On the sample app the static page downloads 6.8 KB before the visitor acts, against 2.8 MB when the same app boots the usual way. Real content is on screen in 72 to 100 ms on desktop and 416 to 484 ms on the phone profile, against 748 to 1,165 ms and 13.2 to 15.5 s. After the visitor presses Start the runtime takes 710 to 1,170 ms on desktop and 12.7 to 15.4 s on the phone profile to reach a working page, the same wait as the usual boot.

Page: https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/blazier/evidence/

Method:
- Workload: The Blazier sample app, the sample app published with the trimmed interpreter build, is loaded in headless Microsoft Edge from a local server shaped like GitHub Pages, with gzip. The same page is loaded two ways: booted the usual way, and as a Blazier static shell that starts the runtime when the visitor presses Start. The worker rows run a prime count to 600,000 in a worker service.
- Engines: Blazier static shell; Blazor WebAssembly booted the usual way
- Check: On a page with a click target, a touch scroll, a tap on text and a Tab key press make 0 requests for the runtime, while the control page starts it.
- Statistic: Desktop is unthrottled, 3 runs. The phone profile is 4 Mbit/s, 100 ms round trip, CPU slowed 6 times, 2 runs. A range runs from the fastest to the slowest run.
- Machine: An Intel Core i9-11950H laptop with 32 GB of memory.

Where it loses:
- Pressing Start does not shorten the wait for the runtime: a working page takes 12.7 to 15.4 s after the press on the phone profile, against 13.2 to 15.5 s for the usual boot. Blazier moves the wait behind a readable page and does not remove it.

#### Results

Booted the usual way and as a Blazier static shell

| Measure | Profile | Booted the usual way | Blazier static shell |
|---|---|---|---|
| Downloaded before the visitor does anything | Both | 2.8 MB | 6.8 KB in 6 requests |
| Until real content is on screen | Desktop | 748 to 1,165 ms | 72 to 100 ms |
| Until real content is on screen | Phone profile | 13.2 to 15.5 s | 416 to 484 ms |
| Until the page works (usual boot from loading the page, Blazier from pressing Start) | Desktop | 748 to 1,165 ms | 710 to 1,170 ms |
| Until the page works (usual boot from loading the page, Blazier from pressing Start) | Phone profile | 13.2 to 15.5 s | 12.7 to 15.4 s |

Worker bridge, desktop

| Measure | Recorded |
|---|---|
| Start a worker runtime from cached files | 190 to 210 ms |
| One call to a worker service, round trip | 0.49 to 0.57 ms |
| Worst gap on the page's timers during a long job | 14 to 19 ms |
| Long tasks on the page during that job | 0 |
| Stop a job that yields | 12 to 17 ms |
| Stop a job that never yields, until the worker is usable again | 730 to 800 ms |
| Restart the worker | 170 to 180 ms |
| Stream 2,000 items, first item | 16 to 21 ms |
| Stream 2,000 items, all of them | 250 to 272 ms |
| Memory of a worker runtime | 32 MiB |
| Worker start on a shared bundle | 132 requests, all served from the browser cache (0 KB over the network) |

Limits:
- One sample app on one machine. The figures describe that app, not a forecast for another.
- The sample app uses the trimmed interpreter build. In an ahead-of-time build the lazy-assembly saving is small, because that native code lives in the main runtime file either way.
- The worker rows are desktop only. The phone profile slows the page and not the worker, so a phone worker figure would describe the page. A worker runtime starts at about 32 MiB of memory.
- Headless Edge only. Firefox and Safari have not been run, and the memory and battery cost on a phone are not measured.
- The worker bridge was measured with a shared bundle. A separate worker bundle has been built but not run in a browser.
- The Showroom tool pages are built this way, but their shell sizes and timings are not part of this record.

### What a gate bound does

The gate never admitted more downloads than its bound: in every recorded run the most in flight equalled the bound. The time to finish 24 queued jobs fell from 1,113 ms at a bound of 1 to 139 ms at 8, then rose again to 410 ms when all 24 ran at once, because the simulated service slows when it is crowded.

Page: https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/evalapp/evidence/

Method:
- Workload: 24 jobs are queued at once through a ForEach. Each passes a Network gate and awaits a simulated download of 40 ms. The simulated service stretches the wait once more than 6 downloads are in flight. 7 fixed gate bounds from 1 to 24, one recorded run each, after a warm-up run.
- Engines: EvalApp pipeline with Gate and ForEach
- Check: Every job records its own timestamps, and the number of downloads in flight is counted inside the gated step, so the bound is checked against what actually ran.
- Statistic: One recording per bound, in milliseconds. A repeated recording varies by a few percent.
- Memory and logging: Nothing is retained between runs.

Where it loses:
- A bound of 1 took 1,113 ms, 8.0 times the best bound. The gate does not choose its bound for you, and a bound set too low is the slowest result here.
- A bound of 24, the whole batch at once, took 410 ms, 2.9 times the best bound. A higher bound is not faster when the thing behind the gate slows under load.

#### Results

24 queued jobs, by gate bound

| Gate bound | All jobs finished in (ms) | Most running at once | Longest wait at the gate (ms) | Jobs per second |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1,113 | 1 | 1,067 | 22 |
| 2 | 557 | 2 | 511 | 43 |
| 4 | 280 | 4 | 233 | 86 |
| 6 | 189 | 6 | 143 | 127 |
| 8 | 139 | 8 | 92 | 173 |
| 12 | 187 | 12 | 93 | 128 |
| 24 | 410 | 24 | 0 | 59 |

Limits:
- The work is a simulated wait, not a real network. It shows how the gate and its queue behave, not the speed of any real service.
- The best bound here is a property of the simulated service, which slows past 6 in flight. A real service has its own shape, which is what the tuner exists to find.
- It measures the gate and does not compare EvalApp with another library.

### HoloDb benchmarks

Totals over 100,000,000 invoices in 0.12 ms and four joins to two million customers in 0.19 to 0.25 ms, against tuned DuckDB and tuned SQL Server on the same machine and data. Out of the box, scans that no structure covers are slower, and the chart shows each of them as an amber bar.

Page: https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/holodb/evidence/

- 0.12 ms: to add up 100,000,000 invoices (HoloDb restored, warm median). Tuned DuckDB scanning them: 23.17 ms. Tuned SQL Server with an indexed view: 0.65 ms.
- 0.19 to 0.25 ms: for the four joins to 2,000,000 customers (HoloDb restored, warm median). Tuned SQL Server: 0.62 to 0.77 ms. Tuned DuckDB: 102.06 to 603.65 ms.
- 16 of 16: queries where HoloDb restored is ahead of tuned DuckDB, and 16 of 16 where it is ahead of tuned SQL Server. Ahead means more than 20 percent faster in both runs.
- 10 of 16: queries where HoloDb out of the box is ahead of tuned DuckDB. It is behind on 5 and too close to call on 1: scans that no structure covers. Against tuned SQL Server it is ahead on 7 and behind on 9.

One size: 100,000,000 invoices and 2,000,000 customers. One machine: an Intel Core i9-11950H laptop with 16 logical cores. Warm means the median of three runs. Ahead or behind means more than 20 percent in both runs of each engine.

Warm median milliseconds at 100,000,000 invoices (HoloDb restored | HoloDb out of the box | DuckDB tuned | SQL Server tuned):
- invoices by status: 0.15 | 0.13 | 77.60 | 1.12
- revenue by month: 0.23 | 0.20 | 69.35 | 1.20
- revenue by region: 0.26 | 0.13 | 67.54 | 1.06
- total invoiced: 0.12 | 0.13 | 23.17 | 0.65
- invoice count: 0.18 | 0.10 | 0.67 | 0.62
- look up one invoice: 0.15 | 0.16 | 0.76 | 0.58
- overdue outstanding: 0.26 | 198.84 | 67.76 | 0.64
- big-ticket invoices (>$5k): 0.19 | 111.31 | 35.02 | 17.21
- largest invoices: 0.30 | 281.64 | 6.70 | 0.81
- top customers by revenue: 0.58 | 3087.82 | 190.14 | 38.50
- revenue by region & status: 0.28 | 355.86 | 261.46 | 0.91
- revenue by segment (JOIN): 0.19 | 6.62 | 488.31 | 0.65
- enterprise revenue (JOIN): 0.20 | 7.40 | 102.06 | 0.64
- revenue by signup cohort (JOIN): 0.23 | 9.05 | 285.55 | 0.62
- top named customers (JOIN): 0.93 | 33.60 | 576.07 | 121.54
- revenue by segment & status (JOIN): 0.25 | 715.47 | 603.65 | 0.77

HoloDb restored ran in a separate session on the same machine and data, the same day as the other three arms. HoloDb restored has its summary, sorted index and keyed summary declared and saved beside the data; the tuned rivals have the matching structures built by hand. Out of the box, nothing is declared and the planner saw each statement four times.

How we measured:
- Machine: An 11th Gen Intel Core i9-11950H at 2.60 GHz, 16 logical cores, 34.1 GB of memory, Windows 11, .NET 8.0.27. Each engine ran in its own process.
- Data and queries: 100,000,000 invoices and 2,000,000 customers; 16 billing queries: five rollups, a lookup, five scans and five joins to the customers.
- Tuned DuckDB: DuckDB 1.5.5: table written in customer_id order, ANALYZE, 16 threads, 12 GB memory limit.
- Tuned SQL Server: SQL Server 2022 Developer: a columnstore index, a descending index on amount_cents and indexed views, max server memory 5,120 MB, in a container.
- Tuning: We chose the rivals' tuning after a 10,000,000-row trial and fixed it before the 100,000,000-row build. A different tuning is untested.
- Same answers: Before any query is timed, its rows are hashed. All four arms return identical results on all 16 queries, including where HoloDb is slower.
- Warm and cold: Warm is the median of three runs. Cold is the first run after the file cache was cleared by reading a 34 GB file (for SQL Server, dropping its buffers).
- Repeats: Each engine ran the whole set twice. A tilde marks a figure whose repeat differed by more than 20 percent, and a query counts as ahead or behind only when both runs agree.

What HoloDb does not do:
- Joins: INNER JOIN only. Several in one statement on in-memory tables, one on a paged table. LEFT, RIGHT, FULL, CROSS, NATURAL, USING and comma joins are refused.
- Aliases: No AS on columns or tables. Aggregate columns are named agg(col), such as count(*).
- ALTER TABLE: ADD COLUMN only, with a DEFAULT or NULL. No DROP COLUMN, RENAME COLUMN or RENAME TO.
- Expressions: No CASE, LENGTH(), OFFSET or UNION, and no arithmetic in the select list or inside SUM(v * 2). COUNT(DISTINCT col), LIKE and IN (SELECT ...) work on in-memory tables.
- Money: Constant-time totals are for INT columns. REAL SUM is a SIMD scan, and DECIMAL and NUMERIC are REAL (a double), so hold money as integer cents. There is no fixed-point type.
- Saved summaries: A summary made with CREATE INDEX ... USING SUMMARY, or built by the planner, is saved with the table and restored on open. A plane attached with the EnablePleroma call on an in-memory table is not saved: call it again after Open.
- Summary limits: A declared summary takes up to 4,095 distinct values per column (1,024 for one the planner builds) and a joint of 12 bits. A column over its limit goes to a scan and is never approximated.
- Joins on paged tables: The keyed summary holds up to 4,194,304 consecutive INT keys. The 100,000,000-invoice run joins 2,000,000 customers.
- Languages: A .NET library. The server speaks a TCP and TLS binary protocol whose only client is .NET. No JDBC, ODBC, Python, Node or Go client, and no PostgreSQL or MySQL wire.
- Concurrency: One process per database and one writer at a time. Simple aggregate reads run off a snapshot without the lock. A second process cannot open a paged database's files, and there is no MVCC: a long transaction blocks other writers.
- Table size: Tested to 100,000,000 rows (4.94 GB paged, 165 s to load). In-memory tables are bounded by RAM at about 110 bytes per row. A paged primary key loaded out of order keeps a RAM dictionary of about 35 bytes per row. Beyond 100,000,000 rows is untested.
- Backup: Offline: copy the files of a closed database. There is no online backup and no point-in-time recovery.
- Crash safety: One fsync per commit. Tests cut the log at every record boundary, flip bits in the log and the data file, and tear a page during a checkpoint. A real power cut, a disk that lies about fsync, a full disk and several processes are not tested.

When to use it: https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/holodb/#fit. Trade-offs:
- Read speed against write cost. Reads: A total over 100,000,000 invoices reads in 0.12 ms, because totals are kept up to date as rows are written. Writes and space: Single-row INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE took 1.5 to 2.1 times SQLite's time (engine alone, in memory). The structures take space: 6.84 GB restored, 4.94 GB out of the box, 2.46 GB for tuned DuckDB.
- Exact against approximate. Exact: Integer sums are 128-bit and identical on all four engines for all 16 queries. A sum past 64 bits throws; it never wraps. Approximate: Only similarity search: from 8,000 rows an approximate index picks the candidates. Money is integer cents, because DECIMAL is a double.
- Automatic against hand-tuned. Automatic: The planner builds a summary or index when repeats pay for it, and drops it when writes cost more than it saves. Hand-tuned: A DBA can declare structures, which are saved and never dropped. Without them, scans no structure covers are slower than tuned DuckDB: 5 of 16 queries at 100,000,000 invoices.
- Embedded against server. Embedded: In process: a point query takes 1 to 3 microseconds. One process owns the files and one writer runs at a time. Server: TCP and TLS with a typed .NET client: about 0.07 ms more per point query. No JDBC, ODBC or PostgreSQL wire.
- Memory against disk. In memory: The fastest path, bounded by RAM at about 110 bytes per row. Paged: Tables bigger than memory through an 8 KB buffer pool: 100,000,000 invoices in 4.94 GB, 165 s to load, a 3.16 GB peak working set out of the box and 1.26 GB restored.

### How HoloGenome scores against the lab

A linear readout trained on 12,472 random-sequence constructs and tested on 82,368 yeast-gene constructs (no shared sequence, forward or reverse complement) scores r = 0.529 with vectors that use the measured twist, against 0.483 with one constant twist (difference 0.046, 95% interval 0.041 to 0.050). Adding the local-shape layer lifts it to 0.600, a further 0.071. A small phasor model that chose its own period, starting from 12 bases, settled at 10.49, 10.51, 10.48 and 10.51 bases per turn on four independent libraries, against the crystallographic 10.534. The best trained network scores higher: the 22-parameter fit trails it by 0.28 to 0.39.

Page: https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/hologenome/evidence/

Method:
- Workload: Loop-seq DNA cyclizability: how readily a 50-base stretch of DNA bends into a loop (Basu et al. 2021, Nature 589:462). Each vector is one window of sequence encoded by HoloGenome. A linear readout is trained on 12,472 random-sequence constructs and tested on 82,368 yeast-gene constructs with no shared sequence, forward or reverse complement. The period search fits a small phasor model to one library's measurements, starting from 12 bases per turn, and is repeated on independent libraries.
- Engines: HoloGenome vectors with a linear readout; A fitted phasor model; A zero-parameter score; DNAcycP, an approximately 94,000-parameter trained neural network (published scores)
- Check: Each score is a correlation on sequences the model had not seen. Label-permutation checks land at zero, as designed, and scrambled-order controls fall to the level of base counts alone. The period search is repeated with the base order scrambled and with the labels scrambled.
- Statistic: Pearson correlation between prediction and measurement, on sequences the model had not seen, with a 95% interval from resampling whole gene blocks. The DNAcycP figures are published.
- Memory and logging: The Loop-seq measurements are not redistributed.

Where it loses:
- It does not beat the best trained model. DNAcycP, an approximately 94,000-parameter trained neural network, reaches r = 0.93, 0.77 and 0.89 on the libraries where it has published scores. The best 22-parameter model here reached 0.54, 0.50 and 0.60 on the same libraries, trailing by 0.28 to 0.39.
- More training did not help. Training the vector readouts with iterative optimisation left accuracy where it was (r 0.46 to 0.62 across the libraries tested), and running the phasor models for 2.5 times as many steps moved their scores by at most 0.0001.
- The measurement itself has a ceiling. Loop-seq replicates agree at roughly r = 0.84 to 0.87, so no model can score near 1.0 on it.
- The simplest zero-parameter score is modest. At r = 0.22 to 0.46 it is well below any trained readout. Its value is that it needs no fitting and matches the known periodicity of the double helix.

#### Results

Linear readout on vectors, held-out correlation. Trained on random sequence, tested on yeast genes it never saw

| Vectors built with | Correlation r | 95% interval |
|---|---|---|
| Measured twist plus shape | 0.600 | 0.591 to 0.609 |
| Measured twist | 0.529 | 0.520 to 0.539 |
| One constant twist | 0.483 | 0.473 to 0.494 |
| Dinucleotide-shuffled sequence | 0.260 | 0.249 to 0.272 |
| Counts of 1-, 2- and 3-base words | 0.253 | 0.239 to 0.267 |

Differences between those readouts

| Contrast | Difference in r | 95% interval |
|---|---|---|
| Measured twist over constant twist | 0.046 | 0.041 to 0.050 |
| Shape layer over measured twist | 0.071 | 0.063 to 0.078 |

Held-out correlation, by library. The fitted model was trained on the yeast tiling library and scored on each library with shared sequence removed. The DNAcycP scores are published figures

| Library | DNAcycP, trained network | 22-parameter fit | Zero-parameter score |
|---|---|---|---|
| Random sequence | 0.93 | 0.54 | 0.31 |
| Chromosome V tiling | 0.77 | 0.50 | 0.36 |
| Nucleosome | 0.89 | 0.60 | 0.46 |

| Library | Found from real data | Order scrambled | Labels scrambled |
|---|---|---|---|
| Yeast tiling | 10.49 | 12.03 | 12.05 |
| Random sequence | 10.51 | 12.01 | 12.01 |
| Chromosome V tiling | 10.48 | 12.03 | 12.04 |
| Nucleosome | 10.51 | 11.96 | 12.03 |

| Started at (bases per turn) | Settled at (bases per turn) |
|---|---|
| 6 | 6.01 |
| 9 | 10.49 |
| 12 | 10.49 |
| 18 | 18.01 |
| 24 | 24.48 |

Zero-parameter score: strength of the AA/TT step pattern at three periods, correlation with bendability

| Library | Helical period | 7 bases | 15 bases |
|---|---|---|---|
| Random sequence | 0.307 | -0.013 | -0.022 |
| Yeast tiling | 0.430 | -0.065 | -0.090 |
| Chromosome V tiling | 0.364 | -0.060 | -0.065 |
| Nucleosome | 0.465 | -0.037 | -0.053 |
| 50-base library | 0.221 | -0.058 | -0.054 |

More training, same accuracy: held-out correlation after training the readouts with iterative optimisation

| Vectors built with | Random sequence | Chromosome V tiling | Nucleosome |
|---|---|---|---|
| Measured twist plus shape | 0.544 | 0.524 | 0.620 |
| Measured twist | 0.570 | 0.483 | 0.578 |
| One constant twist | 0.529 | 0.462 | 0.558 |

Limits:
- The period search has a narrow basin. Runs started at 9 or 12 bases found the helical period, and runs started at 6, 18 or 24 bases found nothing.
- All grading uses one kind of measurement: Loop-seq bendability in yeast-derived and random sequence. Nothing is claimed for other organisms, other assays or chromatin in the living cell.
- The graded readouts (the linear model, the zero-parameter helical score and the fitted phasor models) run in the research harness and are not in the shipped package. The package ships the encoder, the twist tables and the window store.
- The shape layer was graded with a pentamer table from the DNAshapeR project. That table is not shipped because its licence does not allow it, so you load your own.
- The correlations are Pearson r. The intervals come from resampling whole gene blocks, because neighbouring windows overlap.

### Detail against components read

One 16 by 16 chunk stored as a single hologram decodes 98.4 percent of its cells correctly at the full budget of 8,192 components, 131,072 bytes and 17.0 ms. Reading fewer components is cheaper and fuzzier: 67.1 percent at 1,568 components, and 19.5 percent at 24, which takes 384 bytes and 0.09 ms.

Page: https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/holovoxel/evidence/

Method:
- Workload: A chunk of a fixed procedural world is built at full fidelity. For each component budget it is decoded as a colour field and checked cell by cell against the stored block (Chunk.Accuracy). The hologram size is the number of bytes CapacityProbe reports for that budget.
- Engines: HoloVoxel Chunk.DecodeField at ten component budgets
- Check: Accuracy is the share of surface cells whose strongest decoded block equals the block that was stored.
- Statistic: Accuracy is one measurement of one chunk. Decode time is the median of 15 runs after warm-up.
- Memory and logging: Hologram size is sixteen bytes per component read.
- Ties: Eight blocks are possible, so a random guess is right 12.5 percent of the time.

Where it loses:
- Accuracy is low at small budgets by design: 19.5 percent at 24 components, against 12.5 percent for a random guess. A far read is a soft blend, not a smaller copy of the near one.

#### Results

One chunk, by component budget

| Components read | Cells correct (percent) | Hologram size (bytes) | Decode time (ms) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 24 | 19.5 | 384 | 0.09 |
| 48 | 19.7 | 768 | 0.15 |
| 98 | 23.4 | 1,600 | 0.26 |
| 196 | 28.7 | 3,136 | 0.41 |
| 392 | 34.0 | 6,272 | 0.71 |
| 784 | 49.2 | 12,544 | 1.58 |
| 1,568 | 67.1 | 25,088 | 3.19 |
| 3,136 | 83.3 | 50,176 | 6.25 |
| 6,272 | 96.4 | 100,352 | 13.09 |
| 8,192 | 98.4 | 131,072 | 17.04 |

Limits:
- One chunk of one world. Terrain with other block mixes will score differently.
- Accuracy is measured at full resolution for each budget. The scene on the product page also coarsens the grid with distance, which this table does not measure.
- Decode time is for one chunk on one machine.

### Exact recall and refusal

At equal storage the exact key view recovered 64 items with no errors where holographic reduced representations held 95 percent or better only up to 4. Past capacity the exact store refused every time, while the baseline answered wrongly every time.

Page: https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/phasor/evidence/

Method:
- Workload: Two measurements of a keys-only store, the Pleroma's single-face special case. Exact recovery: store k distinct symbols from vocabularies of 4,096 and 2^20 symbols and read them back, at capacities from 1 to 96. Associative recall: store n key and value pairs from a codebook of 256 values and recall each value from its key.
- Engines: Pleroma keys-only store (CycleHologram); Plate's holographic reduced representations with correlation clean-up; The same representations with a stronger peeling decoder (orthogonal matching pursuit); A float bundle of complex phasors, at full and half the bits (recall table)
- Check: Every exact decode is re-encoded and must reproduce every stored element before it is returned.
- Statistic: 200 trials per capacity point. Associative recall uses 20 random seeds, with a chance level of 0.39 percent.
- Machine: CPU only, one core.
- Memory and logging: Stores are compared at equal storage: about 2,064 and 2,580 bits for exact recovery, and 3,965 bits for the exact arm against 3,904 bits for the float arm in the recall table. The 7,869-bit budget was not measured.
- Ties: The exact read in the recall table is decode then test, not a ShiftKeys read. It measures recall, not model quality: a trained model can learn around float noise.

Where it loses:
- At 64 pairs the exact store is past its capacity and refuses every query, so it recalls none, while the float bundle still recalls 9.5 percent of values, though it never says when it is wrong.
- Exact arithmetic is not faster in general. A Pleroma read costs one or more transforms, while a float bundle read is one correlation. At equal bits float reads are often faster.

#### Results

Associative recall at equal bits: share of values recalled correctly

| Pairs stored | Exact store (K=32) | Float bundle (d=61) | Float bundle (d=30, half the bits) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | 100% | 100% | 100% |
| 4 | 100% | 100% | 93.8% |
| 8 | 100% | 87.5% | 53.8% |
| 16 | 100% | 48.1% | 20.9% |
| 32 | 100% | 21.9% | 8.0% |
| 64 | 0 (refuses every query) | 9.5% (never refuses) | 3.1% |

Limits:
- The exact store holds a number of entries proportional to the number of pairs and grows with context, while the float bundle has a fixed size.
- Recall only, not model quality.

### Pleroma costs and checks

A superposed kernel applies in 0.17 to 0.44 ms on a 10,464-cell store whether it holds 1 or 10,368 elements, and the repair and corruption checks recovered or detected every case tried.

Page: https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/phasor/evidence/costs/

Method:
- Workload: Each row is one operation on one store shape, timed or checked on the shape named in the row. Checks are exhaustive or random within the stated count.
- Engines: Pleroma, release build
- Check: Every timed operation is compared with a brute-force or naive implementation, and each check counts the cases that matched.
- Statistic: Per-call times, warmed up, with the range across repeated runs where one is shown.
- Machine: One laptop CPU (Intel i9-11950H), release build, with other work running.
- Memory and logging: Page and kernel figures use the default field.

#### Results

Measured costs and checks

| Operation | Workload | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Superposed kernel apply | 10,464-cell store (GF(13,879), 6 flag bits, S_3, time period 27, joint flags by order by time, key capacity 4, a continuous component, 10 items on four keys), random kernels of 1 to 10,368 elements, the mean of 20 calls after one warm-up | 0.17 to 0.44 ms per call, with no trend in the number of elements |
| The same store built item by item | The same store, rebuilt from the moved items, at 1 element and at 1,000 elements | 3 ms and 1,916 ms |
| Counts on a dense page | 2,925 or 3,150 keys, a full page read | 188 to 246 ns per slot (0.6 to 0.7 ms per page) |
| FromCounts | Build a page from a count vector, 3,150 slots | 758 ns per slot |
| AddCounts | Add a count vector to a page | 758 ns per slot, against 77 to 91 microseconds per slot for sequential Add (about 100 times faster) |
| Sparse page, one key | One key read and sample | 183 bytes, 0.4 microseconds per read |
| Sparse page, 50 keys | 50 keys | About 2.2 KB, 19 to 41 microseconds per read |
| Reserved-key repair | Lost harmonics, r = 5 | Any of 1 to 5 lost harmonics rebuilt, 300 of 300 each |
| Check-prime mirror | One corrupted cell in either copy | Detected 10,000 of 10,000 |
| Exact-sum parity | Any one lost store of a group | Rebuilt 100 of 100, with incremental updates |

Limits:
- Times are warm, single-call figures on one machine. Cold-start costs, including compilation, are larger.
- Every row is the Pleroma alone, without a database or a model around it.

### Generated sentences pass the gate

Of 2,000 sentences requested in one run, 1,966 different ones came back. Every one passed the package's validity gate on a fresh parse, and every word in every one was observed in the corpus.

Page: https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/prose/evidence/

Method:
- Workload: 8,232 sentences from 3 public-domain novels (Alice's Adventures in Wonderland; The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes; Pride and Prejudice) are mined, then 2,000 sentences are generated with a fixed seed.
- Engines: Prose ProseEngine.Generate, checked with ValidityGate.Check and Attested.All
- Check: Every sentence is parsed again by the same rules that mined the text and must have a real subject and a finite verb, with subject and verb agreement and article and noun agreement. A separate check confirms every open-class word was observed in the corpus.
- Statistic: One run with one seed.
- Ties: The corpus is large enough for generation to use observed pairings only.

Where it loses:
- The package returned 1,966 of the 2,000 requested sentences. It returns up to the number asked for and stops when it cannot find more different valid ones.

#### Results

2,000 sentences requested in one run

| Measure | Count |
|---|---|
| Sentences requested | 2,000 |
| Sentences returned | 1,966 |
| Different from every other | 1,966 |
| Passed the validity gate | 1,966 |
| Every word observed in the corpus | 1,966 |

Limits:
- The gate checks form, using the same rules that produced the sentences. It does not check meaning, and a valid sentence can still say something odd.
- One corpus, one seed.

### HoloDb deep dive

The numbers behind the plane: what it serves, what it declines, how its cost grows with size, and the 10,000,000-invoice comparison against engines as they ship. These workloads are built to suit the plane, so they sit apart from the 100,000,000-invoice comparison.

Page: https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/holodb/evidence/deep-dive/

Method:
- Workload: A billing ledger (invoices joined to customers, sixteen queries) at 10,000,000 invoices with every engine out of the box, and three constructed workloads for the plane: a live dashboard, ingest while querying, and multi-tenant slices and joins.
- Engines: SQLite (in memory, always listed first); DuckDB (in process, in memory, default settings); SQL Server 2022 LocalDB (tables in tempdb on disk, primary keys only); HoloDb embedded (in process); HoloDb server (networked over TLS on the loopback interface); HoloDb engine: the same database without a plane; HoloDb plane: a database with the optional plane attached
- Check: Before any query is timed, its full result set is normalised and compared across the engines. Every timed result is identical. After each plane workload the plane is compared with a rebuild from the columns and found equal.
- Statistic: Medians of repeated calls through each engine's typed client API, execute plus consume every row. A cell whose own two timing loops disagree by more than 25 percent is marked noisy, and no ratio is drawn from it. A difference under 1.15x counts as a tie.
- Machine: One 16-core laptop CPU (Intel Core i9-11950H). The billing comparison ran with nothing else heavy open. The plane workloads ran with ordinary desktop applications and the SQL Server service open. The scaling runs used a Release build, and each point is the median of three repetitions.
- Memory and logging: Every figure here is an in-memory HoloDb database with no write-ahead log; SQLite and DuckDB ran in memory and SQL Server LocalDB used tempdb on disk. A database opened with a write-ahead log flushes each committed statement to disk, which adds one flush per commit, set by the disk. Bulk-load rates compare unlike modes: typed arrays into memory, an appender, inserts in one transaction, and a bulk copy into tempdb.

#### Billing ledger at 10,000,000 invoices, every engine out of the box

The ledger has 10,000,000 invoices and 200,000 customers, about 50 invoices each, over 24 months, four regions and five statuses, with money held as integer cents. SQLite and DuckDB run in memory with default settings, SQL Server 2022 LocalDB with primary keys only, and no index or summary table is added for the queries. The optional plane is not attached.

Bulk load, rows per second: DuckDB 1,159,279; HoloDb server 1,051,473; SQLite 726,050; SQL Server 693,231; HoloDb embedded 679,271.

In process, 10,000,000 invoices: HoloDb embedded against DuckDB and SQLite (median milliseconds, in memory, no index or summary added to any engine)

| Query | SQLite | DuckDB | HoloDb embedded | Result |
|---|---|---|---|---|
