| invoices by status | 3719.66 | 41.63 | 0.02 | HoloDb, more than 1,600x (reads a maintained total) |
| revenue by region | 3492.70 | 34.33 | 0.02 | HoloDb, more than 1,300x (reads a maintained total) |
| total invoiced | 414.54 | 2.56 | 0.00 | HoloDb, more than 510x (reads a maintained total) |
| revenue by month | 3584.01 | 5.48 | 0.04 | HoloDb, more than 120x (reads a maintained total) |
| invoice count | 13.90 | 0.68 | 0.00 | HoloDb, more than 130x (reads a maintained total) |
| look up one invoice | 0.01 | 0.60 | 0.02 | SQLite (in memory) ahead, 0.01 ms |
| revenue by segment (JOIN) | 6527.97 | 49.01 | 14.71 | HoloDb 3.3x |
| top named customers (JOIN) | 8944.31 | 291.33 | 132.35 | HoloDb 2.2x |
| revenue by segment and status (JOIN) | 10685.41 | 77.54 | 36.17 | HoloDb 2.1x |
| overdue outstanding | 440.80 | 11.93 | 6.12 | HoloDb 1.9x |
| revenue by region and status | 7495.52 | 58.09 | 35.58 | HoloDb 1.6x |
| top customers by revenue | 4346.30 | 129.61 | 89.87 | HoloDb 1.4x |
| largest invoices | 573.94 | 3.28 | 2.42 | HoloDb 1.4x |
| big-ticket invoices (over $5k) | 382.92 | 2.57 | 2.49 | tie (1.03x) |
| enterprise revenue (JOIN) | 3047.43 | 8.68 | 8.97 | tie (DuckDB 1.03x) |
| revenue by signup cohort (JOIN) | 6469.16 | 11.96 | 14.92 | DuckDB out of the box, 1.25x |

Networked, 10,000,000 invoices: HoloDb server against SQL Server LocalDB and SQLite (median milliseconds, SQL Server with primary keys only)

| Query | SQLite | SQL Server | HoloDb server | Result |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| revenue by region | 3492.70 | 2088.59 | 0.19 | HoloDb, about 11,000x (reads a maintained total) |
| invoices by status | 3719.66 | 2178.58 | 0.20 | HoloDb, about 10,900x (reads a maintained total) |
| revenue by month | 3584.01 | 1485.33 | 0.35 | HoloDb, about 4,200x (reads a maintained total) |
| total invoiced | 414.54 | 943.63 | 0.25 | HoloDb, about 3,800x (reads a maintained total) |
| invoice count | 13.90 | 470.33 | 0.17 | HoloDb, about 2,800x (reads a maintained total) |
| largest invoices | 573.94 | 1472.47 | 2.74 | HoloDb, about 540x |
| revenue by signup cohort (JOIN) | 6469.16 | 2562.84 | 13.88 | HoloDb, about 185x |
| enterprise revenue (JOIN) | 3047.43 | 1550.70 | 8.55 | HoloDb, about 180x |
| revenue by segment (JOIN) | 6527.97 | 2626.84 | 14.65 | HoloDb, about 180x |
| revenue by segment and status (JOIN) | 10685.41 | 5089.70 | 34.35 | HoloDb, about 150x |
| big-ticket invoices (over $5k) | 382.92 | 397.23 | 3.06 | HoloDb, about 130x |
| overdue outstanding | 440.80 | 588.61 | 5.97 | HoloDb, about 100x |
| revenue by region and status | 7495.52 | 2792.44 | 34.46 | HoloDb, about 81x |
| top customers by revenue | 4346.30 | 2426.10 | 87.17 | HoloDb, about 28x |
| top named customers (JOIN) | 8944.31 | 2616.03 | 127.51 | HoloDb, about 21x |
| look up one invoice | 0.01 | 0.07 | 0.18 | SQL Server (primary keys only), 2.6x |

HoloDb embedded is faster than in-memory SQLite on 15 of the 16 queries. Against DuckDB out of the box, counting a difference under 1.15x as a tie, it is faster on 13 queries, tied on 2 and slower on 1. The rollups and the lookup read a maintained total or the primary-key index, so they take microseconds and do not grow with the ledger, while the other engines scan. The benchmark prints two decimals, so those cells are lower bounds. The joins and scans are the rows where the engines do the same work.

HoloDb server is faster than SQL Server with primary keys only on 15 of the 16 queries, including all five joins. Both are networked services paying a client and server round trip. The server figures are medians of five calls, so they include the first-call cost of the network path: a longer loop through the same client measures the rollups and the lookup at a steady 0.06 to 0.10 ms, and a point query pays a fixed 0.07 ms of client, TLS, socket and result encoding that the same query does not pay embedded (1 to 3 microseconds).

Total invoiced across 10,000,000 invoices (SELECT SUM(amount_cents)): SQLite 414.54 ms, DuckDB 2.56 ms, SQL Server 943.63 ms, HoloDb under 0.01 ms, because a maintained total is read instead of 10 million rows.

What it costs:
- Look up one invoice: SQLite is ahead of embedded HoloDb, 0.01 ms against 0.02 ms at the benchmark's two-decimal resolution.
- Revenue by signup cohort (a join): DuckDB is ahead of embedded HoloDb by 1.25x, a parallel scan of the 10 million invoices against DuckDB's columnar engine. Two other queries tie with DuckDB (big-ticket invoices and enterprise revenue).
- Look up one invoice over the network: SQL Server answers in 0.07 ms and HoloDb server in 0.18 ms. About 0.07 ms of HoloDb's time is client, TLS and socket cost outside the engine.

#### The optional plane on the billing ledger

The plane is opt-in per table. This run attaches one to the invoices table: dimensions region (4 values), status (5) and month (24), a 10-bit joint, and the measure amount_cents. Building it for 10,000,000 rows takes 741 ms (749 ms on the server's database) and its cells take 34,528 bytes. All 16 results are identical across the engines.

Plane off and plane on, 10,000,000 invoices, median milliseconds (SQLite and DuckDB out of the box, in memory)

| Query | SQLite | DuckDB | HoloDb, plane off | HoloDb, plane on | Plane vs off |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| overdue outstanding | 429.30 | 11.43 | 5.93 | 0.01 | about 600x faster |
| revenue by region and status | 7,381.34 | 56.66 | 32.30 | 0.18 | about 180x faster |

Through the server the same two queries take 6.30 ms and 34.58 ms with the plane off and 0.11 ms and 0.45 ms with it on (SQL Server: 611.59 ms and 2,898.13 ms).

What the plane serves: filters and multi-column GROUP BY over its dimension columns. What it declines, and why: the big-ticket count (the filter is on a measure, not a dimension), top customers (200,000 distinct customer ids, far over the 1,024-value dimension limit), the five joins (200,000 join keys against a limit of 4,095) and the lookup and largest-invoices queries (no aggregate). The five rollups are left to the engine on purpose, because it reads a maintained total there in microseconds and the plane is slower. Per database, 12 calls were served by the plane and 42 declined.

The cells the plane does not touch run the identical engine path in both columns and differ by 1 to 13 percent typically and by up to 33 percent (big-ticket: 3.01 ms off, 2.26 ms on), so differences of that size are noise.

What it costs:
- The plane is not used for the rollups: whole-table counts and sums, single-column GROUP BY and MIN and MAX, where the engine already reads a maintained total in microseconds.

#### Constructed workload: a live dashboard

The filter combinations cannot be pre-indexed because nobody knows in advance which dimensions a person will cut by, the answers must be exact, and the table keeps changing while it is queried. The workload is 10,000,000 events and 32 ad-hoc slices over six small-domain dimensions (a 14-bit joint) and the measures. Building the plane takes 1,759 ms and its cells take 920,248 bytes. The slices are scalar filters (W), group-bys with and without a filter (G), HAVING (H), COUNT DISTINCT and MIN and MAX with a filter (D), queries outside the plane (X) and whole-table queries the engine already answers from a maintained total.

Plane against the engine and against the best other engine (SQLite, DuckDB and SQL Server, each out of the box), by class of slice

| Class (queries) | Plane vs engine, median | Plane vs best of SQLite, DuckDB, SQL Server, median |
|---|---|---|
| W scalar slices (9) | 121.40x | 191.5x |
| G group by (7) | 20.90x | 27.4x |
| H having (2) | 24.57x | 42.2x |
| D distinct, min/max with a filter (3) | 18.42x | 36.0x |
| X outside the plane (7) | 0.97x (tie) | 1.5x |

First call of each query, median milliseconds (DuckDB and SQL Server out of the box)

| Query | DuckDB | SQL Server | HoloDb engine | HoloDb plane |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| WHERE region = 'north' AND device = 'mobile', COUNT and SUM | 25.185 | 827.218 | 18.526 | 0.153 |
| GROUP BY region, device, COUNT and SUM | 56.712 | 3,012.047 | 43.222 | 2.068 |
| GROUP BY region, channel HAVING COUNT(*) > ... | 67.130 | 3,047.374 | 43.815 | 2.110 |
| COUNT(DISTINCT channel), COUNT(DISTINCT device) with a WHERE | 37.506 | 2,336.280 | 50.189 | 0.803 |
| (outside the plane: filter on user_id, a column that is not a dimension) | 12.139 | 486.466 | 11.300 | 11.484 |

The best other engine on the W, G, H and D slices is DuckDB in every row shown, out of the box: no indexes added and no summary table built. Three of the nine W cells are noisy, because the engine's own two timing loops disagree by more than 25 percent; the class median is as printed.

The first call of each query, which pays any one-time work, is also faster with the plane: the median first-call speed-up over the engine is 16.99x for W, 10.90x for G, 13.97x for H and 10.17x for D.

What it costs:
- The queries the plane declines or leaves to the engine (the X class: a filter on a non-dimension column, COUNT(DISTINCT user_id), a sum of a non-measure column, a top-10 by user, a filter on a measure, a row list and a point lookup by event id) run the engine's own path and tie with it: the seven X queries read 0.95x to 1.04x warm. On the first call five of the seven are slower with the plane attached, at 0.42x to 0.84x of the engine's first call (single samples).

#### Constructed workload: ingest while querying

A 2,000,000-row base table, then 20 rounds of a 10,000-row bulk load, 200 single-row INSERTs and an eight-query dashboard panel. The panel's results match in every round. How an insert followed by a query scales with the size of the table is under Scaling.

Per round, median milliseconds (SQLite, DuckDB and SQL Server out of the box)

| Per round (ms) | SQLite | DuckDB | SQL Server | HoloDb engine | HoloDb plane |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| panel (8 queries) | 3,794.93 | 112.30 | 3,057.90 | 137.90 | 11.53 |
| round total (bulk load, INSERTs, panel) | 3,816.72 | 239.88 | 3,109.90 | 149.47 | 25.84 |

What it costs:
- Writes cost more with the plane attached: the 10,000-row bulk load takes 11.62 ms against 9.85 ms (1.18x), and 200 single-row INSERTs take 1.55 ms against 1.23 ms (1.26x), about 7.8 microseconds against 6.2 per INSERT.

#### Constructed workload: multi-tenant slices and joins

Five million events spread over six tenant tables (2,000,000 down to 150,000 rows) and a 2,000-product dimension table. A filter with a COUNT and SUM on one tenant is a median 11.70x faster than the engine and 25.0x faster than the best other engine (DuckDB, SQLite and SQL Server each out of the box). The largest tenant reads 0.171 ms with the plane, 4.263 ms for the engine, 6.312 ms for DuckDB and 195.195 ms for SQL Server.

The same join repeated, median milliseconds (DuckDB and SQL Server out of the box)

| Query | DuckDB | SQL Server | HoloDb engine | HoloDb plane, embedded | HoloDb plane, server |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| join COUNT, largest tenant (2,000,000 rows) | 1.749 | 307.039 | 0.380 | 0.002 | 0.078 |
| join COUNT and two SUMs, largest tenant | 2.906 | 477.043 | 2.716 | 0.003 | 0.079 |
| join COUNT, smallest tenant (150,000 rows) | 0.947 | 23.678 | 0.110 | 0.002 | 0.071 |
| join COUNT and two SUMs, smallest tenant | 1.392 | 37.158 | 0.999 | 0.003 | 0.073 |

The join is one statement repeated: tenant events joined to the products table on the product key (about 2,000 keys), with COUNT(*) alone or with two SUMs. The plane serves a repeat from a memo of the exact answer, valid until either of the two tables is written, so the very low figures are for a repeated identical statement with no write in between. A memo hit takes 0.001 to 0.003 ms embedded and 0.071 to 0.084 ms through the server.

Joins with a WHERE or a GROUP BY on the dimension table are not served by the plane; they run the engine's path and tie with it (0.93x to 1.02x).

What it costs:
- A join that is not a memo hit usually costs more through the plane than the engine's own join. The first call of a statement costs more through the plane than through the engine in 11 of the 12 join cells: join COUNT 1.016 to 2.921 ms through the plane on the five smaller tenants against 0.179 to 0.573 ms for the engine, and join COUNT with two SUMs 2.348 to 8.134 ms against 1.364 to 3.076 ms. If the tables are written between nearly every read, expect the plane join to cost more than the engine's own join; the plane's value on such a workload comes from the filters and group-bys.

#### The plane against the engine at 1,000,000 rows

Seventeen query classes on a 1,000,000-row table, with the engine alone, the engine with the plane, and SQLite. The control query (one the plane declines, so both sides run the same engine path) reads 0.81, inside the band of 0.8 to 1.25. The join rows use a very small dimension table: 40 distinct join keys for the two INT joins and 4 for the TEXT join, so they say little about joins over many keys.

Seventeen query classes at 1,000,000 rows (SQLite in memory; the two INT joins have 40 distinct join keys and the TEXT join has 4)

| Query class | SQLite | HoloDb engine | HoloDb plane | Plane vs engine |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| COUNT(*) whole table | 417.4 us | 1.6 us | 3.3 us | slower (0.48x) |
| SUM(qty) whole table | 40.25 ms | 1.8 us | 3.8 us | slower (0.47x) |
| GROUP BY 1 column | 288.46 ms | 4.4 us | 10.2 us | slower (0.43x) |
| GROUP BY 2 columns | 484.34 ms | 2.88 ms | 2.40 ms | tie (1.20x) |
| WHERE = on 1 column | 48.11 ms | 1.28 ms | 3.8 us | 336x faster |
| WHERE BETWEEN | 52.23 ms | 620.0 us | 9.2 us | noisy, no ratio |
| WHERE on 3 columns (AND/IN) | 65.19 ms | 1.63 ms | 144.2 us | 11x faster |
| WHERE LIKE ... OR | 61.37 ms | 1.24 ms | 37.2 us | 33x faster |
| GROUP BY with WHERE | 126.79 ms | 3.10 ms | 2.32 ms | 1.34x faster |
| COUNT DISTINCT whole table | 81.41 ms | 2.1 us | 1.7 us | tie (1.24x) |
| COUNT DISTINCT with WHERE | 71.71 ms | 1.91 ms | 630.7 us | 3.0x faster |
| MIN/MAX of an INT column | 51.34 ms | 1.8 us | 3.4 us | slower (0.53x) |
| Range count | 44.39 ms | 343.4 us | 2.7 us | 127x faster |
| Join COUNT | 69.68 ms | 3.75 ms | 15.9 us | noisy, no ratio |
| Join SUM (both sides) | 108.23 ms | 4.92 ms | 85.5 us | 58x faster |
| Join on a TEXT key | 327.89 ms | 37.36 ms | 8.0 us | 4,670x faster |
| Query outside the plane (control) | 48.55 ms | 938.1 us | 1.16 ms (declined, engine path) | tie (0.81x) |

The engine alone is faster than in-memory SQLite on every class; the whole-table classes compare a maintained total with a scan. The plane is faster than SQLite on every class it serves. Against the engine it wins where there is a real scan or join to avoid. Outcome counts for the plane against the engine: 7 classes at least 2x faster, 3 ties, 1 between 1.25x and 2x, 4 slower, 2 noisy.

At 100,000 rows the engine is faster than the plane on seven of the 17 classes: the whole-table classes, the single-column GROUP BY and MIN and MAX (0.33x to 0.51x), the two-column GROUP BY (0.26x), GROUP BY with a WHERE (0.41x) and COUNT DISTINCT with a WHERE (0.58x). At 300,000 rows the plane is faster on every filter and join (24x to 1,887x) and on the two-column GROUP BY (1.77x). Default routing sends GROUP BY with a WHERE to the engine below 140,000 rows.

The plane's cost when attached, against the engine alone: single-row INSERT 1.4x to 1.9x, UPDATE 1.6x to 1.8x (microseconds that move with the order the two arms run in); batch load of the whole table 1.93 s with the plane against 1.80 s without at 1,000,000 rows; rebuilding the plane from the columns 131 ms; a heap of 139.7 bytes per row with the plane against 135.2 without; the plane's cells are a flat 0.92 MB joint slice whatever the row count.

The TEXT-key join is faster than SQLite in the engine alone (39.98 ms against 322.17 ms at 1,000,000 rows, rows identical). It requires both join columns to be TEXT; a join between an INT column and a TEXT column takes the general path and is much slower.

What it costs:
- With the plane attached, whole-table COUNT(*) (0.48x), whole-table SUM (0.47x), single-column GROUP BY (0.43x) and MIN and MAX (0.53x) are slower than the engine alone, because the engine reads a maintained total in microseconds.

#### Scaling

Each line is a recorded run on logarithmic axes, and its slope says how the cost grows: a slope of 1.00 is one step for every item, and a slope near zero is a cost that does not depend on how many items there are. Only the engine and the plane appear here; no other database is timed in this section.

The control, a fixed amount of work repeated at each size, fits a slope of -0.47 because its first point includes start-up compilation (165 microseconds against 9 to 24 for the other four). The first point of every time series carries the same start-up cost, so a time slope under about 0.4 is shown as nearly flat and is not read as an exact exponent. Counts (commit groups, transform passes) carry no such noise and are exact. The write-then-read pairs are 200 repetitions of one insert followed by the same two-column group-by at each table size, one run per size, with a placebo pair beside them.

Fitted slope of log cost on log size: one step per item, and one step for the whole set

| What grows, and what is measured | One step per item | One step for the whole set |
|---|---|---|
| Changes in a batch, time | 0.96 | 0.21 (nearly flat) |
| Changes in a batch, commit groups written | 1.00 | 0.00 |
| Flag words added to a plane, time | 0.98 | 0.04 (nearly flat) |
| Measures in a group-by, transform passes | 0.88 | 0.00 |
| Measures in a group-by, time | 0.62 | 0.43 |
| Group-bys in one refresh, transform passes | 1.00 | 1.00 |
| Group-bys in one refresh, time | 1.03 | 0.97 |

One insert, then the same two-column group-by, per pair, as the table grows

| Rows in the table | Engine alone | With the plane | Placebo ratio (a query the plane declines; the band is 0.8 to 1.25) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 100,000 | 1.03 ms | 385 us | 1.04 |
| 300,000 | 1.44 ms | 343 us | 1.03 |
| 1,000,000 | 3.54 ms | 354 us | 0.97 |

Write, then read. With the plane attached, one insert followed by one two-column group-by costs 385 us, 343 us and 354 us per pair at 100,000, 300,000 and 1,000,000 rows: flat across a tenfold growth in the table. The engine alone costs 1.03 ms, 1.44 ms and 3.54 ms for the same pair, a slope of 0.54, because the group-by scans the table. A placebo pair that runs a query the plane declines (so both arms take the same path) reads 1.04, 1.03, 0.97, inside its band.

Changes in a batch. B changes applied one statement at a time cost one lock, one log commit and one plane update each: the time slope is 0.96, and the commit groups written equal the changes made (slope 1.00). One ApplyChanges call writes exactly one commit group at every B (slope 0.00), and its time grows far more slowly than the statements do. It keeps growing: from 512 to 2,048 changes its slope is 0.69, because the per-row work on the table remains and only the fixed costs are shared.

Flag words. Adding k flag words to a 14-bit plane with k separate Add calls has a slope of 0.98. One AddFlagWords call, which is a Phasor Pleroma operation, takes 169 to 211 microseconds from k = 16 to k = 4,096, nearly flat.

Measures in a group-by. A group-by that sums M measures reads 1 + 3M planes, because each measure is held as three limbs beside the count plane: 4 planes at M = 1 and 25 at M = 8. Read plane by plane, the transform passes grow with a slope of 0.88; read by one multi-plane call (Pleroma FlagsMany) they are 1 at every M (slope 0.00). Time falls from a slope of 0.62 to 0.43, and no lower, because the answer itself grows with M: a repeat that skips the transform and only builds the result takes 23 to 42 microseconds.

Group-bys in one refresh. With four measures, refreshing G group-bys together still costs one transform per group-by: the passes grow with a slope of 1.00 read plane by plane and 1.00 read by one multi-plane call, and the time with 1.03 and 0.97. Each distinct group-by is its own read.

What it costs:
- Group-bys in one refresh: each distinct group-by is its own read, so the time and the transform passes grow in proportion to the number of group-bys (time slope 0.97 with the multi-plane read).
- Measures in a group-by: the transform passes stay at one, but the time still grows (slope 0.43), because the answer grows with the number of measures.
- Changes in a batch: a bigger batch costs more (slope 0.69 from 512 to 2,048 changes); only the fixed costs, one lock, one commit and one plane pass, are shared.

#### Dashboard reads during live ingest, and opening a database

Whole-table counts and sums, and GROUP BY on a column with up to 64 distinct values, are served from a snapshot republished after every write, without taking the engine's write lock. On a 16-core laptop that was not idle, 2,000,000 events ingested in 1,000-row batches at 1.16 million events a second while 4 concurrent readers queried: median read 0.009 to 0.09 ms, p99 0.8 ms (group by region), 1.1 ms (sum) and 6.6 ms (count), worst single read 6.7 ms.

Opening a database of 1,000,000 rows (a 43 MB log) takes about 2.0 s by replaying its write-ahead log (1.95 to 2.05 s across two runs) and about 1.1 s from a checkpoint (1.09 to 1.11 s), with the loaded state checked correct and a heap of about 110 bytes per row, in a newly started process. This is the engine's own recovery and checkpoint; it does not use the plane or the page store.

What it costs:
- A GROUP BY with more than 64 distinct values (the per-minute series in the same test has 167) takes the normal locked path and waits behind the ingest for up to 0.9 s (p99 0.9 s).

#### Checks behind the figures

Every release is measured against the one before it: each benchmark cell is run twice on each build, and a cell counts as a regression only if it is worse than 25 percent (or the baseline's own spread) in both pairs. The check covers the 10,000,000-invoice comparison, the plane benchmark at 100,000, 300,000 and 1,000,000 rows, and opening a 1,000,000-row database from its log and from a checkpoint, and finds no cell slower.

Queries the plane declines or leaves to the engine stay within noise: of the 16 queries that run the same path in both arms, none falls outside a band of 0.8x to 1.25x, with class medians of 0.97 and 0.99. A deliberately wrong plane (the measure column shuffled at 1,000,000 rows) is caught on every query it changes and matches on every query it does not: 0 failures of 32.

The aggregate plane returns row-for-row the same answers as the engine and SQLite across the parity suite (2,853 checks at 2,000 rows, and the suite also passes at 5,000 and 100,000 rows), including a random insert, update, delete, rollback and reopen log, and sums past 64 bits. Nine deliberate mutations (a dropped carry, a missed delete, a stale join limb and others) each turn the suite red. Sums past 64 bits are never wrapped: the plane raises an error and PleromaSumExact returns the exact 128-bit total.

The page store passes 72 of 72 checks: exactly-once replay after a crash, a torn journal tail discarded, restore points that rewind without recounting, and repair of a lost page from its parity group. Eight deliberate mutations and a tiny-cache case each turn the suite red.

A paged table checks every 8 KB data page against a checksum kept in a small side file. In a test that flipped 61 bits in the data file of a 91 MB paged table, none gave a silently different answer: 36 were reported with an error that names the page, and 25 were in pages never read.

Atomicity and crash recovery are covered by a 48-check suite (a failing log append is undone in full, a reopen from the log reproduces the committed state) and a 58-check transaction suite plus about 600 randomised comparisons against SQLite; three deliberate mutations each turn it red.

Limits:
- Each figure comes from a single run on a single machine, and the plane sections use constructed workloads: one synthetic table (9 columns, four small-domain dimensions, a 14-bit joint). The plane serves only the columns you attach. A plane made with EnablePleroma lives in RAM and is not persisted; a plane made with SQL, and the summaries the planner builds by itself, are saved with the table.
- In the engine alone, GROUP BY with a WHERE is about 3 ms at 1,000,000 rows because the filter and the grouping are separate passes. The dense-code GROUP BY covers INT and TEXT columns whose combined distinct count is at most 65,536, and anything else uses a slower string-key path. REAL aggregates over a filter use a scan.
- The first DDL statement inside a transaction takes a snapshot of every in-memory table, so it costs time proportional to the data. After a ROLLBACK of deleted rows the table holds the same rows but not necessarily in the same internal order.
- The aggregate plane does not serve the billing joins at 10,000,000 invoices (200,000 join keys against its limit of 4,095) or the top-customers query; the keyed summary and the pre-grouped join totals of paged tables do. A plane join over fewer keys is served, as in the tenant workload.
- The scaling lines are fits over four or five sizes on one machine, and the write-then-read pairs are one run per table size of one repeated group-by. Time slopes under about 0.4 are not read as exact exponents.

## Research

### Fifty reads, one store

Page: https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/research/one-store-many-reads/
Topics: exact stores, Pleroma

Finding: Fifty reads, one store. One fixed-size array of exact integers answers fifty different questions, each in a single pass over the array. The one exception is `CausalReads`, which takes one read per prefix. Counts by key. Counts by flag word. The nearest stored words. Arrangement order. Parity. Time. Joint counts across any chosen faces. Every count it returns is exact within the field's range (about 1.15 x 10^18 on the default field), and when the store is full the key views refuse rather than guess.

#### In brief

The Pleroma is a new construction and a mathematical discovery. Its proof is the code.

The numbers were measured against the standard. At 2,064 and 2,580 bits, the two budgets the benchmark ran, the Pleroma recovered 64 items exactly, in 200 of 200 trials. Plate's holographic memory (HRR), and its phase form (FHRR), with the best decoder tried, recovered 4 items reliably and none from 16 upward. Past the Pleroma's capacity, 65 to 96 items, it refused all 12,800 trials and gave no wrong answer. The baselines answered every time, and every answer was wrong.

#### How it was found

The project starts where its philosophy and ethics start, and reduces to the fewest axioms that reasoning needs. In its own words:

It is how we start from philosophy and ethics to figure out the most minimal set of axioms for reasoning, and build up from that on first principles.

Three of its statements carry the reduction: "Consciousness exists.", "Non-contradiction is necessary for coherent reasoning.", and "Claims about reality are more reliable when tested against reality."

Two axioms follow: there is an observer, and a resolved state does not contain both P and not-P. From them comes the first distinction. Whatever appears from the void comes with its opposite, so 0 = (+1) + (−1). The project calls this pair the syzygy.

Once the syzygy is in hand, its symmetries can be counted. They are the signed permutations of the cross-polytope, and they split exactly into two parts: sign flips, each its own inverse, and permutations. The flips form the ouroboros, and the permutations form the monad.

The project's rule for climbing from here: "A tick therefore adds one symmetry, and climbing the ladder is mapping the lineage of symmetries in order."

The thesis comes next. The project states it as: "The Pleroma ... is the one object all their holograms are shadows of." A shadow is what the larger object shows when it is read on some of its faces and not others.

The search for that object gives a map: the ladder laid out as rungs, each read across three faces. The map is predictive. It says what each cell should be, and each cell is then built and proved.

The ladder: eight rungs, each read across three faces

| Rung | Counts (syzygy) | Choices (monad) | Parities (ouroboros) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 Pair | ±1 | one of two | the toggle |
| 2 Identity | a position | a corner | a truth assignment |
| 3 Relation | counts | order | parity |
| 4 Function | table, Fourier | a map | Boolean function, Walsh |
| 5 Symmetry | h → u·h | conjugation | Frobenius |
| 6 Composition | Chinese remainder | independent choices | Hamming codes |
| 7 Turning | the spiral | mixing | shift-register cycles |
| 8 Circulation | winding | probability current | frustration |

The method is the same for every cell. The prediction and its null are written first. The operation is built as a public member of the store. Its answer is checked against a brute-force rebuild, and the test is broken on purpose to confirm it fails for the right reason. For rung 3, ten symbols bound as four-symbol sequences give 715 distinct multisets, 10,000 distinct orders, and 256 parity classes, each checked against the rebuilt store.

#### The rungs said which operations superpose

The derivation's operator rule: a symmetry is a group element, and a weighted sum of group elements is one kernel. It acts on each harmonic with one multiplication, so its cost is one pass whatever the size of the sum. The same rule says choosing is not linear, so the one choice is made at the read.

The code was measured against that rule across the public surface. Eight of the 41 operators that change the store join one kernel and apply in one pass; key shifts do so on a keyed kernel. Sixteen take one pass per term in a mix. Seventeen are writes that are not kernel elements. The 50 reads are separate, each one pass, and nine of them are answered through a read set.

On a 10,464-cell store, `Apply` takes 0.17 to 0.44 ms per call, for a kernel of anything from 1 operator up to 10,368, with no trend across that range. Building the same store from the moved items takes 1,916 ms at 1,000 operators. The figures are a Release build on a loaded machine, two runs.

#### Twenty-four cells, each an operation

Every cell is a public member of `Pleroma`. The grid covers eight rungs by three faces, and the lid. Each cell has its own brute-force check.

The 24 cells: the public member for each rung and face, and the lid

| Rung | Counts (syzygy) | Choices (monad) | Parities (ouroboros) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 Pair | `Add`, `Remove` | `SignBalance` | `RelabelFlags` (XOR mask) |
| 2 Identity | `TryKeys`, `TryItems`, `Counts` | `Arrangements`, `ArrangementIndex` | `Flags`, `Near`, `Nearest` |
| 3 Relation | `Bind`, `JointCounts`, `Attend` | `ComposeArrangements`, `Attend` | `BitCounts`, `FlagParity`, `Attend` |
| 4 Function | `ShiftKeys`, `ModulateKeys` | `TimeMap`, `MapTimes` | `CountWhere` (Walsh spectrum) |
| 5 Symmetry | `ScaleKeys` | `RelabelArrangements` | `Frobenius`, `Apply(FlagOperator)` |
| 6 Composition | `CombineCycles` | `IsIndependent` | `Syndrome` |
| 7 Turning | `Tick`, `FadedTimes` | `Diffuse` | `ShiftRegister` |
| 8 Circulation | `Holonomy`, `ReadLoop` | `Current` | `Frustration` |
| Lid | `Sample`, a read-time draw over all three faces |  |  |

#### Protection and size

Each face protects its own store in its own way.

- Counts: a page on a larger cycle, with r keys known to be empty, rebuilds any r lost harmonics exactly: 300 of 300 at each erasure size from 1 to 5. It detects corrupted harmonics and corrects up to half that many at unknown positions.
- Choices: a second prime holds a mirror of every cell. One corrupted cell in either copy is detected, 10,000 of 10,000.
- Parities: a parity page, the sum of the pages, rebuilds any one lost page, 100 of 100.

The unit workload is 53,031 pages of 110 cells each, and it fits in 49.6 MB. A plane of 14 flag bits and 16,386 cells stores at 8.02 bytes per cell. A sparse page holding one key takes 183 bytes and reads in 0.4 µs.

#### Built on

The Pleroma is a new construction. Each brick it stands on is established mathematics or an established algorithm, credited here:

- Plate's Holographic Reduced Representations (1995), and its phase form FHRR. The continuous component is the bundle, and both are the equal-storage baselines.
- Reed and Solomon (1960), with Bose and Ray-Chaudhuri (1960): syndrome decoding of power sums, which the key view uses.
- Berlekamp (1968) and Massey (1969): the Berlekamp-Massey recurrence, with a re-encode check.
- PinSketch (Talbot et al., 2012) and minisketch (Poinsot et al., 2017): exact set sketches that subtract and decode the difference.
- The Walsh-Hadamard transform: counts under any predicate of the flag word, in one read.
- Fourier analysis on finite groups: binding as convolution.
- The Chinese remainder theorem: joining coprime key cycles.
- Hamming codes (1950): syndromes that locate a single error.
- Galois linear feedback shift registers and the Frobenius map on GF(2^m).
- Time diffusion on a cycle, from Markov chains.
- Krawtchouk polynomials, which underlie the views.
- The universal coefficient theorem, Schläfli's classification of regular polytopes, Galois and Abel-Ruffini on the simplicity of A_5, Kolmogorov's criterion for circulation, Bott periodicity, and the Altland-Zirnbauer and Kitaev symmetry classes.

#### Where the code does not superpose today

- Key scaling costs one pass per term in a mix. A key shift joins a kernel only on a keyed kernel; on an unkeyed one a mix of key shifts costs one pass per term.
- Right relabelling, conjugation and flag sign flips cost one pass per term.
- Bit maps on the flag cube, and fixed per-key or per-tick weights, are not kernel elements. A mix of them costs one pass per term.
- Commuting with the symmetry is necessary for a kernel and not sufficient. `Hadamard` commutes and is not a kernel element, and `ShiftKeys` is one only through a keyed kernel.
- Each read makes its own transform by default. A transform is shared between reads only inside an internal planner that is not exposed.
- A kernel on a store with a check prime runs through a mirror kernel in the check prime, built from the same elements; a kernel built from a shape without that check prime is refused.
- Key reads refuse past their capacity. A store keeps 2K+1 harmonics per key line, so K+1 distinct keys always refuse. A complete key band goes to 4,096 keys.
- Counts are exact within the field's signed range. A plain read does not check for a wrap. On a store with a check prime, `VerifyCheck` detects one within the check bound.
- The store runs on the CPU. Its gain is exactness and many views on one array, not raw speed for a single read.
- Rung 8's contradiction location is not built, and reunification, the rung where observers merge, is open.

#### The four families and the order face

The store holds the harmonic transform of its items on one product of four families: the key cycle, the flag cube, the symmetric group and the time cycle. Each view reads its own slice of the same cells, because each view is a shadow on some of the faces.

The search found the flags and the permutations as the two halves of the root's symmetry. The key cycle is the syzygy's own cycle, realised on a finite field. The time family is the rung-7 step repeated. A direct product does not depend on the order of its factors. The listing follows the order in which the search met them.

The order face is built for S_2 to S_5, up to 120 arrangements. The shape definition sets the cap, and the record gives no further reason for it.

Five is also where repeated splitting first meets a part it cannot split: the alternating group A_5, of order 60, the rotation group of the icosahedron. That is a coincidence of the two facts, and the cap is not derived from it.

The splitting chains are: 2 to 1; 6 to 3 to 1; 24 to 12 to 4 to 1; 120 to 60 to 60. The shadow of the root holds on sequences, 10,000 of 10,000, and on loops, 9,000 of 9,000.

#### Signed removal and plus and minus

Removal adds the opposite count. This fits the project's rule that a distinction, once made, is not unmade. The cell layout keeps its size, and a removed item leaves its cells at zero.

The cancellation test adds an item and then its opposite, and every cell is zero afterwards, with the default field and with three primes.

A plus and a minus of the same item share one cell and cancel there exactly.

#### Closeness on the cube

Closeness on the flag cube is Hamming distance. `Near(query, r)` counts the stored items whose flag word lies within r bits of the query, and `Nearest` returns the nearest stored words with their distances. Both are exact at 200 keys. The key view refuses past its capacity, but the flag-cube read does not depend on the key count.

#### The lid

`Sample` is a read-time draw. It returns a value with probability count over total, taken from the exact counts, and it leaves the store unchanged. A check confirms that every draw lands on its exact share.

The map places the lid at the top of the ladder: the top rung iterated, with the faces divergence, forgetting and pseudo-randomness.

#### The map and where the code stands

The map says what each cell should be. Each row below is a place where the map's statement and the code are checked against each other, and what the code does today.

Held as mapped

- Rung 3: 715 distinct multisets, 10,000 distinct orders, 256 parity classes.
- A complete cycle sums to exactly zero, and a symbol read on coprime cycles decodes exactly, 20,000 of 20,000.
- Relation networks stored as bound facts give exact loop sums, and planted contradictions are found: 40 of 40 networks, no false alarms in 20.
- Nested structure answers every path question exactly, 851 of 851.
- The mirror cells that label the ten symmetry classes hold on every realisation: 10 of 10 classes, 11,995 relation checks over 2,079 realisations.
- Four composition recipes, built only from existing operations, are exact against brute force, 4 of 4.

Where the code stands against the map

Where the map's statement and the code were checked against each other

| The map says | The code today |
|---|---|
| The continuous circle holds the rungs exactly. | It holds them up to its dimension. Exact storage is the finite field: with p = 65,537 and d = 128, recovery is 100% for 8 to 64 items and 0% at 65. The continuous circle is the graded-similarity component. |
| The spiral's eight steps are the eight named rungs. | They are two ladders. Each spiral step adds an operator of order 2 or 4; the rungs add cycles of every order. |
| The anti-universe starts at three states. | Groups of two gain as much as groups of three. |
| The lid has an ordered regime before chaos, and entropy rises steadily. | The lid has no ordered regime before chaos. The divergence from the settled state is monotone; entropy is not. |
| Reunification, the rung where observers merge by exact difference, is the next rung. | It is open. |
| A wrap is detected while the true value lies inside both check ranges. | `VerifyCheck` detects a wrap on a store with a check prime, within the check bound. A plain read does not check. The parity claim for the running bundle is not measured. |

#### The gaps, grouped

The theory says these should superpose, and the code does not:

- Key shifts and key scaling permute the key harmonics. A keyed kernel has the key-harmonic axis, so a key shift is one of its elements; key scaling is not.
- Right relabelling and conjugation act from the right on the order face. The kernel holds the left action only. A superposed conjugation exists in an experiment record and not in the library.
- Flag sign flips and per-key or per-tick weights cost one pass per term.
- Relation faces under projection and under the Chinese remainder theorem.
- Causal reads take one read per prefix. A prefix structure over the sequence is not built.

Design limits, set by the data rather than a missing operation:

- A complete key band costs one cell per key, up to 4,096 keys. A truncated band holds 2K+1 harmonics per key line.
- Exact keys carry no metric, so a nearest-key read needs the continuous component, which is approximate.
- Choosing (argmax, sampling, a decode that refuses) happens once, at the read.

Other boundaries:

- Exact within the signed range. A plain read does not check for a wrap; `VerifyCheck` does on a store with a check prime, within the check bound.
- `Bind` is refused with several primes, and `ShiftKeys` on several primes needs an explicit key cycle.
- `CombineCycles` refuses a store with a relation face.
- The joint slice is capped at 2^24 cells.
- Tenants as flag bits share one store while tenant bits plus data bits stay at 16 or fewer.

#### Cost of exactness, one page per context against a hash map

In a sequence-model test, the same exact counts were held two ways: a hash map, and one dense Pleroma page per context. The two agree on every cell, 5,037,945 of 5,037,945.

The same exact counts held two ways: a hash map and one dense Pleroma page per context

| Measure | Hash map | Pleroma pages, one per context |
|---|---|---|
| memory | 22.3 MB | 757.8 MB (44.5 MB of cells) |
| read, 8 subsets per position | 0.67 µs | 131 µs |
| build | 0.45 s | 2.06 s |
| training step, 32 by 128 | 6.8 s | 6.2 s |

With the shared layout, the same pages occupy 66.2 MB as standalone stores, and 49.6 MB as one page set.

A long-context store still sits in a sorted host index, which is exact up to 16 subwords and reads in microseconds. The sparse page class exists, but the page store's keys are 63 bits, and a context of four or more subwords needs 128.

### The Four-Token Ceiling

Page: https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/research/context-four/
Topics: context length, small models

Finding: A holographic language model pinned to four tokens of context stops improving its top-guess margin at about round 48,000 and stops adding spelled words between rounds 15,000 and 21,000, while calibration and the specialisation of one weight bank keep changing through more than 80,000 rounds.

#### Setup

The model is a fresh set of weights with the same shape and the same real corpus as the main lineage. Its context is fixed at exactly 4 tokens for the whole run, and no schedule grows it. The architecture runs one fixed weight matrix through eight refinement passes on every token, and the state after each pass can be inspected as well as the final answer.

Four tokens of context cannot carry long-range coherence: a model that sees only the last four tokens has no mechanism for staying consistent with a subject from six tokens back. The run is therefore graded on spelling and on local structure, not on whether it writes a sensible paragraph.

The extrapolation multiplier is the length of the longest correct stretch of output divided by the four-token window. A correct stretch longer than the window cannot be read off the input and has to be reconstructed from the weights, so the multiplier separates building from repeating within the window.

A permanent battery of tests runs directly against saved checkpoints. It was run every 3,000 rounds on a fresh checkpoint out past 80,000 rounds, and every snapshot from the run is kept.

#### Evidence: what stopped moving

Three measures stopped moving. The primary signal is the gap between the model's top guess and its second-best guess, a proxy for whether the runner-up is still catching the winner. It plateaued at about round 48,000. Splitting the run into thirds and comparing the middle third's average with the final third's gives equal values: the signal is flat, not slowly rising.

The effective vocabulary, the set of corpus words the model reliably spells, capped between rounds 15,000 and 21,000 and did not grow in the 60,000 or more rounds after. The measurement was made twice, independently, and both gave the same result.

The rate at which plain generation falls into a repeat loop reached a floor. At the latest checkpoints a plain generation run falls into a repeat loop in the large majority of runs. A long-form test on this run shows the collapse rate was already high at the earliest checkpoints and stayed in that band. A lower collapse rate at larger contexts, seen in a different and longer run, does not carry over to this one.

Measures that stopped moving at a context of four tokens

| Measure | Behaviour | Round |
|---|---|---|
| Gap between top and second-best guess | Flat; middle-third average equals final-third average | about 48,000 |
| Effective vocabulary | Capped; no growth in the following 60,000 or more rounds; confirmed by two independent measurements | 15,000 to 21,000 |
| Collapse into a repeat loop | High at the earliest checkpoints and unchanged through the run | Present from the first checkpoint |

#### Evidence: what kept moving

Two things never plateaued across the 80,000 or more rounds. The first is the specialisation of one weight bank: its channels specialise harder throughout the run, with zero reversals. One channel in that bank, the no-relative-shift channel, was the most active channel in two separate investigations on two different checkpoints.

That channel is consistent with a gate: it appears to decide, per token, how much of the eight-pass iterative budget is spent on real work and how much is served from an embedding-level guess. Part of the model's numeric encoding is a fixed codec that has not been trained since round one, and the model routes through it more over time. The codec does not change; the model leans on it more. This reading is an interpretation of the channel's activity, not a separately measured result.

The second is calibration. When the top guess is wrong, the rank of the correct answer and the probability mass placed near it kept improving after the primary metric went flat. The model did not get better at being right; it got better at being usefully wrong.

The specialisation trend is steady and linear, not accelerating. Acceleration is the signature of an approaching sudden transition of the kind called grokking, so the trend gives no sign of one approaching. The general phenomenon of a flat visible output over a reorganising interior is the grokking pattern; what this run adds is its observation in this architecture.

Measures that kept changing after the primary metric went flat

| Measure | Behaviour over 80,000 or more rounds |
|---|---|
| Specialisation of one weight bank | Rises throughout, zero reversals, linear and not accelerating |
| No-relative-shift channel | Most active channel on two checkpoints in two separate investigations |
| Calibration (rank and probability mass of the correct answer when the top guess is wrong) | Keeps improving after the primary metric is flat |

#### Evidence: measurements that did not measure what they appeared to

Raw accuracy under corrupted input rises with more training, which reads as growing robustness. It is not robustness: the model increasingly echoes the last visible token regardless of what was corrupted, and the corruption filler used coincided with the model's favourite echo target. The rise is an artefact of the test design.

The reduced collapse rate remembered from a different run does not appear in this run when tested directly with a long-form test (see the plateau section).

#### What this means for a small model

Compare the middle and final thirds of the margin signal before deciding a size is finished; a slow climb and a plateau look alike on a curve and differ in that comparison.

Once the effective vocabulary has capped, more rounds at the same context do not add spelled words. Further capability needs a change other than more rounds at that size.

Track calibration separately from top-guess accuracy. It can keep improving under a flat headline metric.

Do not read a rise in accuracy under corrupted input as robustness unless the filler is different from the token the model echoes.

#### Limits

One lineage, one shape and one corpus. The window is four tokens, so nothing here concerns long-range coherence. The extrapolation multiplier is defined here and used as the stopping test, but its measured values are not reported in this article. The gating and codec-reliance readings of the no-relative-shift channel are interpretations of activity, not isolated causal tests.

#### Refuted by

A longer run in which the margin between the top and second-best guess is higher in the final third than in the middle third; a count of reliably spelled words that grows after round 21,000; or a reversal in the specialisation trend of the weight bank.

Related: Growing the Wrong Way https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/research/context-eight/

### Growing the Wrong Way

Page: https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/research/context-eight/
Topics: context length, growth

Finding: Growing a four-token model that had plateaued to eight tokens of context gave no recovery in about 100,000 rounds, and growth by appending new position slots after the most-trained one demotes that slot on every grow, whereas inserting new slots before the oldest one keeps it in place.

#### Setup

The starting point is the final trained weights of the four-token run described in the article The Four-Token Ceiling, whose top-guess margin had plateaued. A new model is seeded from those weights and its context is grown to eight tokens. The test is whether training a context fully at the smaller size makes the larger one easier to absorb.

The main metric is the same top-guess margin used at four tokens. Other measures are calibration, long-form generation sampled at dozens of checkpoints, and the specialisation of the weight bank that kept changing at four tokens.

#### Evidence: no payoff from a finished seed

No recovery appeared in the first 20,000 rounds after the grow, or in the next 70,000. The margin oscillated in a wide band for the whole period, past the point where the four-token run's own training life would have finished. Calibration got worse before it improved. Long-form generation stayed collapsed into repeat loops at every checkpoint pulled, dozens of them, spread over nearly 100,000 rounds.

One measure held: the weight bank that specialises at four tokens kept specialising, checkpoint after checkpoint, through the grow. It behaves as a general mechanism and not a context-specific one.

Measures after growing from four to eight tokens

| Measure | Outcome |
|---|---|
| Top-guess margin | Oscillates in a wide band; no settled recovery in about 100,000 rounds |
| Calibration | Worse before better |
| Long-form generation | Repeat-loop collapse at every checkpoint, dozens over nearly 100,000 rounds |
| Specialisation of the general weight bank | Keeps rising through the grow |

#### Evidence: the learning rate does not explain the stall

A learning-rate boost that the training engine gives a model after a context grow did not fire in this run, because the fork bypassed the normal path that triggers it. That does not explain the stall. The four-token model produced all of its own improvement at that same floor learning rate, so a starved rate would have stopped the four-token run as well, and it did not.

With the learning rate excluded, the premise is not supported: fully mining a small context before growing did not make the bigger context easier to absorb.

#### Evidence: growth is not the problem

The one measure that never stopped improving through the eight-token run was the general, non-position-specific structure. Content that is generic should not need a context size to be finished before it is worth having, and the record is consistent with that.

On that basis the schedule was changed from a context tier every 20,000 rounds to a context tier every 200 rounds, on the reasoning that cheap early token-level structure does not need relearning at each size. Comparable capability appeared at comparable round counts to the four-token run, as generic transfer predicts. These early results are not tabulated here.

#### Evidence: appending slots demotes the most important one

Every position slot in the context window has its own separately trained representation. The highest-indexed slot always means the token immediately before the one being predicted, the most load-bearing position. Growing by appending capacity past that slot demotes it to the middle of the window and puts a new untrained slot in the role that matters most.

This happens on every grow. Pacing the growth more slowly spreads the damage and does not remove it. After growth to a thousand tokens, the slot that reads what was just said has had less training than almost any other slot in the window. The cause is structural, not a training-procedure problem.

The alternative is to insert new capacity before the oldest slot and shift every existing position up. The slot meaning immediately before prediction keeps its trained values through any number of grows, and new capacity lands on context further in the past, where starting from zero is cheapest.

This is safe for a specific reason, checked against the code: the attention mechanism does not work on relative position. The model's sense of position lives in exactly one place, a lookup table added onto each token, so nothing else depends on slot order.

Newly built models use front insertion by default. Existing checkpoints are pinned to the old behaviour when loaded, so a trained model does not change under itself, and old and new can coexist.

#### What this means for a small model

Do not expect a model converged at a small context to absorb a larger one faster. Treat context growth as its own change and measure it.

Before blaming a stall on the learning rate, check whether a model that did improve ran at the same rate.

When a model will grow repeatedly, insert new position slots before the oldest slot and shift existing slots up. Appending demotes the most trained slot on every grow, however slowly the model grows.

Pin loaded checkpoints to the convention they were trained under, so a change of growth default does not alter a trained model.

#### Limits

The no-payoff result comes from one seeded run at one grow, from four to eight tokens. Whether a less-settled seed would have absorbed the grow better is a conjecture the run does not test.

The effect of front insertion on the long-form repeat collapse over many grows is unmeasured. A model trained from scratch under the new convention has run for a few hundred rounds. Its generation shows cleanly space-separated word-shaped chunks with the individual words misspelled, and its raw numbers match the old approach at the same age, which is expected because the cost accrues over many grows, not the first.

The faster growth schedule's results are reported in words only.

#### Refuted by

A grown model seeded from fully trained weights that reaches a settled margin sooner than a less-trained seed under the same learning rate; or a model grown by front insertion that still shows the long-form repeat collapse after many grows.

Related: The Four-Token Ceiling https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/research/context-four/

### The Model Learns Back To Front

Page: https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/research/back-to-front/
Topics: growth, layers

Finding: In a holographic model grown from one layer to six, only the last layer's two passes carried information: reading every intermediate state against the vocabulary shows the earlier passes name a single token at confidence 0.9740 to 1.0000, and the four-layer and six-layer snapshots are identical to two decimal places over their last four read points.

#### Setup

The models grow while they train. They start as a single layer and gain layers as they go, each new layer inserted at the front and initialised to be an exact no-op so it cannot disturb what already works. One lineage went from one layer to six.

Every intermediate state in this architecture can be read against the vocabulary directly, because the table that turns a state into a prediction is the same table that turns a token into a state. In a conventional transformer an intermediate activation has no privileged interpretation; here it has one, and reading it costs nothing.

Two numbers are taken at every step of the computation. Confidence is how strongly the state names a single token. At 1.0000 nothing has been computed and the state is a copy of its input. Effective candidates is two to the power of the entropy of that reading: 1 means pinned to a single token, 3 means weighing three, and several hundred means the state has fallen off the vocabulary and resolves to nothing useful. Together they separate three kinds of state: a copy, a real computation and noise.

The six-layer snapshot has thirteen read points: the raw embedding, then the state after each of its twelve passes (two passes per layer). A snapshot of the four-layer model from earlier in the same run is compared against it.

#### Evidence: the work sits in the last layer

Six-layer snapshot, confidence and effective candidates at each read point: embedding 1.0000 and 1.00; layer 0 pass 0, 1.0000 and 1.00; layer 0 pass 1, 1.0000 and 1.00; layer 1 pass 0, 1.0000 and 1.00; layer 1 pass 1, 1.0000 and 1.00; layer 2 pass 0, 0.9992 and 1.00; layer 2 pass 1, 0.9999 and 1.00; layer 3 pass 0, 0.9952 and 1.02; layer 3 pass 1, 0.9916 and 1.03; layer 4 pass 0, 0.9740 and 1.11; layer 4 pass 1, 0.9622 and 1.20; layer 5 pass 0, 0.4785 and 11.94; final, 0.3124 and 27.14.

Four consecutive passes sit at 1.0000 to four decimal places. That is a copy, not an approximation of one. Two entire layers and most of a third contribute nothing measurable. The last layer's two passes take the state from naming one token to weighing 27, and everything before them is padding.

Six-layer snapshot, read at each of thirteen points

| Point | Confidence | Effective candidates |
|---|---|---|
| embedding | 1.0000 | 1.00 |
| layer 0, pass 0 | 1.0000 | 1.00 |
| layer 0, pass 1 | 1.0000 | 1.00 |
| layer 1, pass 0 | 1.0000 | 1.00 |
| layer 1, pass 1 | 1.0000 | 1.00 |
| layer 2, pass 0 | 0.9992 | 1.00 |
| layer 2, pass 1 | 0.9999 | 1.00 |
| layer 3, pass 0 | 0.9952 | 1.02 |
| layer 3, pass 1 | 0.9916 | 1.03 |
| layer 4, pass 0 | 0.9740 | 1.11 |
| layer 4, pass 1 | 0.9622 | 1.20 |
| layer 5, pass 0 | 0.4785 | 11.94 |
| final | 0.3124 | 27.14 |

#### Evidence: growing added padding

The last four read points of the four-layer and six-layer snapshots, as confidence and effective candidates. Fourth from last: 0.9774 and 1.11 against 0.9740 and 1.11. Third from last: 0.9592 and 1.22 against 0.9622 and 1.20. Second from last: 0.4771 and 12.35 against 0.4785 and 11.94. Final: 0.3135 and 27.03 against 0.3124 and 27.14. The two are identical to two decimal places across all four.

Going from four layers to six did not make the model deeper in any sense that mattered. It reproduced the same working window and prepended four passes that did nothing. The part computing stayed the same size, and what grew was the number of weight matrices taking gradient, competing, and perturbing a stream they were contributing nothing to.

Passes carrying real information: the six-layer model has 2 of 12, the four-layer model has 2 of 8, and a two-layer model has 4 of 4. The two-layer model uses every pass it has, and the six-layer model used a sixth of itself. By that measure the small model is the bigger one.

Last four read points, confidence / effective candidates

| Position from the end | Four-layer | Six-layer |
|---|---|---|
| fourth from last | 0.9774 / 1.11 | 0.9740 / 1.11 |
| third from last | 0.9592 / 1.22 | 0.9622 / 1.20 |
| second from last | 0.4771 / 12.35 | 0.4785 / 11.94 |
| final | 0.3135 / 27.03 | 0.3124 / 27.14 |

Passes that carry real information

| Model | Passes doing work | Total passes |
|---|---|---|
| six layers | 2 | 12 |
| four layers | 2 | 8 |
| two layers | 4 | 4 |

#### Evidence: the six-layer run diverged

Loss spiked into the thousands and recovered, repeatedly, for about 43,000 rounds. Then in a single step every trainable parameter became NaN: 764,288 values of 829,825. The 65,537 that survived include the frozen numeric identity band of 1024 tokens by 64 fixed dimensions, which survives because nothing writes to it.

Gradient clipping was switched on throughout and delivered the failure. Clipping computes the size of the gradient and scales it down if the size exceeds the limit. If any part of the gradient is NaN, the size is NaN, a NaN is not greater than anything, the test is false, and the gradient is applied at full strength. If the size overflows to infinity, the scale factor is the limit divided by infinity, which is zero, and an infinite gradient multiplied by zero is a new NaN that a skip-if-zero check does not catch.

Two guards close both paths. The step is refused when the gradient size is not a finite number, so a bad batch is dropped and counted instead of being fatal, and the learning-rate schedule does not respond to a loss spike by going to maximum.

The deeper cause was that half the model had never crystallised while more layers were being added.

#### Evidence: a front layer that carries candidates

A two-layer lineage, left alone, has a front layer unlike the front layers of the older models. Front layer, second pass: four-layer snapshot 1.0000 confidence and 1.00 candidates; six-layer snapshot 1.0000 and 1.00; two-layer model 0.8692 and 1.46. A confidence of 1.0000 is zero information, so the front layers of the two older models were absent in effect. The two-layer model's front layer carries a genuine candidate set, and it is better than the best early pass either older model had anywhere in its stack.

The value is 1.46 candidates, not twelve. It has not moved since about round 99,000, so what formed, formed early and has held since. The state is far from one where adding another layer would be justified.

This model is at 320,000 rounds with two layers and a parameter count of 369,664. It answers in complete sentences with correct punctuation and contractions, and loses the thread across more than about fifty characters. Its context reach did not move in three separate measurements.

Front layer, second pass

| Model | Confidence | Effective candidates |
|---|---|---|
| four-layer snapshot | 1.0000 | 1.00 |
| six-layer snapshot | 1.0000 | 1.00 |
| two-layer model | 0.8692 | 1.46 |

#### Evidence: two measurements that misled

Context reach measured with 25 sample windows showed the model still improving at the edge of the window, which implies more context would help. The identical measurement with 220 windows reverses it: the model saturates at roughly 16 tokens and everything past that carries nothing measurable. The 25-window result did not look noisy and was confidently wrong.

Front-layer progress tracked by how often its output names a different token from its input more than doubled over 223,000 rounds. On the confidence and candidates measure, which separates computation from copying, it had not moved. Both are true: the front layer increasingly picks a different single token, and a single token carries no alternatives forward whichever token it is. The rate of change in the named token counts motion, not work.

#### What this means for a small model

Read every intermediate state against the vocabulary before adding a layer. If a pass names one token at 1.0000, it is a copy and a further layer on top of it adds nothing.

Count the passes that carry real information, not the layers. A model with fewer layers all in use can out-compute a deeper one with most layers inert.

Let a layer finish before another starts. The rule is not a round count or schedule: the front layer's candidate count has to stop climbing, then the pair has to settle together, and only then does a new front layer go in at zero.

Check that gradient clipping tests for a finite gradient size. A clip that tests only whether the size exceeds the limit passes a NaN through at full strength and turns an infinity into a NaN.

Measure context reach with hundreds of windows, not tens, and judge a front layer by candidates carried, not by how often its output differs from its input.

#### Limits

One lineage, with snapshots at four, six and two layers. The reading says which passes carry information, not why the front layers failed to crystallise: whether patience is enough, or whether the training data has to change before a front layer forms, is untested. The two-layer front layer sits at 1.46 candidates and has been flat since about round 99,000.

#### Refuted by

A grown layer that, read the same way, shows more than one effective candidate at its first pass while the final layer is unchanged; or a four-layer and a six-layer snapshot from one run that differ in their last four read points.

### Smaller Than TinyStories

Page: https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/research/smaller-than-tinystories/
Topics: small models, evaluation

Finding: A holographic language model with a parameter count of 107,776 is about a tenth the size of the smallest published TinyStories reference model and spells 88.5% of its words correctly, but it does not write readable stories.

#### Setup

The yardstick is TinyStories . That paper trains very small language models on a synthetic corpus of simple children's stories to see how small a model can be while still producing text that reads as coherent English. Its published reference models come in five sizes: 1M, 3M, 8M, 28M and 33M parameters. This lineage asks how much a model can do at a size TinyStories did not try.

The checkpoint is weight-tied and runs entirely in the browser in the Prism tool at /tools/prism/, with nothing server-side. Its shape is d=96, 6 layers, 16 shifts, a context window of 192 tokens, a 256-token vocabulary, and 2 weight-tied passes over the same weights per forward step. The file is 862,244 bytes raw and about 471KB gzipped, which is what a browser downloads to load the tool.

Bits per character is the measure of the model's remaining uncertainty about the next character. It is not comparable to the bits per character the TinyStories paper reports, which uses a different tokenizer and a different measure. No benchmark comparison is made on it.

#### Evidence: size

The checkpoint has a parameter count of 107,776. Against the five TinyStories sizes, that is roughly a tenth the size of the smallest (1M parameters) and roughly a three-hundredth the size of the largest (33M parameters). On parameter count it is smaller than anything in that lineup, by a wide margin.

A second dimension is vocabulary granularity. The tokenizer has 256 entries and is a bigram vocabulary, not a word-level one. Mean token length across the vocabulary is 1.63 characters; 95 tokens are a single character, 160 are two characters, and no token is longer than two. Every word is built a couple of characters at a time, with no lookahead past the current token. The word Once is O, nc, e; upon is u, po, n; little is li, tt, le.

Measured across real prose, it takes an average of 2.84 tokens to produce one word. A word-level TinyStories-style model typically spends one token per word. A five-word phrase such as going to there with them is 5 correct decisions in a row at word granularity and 15 correct token decisions in a row here, three times as many, each made without sight of the next token. Spelling a word of five or more letters takes two or three sequential blind token decisions, each consistent with the ones before it.

Parameter count against the TinyStories reference sizes

| Model | Parameters |
|---|---|
| This checkpoint | 107,776 |
| TinyStories reference | 1M |
| TinyStories reference | 3M |
| TinyStories reference | 8M |
| TinyStories reference | 28M |
| TinyStories reference | 33M |

Vocabulary granularity

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| Vocabulary entries | 256 (bigram, not word-level) |
| Mean token length | 1.63 characters |
| Single-character tokens | 95 |
| Two-character tokens | 160 |
| Longest token | 2 characters |
| Tokens per word, real prose | 2.84 |
| Decisions for the five-word phrase going to there with them | 15 here against 5 at word granularity |

#### Evidence: an unedited sample

A sample from the checkpoint at a middling temperature, unedited: "One doging the saw the started to the started to the very. They w..."

This is not TinyStories-quality prose. No subject survives more than a couple of words, doging is not a word, and the text decays into a repeat loop (the started to the started to). The measured improvements below do not mean the model writes readable stories.

#### Evidence: spelling, loops and bits per character

Across a held-out sample, 88.5% of the words the model produces are spelled correctly. By word length: 94.1% for 3-letter words, 87.4% for 4-letter words, and 49.5% for words of 5 letters or more. Long words are the figure to watch, because short words can be right by luck or by memorising a small closed set. Long-word spelling rose from 16.6% to 49.5%, roughly a tripling.

Degenerate looping, where the model falls into a short repeating cycle and stays, fell sharply. 59.0% of vocabulary-seeded generations produce no repeating loop, up from about 40%.

Bits per character sat flat at 2.6 to 2.7 through several restructures of the architecture that moved it in neither direction, then dropped to about 2.3 at roughly round 190,000 of continuous training.

Share of words spelled correctly on a held-out sample

| Word length | Spelled correctly |
|---|---|
| all words | 88.5% |
| 3 letters | 94.1% |
| 4 letters | 87.4% |
| 5 letters or more | 49.5% (16.6% at the earlier measurement) |

Looping and bits per character

| Measure | Earlier | Current |
|---|---|---|
| Vocabulary-seeded generations with no repeating loop | about 40% | 59.0% |
| Bits per character | 2.6 to 2.7, flat | about 2.3 at roughly round 190,000 |

#### Evidence: the weights rotated, they did not grow

Six checkpoints spanning the stretch were compared on how the weights moved. In all 42 bank-and-layer combinations in the model the weights rotated and did not grow. Every combination moved 10 to 1,000 times more by rotation (a change in the direction a weight vector points) than by rescaling (a change in its size). Cosine similarity between old and new direction sits between 0.977 and 0.999, barely different in raw angle but consistently different in the same direction checkpoint after checkpoint.

Magnitudes changed by under 1.5% on every weight bank across the window, and each layer's share of the total work stayed essentially flat. The token embeddings and the readout geometry stayed fixed: the effective dimensionality of the embeddings held between 14.7 and 14.9, and the readout geometry correlated between 0.996 and 0.998 across checkpoints. The model did not relearn what tokens mean or how to read its internal state back into a prediction. It reorganised how it relates things between those two fixed points, which is restructuring and not accumulation.

The flat stretch of the loss curve was not a stall. Rotation rate during the plateau at 2.6 to 2.7 bits per character was 0.0198 per round, faster than the 0.0159 per round averaged over the whole window that includes the drop to 2.3. Stopping when the loss curve looked flat would have stopped training when the structure was moving fastest.

Weight motion across six checkpoints, 42 bank-and-layer combinations

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| Rotation against rescaling | 10 to 1,000 times more rotation, in all 42 combinations |
| Cosine similarity of old and new direction | 0.977 to 0.999 |
| Magnitude change on every weight bank | under 1.5% |
| Effective dimensionality of the embeddings | 14.7 to 14.9 |
| Readout geometry correlation across checkpoints | 0.996 to 0.998 |
| Rotation rate during the flat loss stretch | 0.0198 per round |
| Rotation rate averaged over the whole window | 0.0159 per round |

#### Evidence: measurements that went the wrong way

Long-form coherence got worse over the same window. The longest run of valid English the model sustains shrank across the checkpoints, and a corruption test (feeding a deliberately broken input and seeing how much the model relies on the good context around the break to recover) suggests it leans less on context than before. That test runs across only 60 windows, too coarse to call either a real regression or noise.

The corpus changed on the same day as some of the measurements. TinyStories data is 55% of the 3.77GB training corpus. The spelling gains predate the corpus change, so they are not an artefact of seeing more TinyStories-shaped text. A later acceleration of roughly six-fold in the rate of weight rotation sits entirely inside the window after the corpus change, and how much of it comes from the architecture and how much from the changed training mix cannot be separated.

#### What this means for a small model

A model under a million parameters can spell most of its words correctly on a held-out sample, while still failing at stringing words into sentences. Spelling and coherence are separate measurements and need separate reports.

Compare size with vocabulary granularity in view. A bigram vocabulary needs about three token decisions where a word-level vocabulary needs one, so a parameter count compares two models only at equal granularity.

Do not stop a run because the loss curve is flat. Measure weight rotation against rescaling, and read a flat loss with a fast rotation rate as reorganisation in progress.

Keep a corruption test at more than 60 windows if it will carry a claim about context use, and record corpus changes against the measurement dates so they can be separated from architecture effects.

#### Limits

The size claim is closed and holds on parameter count and on token granularity. Nothing here shows the model writes like a TinyStories model, and the sample above shows it does not. No quality comparison against the TinyStories models was made, and bits per character is not comparable to theirs. Long-form coherence moved in the wrong direction on a coarse test, and the corpus change confounds the weight-rotation acceleration.

The vocabulary is described as 256 entries but the single-character and two-character counts (95 and 160) sum to 255.

#### Refuted by

A checkpoint whose parameter count is not 107,776, or a TinyStories reference model smaller than 1M parameters; checkpoints from the same window showing magnitude change above 1.5% on a weight bank, or rescaling comparable to rotation; or a held-out spelling measurement on the checkpoint that gives a different rate.

References:
1. Eldan and Li, TinyStories, 2023, arXiv 2305.07759. https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.07759

### Nobody Read the Warning

Page: https://evaluatedapplications.github.io/research/nobody-read-the-warning/
Topics: essay

Finding: The effective number of independent judgements in a group falls as its members become correlated, to about one when they are fully coordinated, and the surviving accounts of collapse are consistent with that mechanism but were preserved as scripture, not read as analysis.

#### Setup

This is an argument from a statistical result and a set of historical cases. It is not a measurement. The statistical result is the design effect . The cases are the collapse of the eastern Mediterranean around 1177 BC, the Babel account in Genesis 11 , the long survival of Egypt and Imperial China, and the Talmudic rule on unanimous verdicts .

The design effect says that the worth of a group's answers is the number of members thinking independently, not the number of members. A thousand people who read the same paper, went to the same school and use the same three websites supply about eleven data points. Pushed to full correlation, a million perfectly coordinated minds have roughly the decision-making power of one.

#### Evidence: the pattern of collapse

Around 1177 BC the eastern Mediterranean fell over, not one kingdom but all of them more or less at once: Mycenae, the Hittite empire, the Levantine trade cities, and Egypt reduced to a shadow of itself. Writing systems vanished. Linear B stopped being written and could not be read for three thousand years. Trade networks that had run for centuries stopped, the palaces burned, and a period followed that historians call the Dark Age.

The people who came out the other side were overwhelmingly the ones who had never mattered: hill villages, herders, and populations too marginal for the palace economies to have integrated. The great houses died with their records, and the marginal populations inherited the ground and then wrote things down.

The pattern generalises: the most sophisticated, most connected and most efficiently organised system fails first, and what survives is whatever was too scattered, rural or unimportant to have been plugged in. In each case the survivors wrote an account of what happened.

#### Evidence: the Babel account

The text of Genesis 11 reads as a statement about capability and names its source precisely. Close to the direct quotation, the people is one, and they have all one language, and now nothing will be restrained from them. The cause given is unity: one people, one language, everybody pulling the same direction with no friction between them.

The response is specific. The tower is not destroyed and no one is killed. Their language is confused and they are scattered. That is the minimum intervention that reduces a population's capability without harming a person: break its ability to coordinate and spread it out.

An observer watched a unified civilisation become catastrophically capable and then come apart, and recorded that the unity was what made it dangerous and that afterwards it was scattered and speaking different languages. The account files this under pride, the vocabulary available, but the observation is preserved unedited and says that coupling was the cause.

#### Evidence: progress is correlation

Progress, mechanically, is shared standards, shared infrastructure, faster communication and everyone reading the same thing at the same time. Getting better at civilisation is the process of becoming more correlated, and the same thing that makes a society powerful reduces its effective size. The empire with the best roads is the empire whose provinces make the same mistake in the same week; the hill villages survive because nothing connected them.

Egypt lasted three thousand years and Imperial China was large, standardised and unified, and both survived. The reason is that until about a hundred and fifty years ago nobody could coordinate anything. An order from the capital took months to reach the frontier, arrived garbled, and was carried out by a governor who was in practice making it up. Ancient empires were centralised on paper and independent in practice, every province ran its own experiment and was wrong in its own local way, and that unplanned diversity kept the effective number of independent units above one. Distance was the immune system. Modern communication removed distance and with it the one thing that kept the effective number above one without cost.

#### Evidence: why the accounts were not read

The survivors wrote accurate accounts, because they were present. They were by definition peripheral to whatever failed, so they saw the event and could not see the mechanism, which is a statistical property of a system they were never inside. They recorded the event correctly and explained it as pride, wickedness or forgetting the old ways. The wrong explanation is the container the correct observation was shipped in.

A text about the end of the world written by the only people who lived through it is made sacred. Sacred texts are recited word for word, in unison, for centuries, with essentially no loss of the words and essentially no comprehension, because reciting something is the opposite of reading it. A congregation asked to say a passage reproduces it exactly. Asked what it means, it returns the explanation from the container and not the content. Veneration is both the best preservation method and the best concealment method, using one mechanism.

#### Evidence: the case that kept a procedure

In the Talmud, a capital case before the Sanhedrin needed a majority to convict, but a unanimous vote of all seventy-one judges meant the accused walked free. The strongest possible evidence is thrown out for being too strong. That is the design effect applied to a jury: seventy-one judges from one tradition, in one room, hearing one presentation, are already heavily correlated, and total unanimity signals that correlation has reached its ceiling. There are not seventy-one opinions but one opinion held seventy-one times, and a man is not hanged on one opinion. A result from 1965 appears in a law book from the second century and is usable as written.

A likely reason this one survived intact is its size. A court that convicted an innocent man is a disaster small enough to leave a procedure behind and not a scripture. Catastrophic collapses leave stories, and stories get sung.

#### What follows in practice

Unanimity among correlated members is a warning and not a confirmation, as it is in the Sanhedrin rule.

The prediction for a society routing a growing share of its thinking through a shrinking set of shared platforms, rankings and models is that individuals become sharper while the population's effective size falls, because mistakes once scattered and cancelling are made once at the source and delivered to everyone at the same time. The symptom is not stupidity. It is that disagreement stops carrying information: two people arguing used to triangulate something because they had been wrong in different ways from different places, and when their inputs share an upstream the disagreement is decorative.

The remedy that follows is to keep some people, methods and sources deliberately unplugged. They are not better; they are wrong differently, and that difference is the only thing that has caught an error the whole system was making together. Better tools alone do not supply it.

#### Limits

The statistics are standard and can be looked up: Leslie Kish, design effect, 1965. The history is also established. The link between the two is a hunch and not a finding. No effective size is measured for any ancient or modern society here, and the figure of about eleven independent data points from a thousand correlated people is an illustration and not a computed value.

Our own civilisation has not completed its trial, so no comparison against the finished cases can be made. The prediction above is recorded so that it can be checked.

Several historical statements carry no citation in this article: the 1177 BC collapse and its extent, Linear B going unread for three thousand years, the speed of communication before the last hundred and fifty years, and the Egyptian and Chinese durations.

#### Refuted by

Measurements showing that correlated groups keep an effective size close to their head count; collapses in societies whose members were weakly coupled; or evidence that disagreement between people sharing the same upstream sources is as informative as disagreement between people who do not. If the link between the statistics and the history is wrong, the cost is a closer reading of Genesis 11.

References:
1. Leslie Kish, design effect, 1965.
2. Genesis 11 (the tower of Babel).
3. The Talmudic rule on unanimous verdicts in capital cases before the Sanhedrin.
